subsystem: The Picker — hover targeting, box-model highlight overlay, HUD, keyboard DOM navigation, and the activation lifecycle (content.js core picker; background.js injection/command path; sidepanel.js key relay)
summary: A DevTools-style element inspector implemented entirely in page-space JavaScript: a Shadow-DOM overlay host draws four absolutely-positioned viewport-fixed rectangles reconstructing the CSS box model (margin/border/padding/content) from one getBoundingClientRect + one getComputedStyle, a floating HUD badge shows tag/id/class/dimensions plus a generated CSS selector, and a full capture-phase event blanket makes the page inert while the picker is live so a click selects instead of navigating. Keyboard arrows step the DOM tree (parent/child/prev-sibling/next-sibling), Esc cancels, Enter picks, D exports, S screenshots. The whole thing is gated by a version+liveness injection guard that solves the "orphaned content script after extension reload" problem. Everything here is pure DOM/CSS/Canvas — it is the single most portable subsystem in the extension, and it is exactly what deliverable (c) needs and what gives deliverable (d) its inspect mode.

mechanisms.name: Injection guard: PICKER_VERSION + isAlive() liveness probe
mechanisms.problem: A naive `if (window.__ALREADY_INJECTED__) return;` guard permanently bricks the picker on any page that was open across an extension reload/update. After a reload Chrome does NOT kill the already-running content script's JavaScript — the closures, timers and event listeners keep executing — but its *extension context* is destroyed. The script becomes a zombie: it still owns the global marker, so it blocks fresh injection, yet every chrome.* call it makes throws "Extension context invalidated". The page is un-pickable until the user hits F5.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 1–9 (guard) and 7500–7517 (marker registration); background.js lines 48–66 (ensureContentScript / CONTENT_VERSION)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker and (d) mini-browser — both inject a long-lived agent into a page they do not own
mechanisms.chrome_apis_used: chrome.runtime.id (as a liveness oracle), chrome.tabs.sendMessage, chrome.scripting.executeScript
mechanisms.electron_equivalent:
Two distinct Electron analogues, both real:

(1) **Injected-agent orphaning.** `webContents.executeJavaScript()` is our executeScript. The exact same zombie exists: our injected picker agent survives a main-process hot-restart or a rebuild of the host app while the guest page keeps running. Replace `chrome.runtime.id` with a probe of the IPC bridge — the agent holds a MessagePort or an `ipcRenderer`-backed callback given to it at injection time, and `isAlive()` returns whether that channel still responds (a `port.postMessage`/`await`-with-timeout ping, or simply comparing a `generation` integer passed in at injection against the current one held in main). Concretely: main keeps `let generation = Date.now()`, bumps it on every host restart, and injects `window.__EXELMJ_PICKER__ = { version: N, gen: <generation>, isAlive: () => gen === CURRENT }` where CURRENT is re-read via a preload-exposed getter.

(2) **Preload + Vite HMR orphaning — the sharper one.** Preload scripts re-evaluate on EVERY navigation and on `webContents.reload()`, so the guard must be per-document, not per-process. And in the EXELMJ dev loop, Vite HMR re-imports the picker module while the previous module instance's capture-phase listeners are still attached to `document` — identical zombie, no chrome.* involved. Fix: `import.meta.hot?.dispose(() => picker.destroy())` plus the same version marker on `window`.

**Bug to fix during the port:** the extension never calls `prev.dispose()` on the orphan it displaces. If the orphan had the picker active, its capture-phase `mousemove`/`click`/`keydown`/`contextmenu` listeners keep swallowing events forever and the page stays half-frozen with two overlays fighting. In the port, the marker must expose `dispose()` and the new instance must call it before taking over.
mechanisms.port_notes: Keep the version+liveness two-factor design verbatim; swap only the oracle. Add the missing `dispose()` handshake. In Electron you additionally get an option the extension did not have: inject via `webContents.debugger` CDP `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument`, which auto-reinjects on every navigation and returns an identifier you can `removeScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` — that removes the whole class of "is my script still there" questions for deliverable (d).

mechanisms.name: Shadow-DOM overlay host (why shadow, why 2147483640)
mechanisms.problem: An inspector overlay drawn into a page it does not own faces three collisions: (a) the page's CSS matching and restyling the overlay's elements (`div { border: … }`, resets, `* { transition }`), (b) the overlay's own <style> leaking into and repainting the page, and (c) the page's own z-index stack (modals, cookie banners, sticky headers) painting over the highlight.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 13–15 (Z constant), 78–100 (host creation), 100–190 (shadow stylesheet), 190–210 (layer assembly + append)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker, (d) mini-browser inspect mode, and reusable for (a) the builder's own canvas selection chrome
mechanisms.electron_equivalent:
Identical code, injected via `webContents.executeJavaScript` into the <webview>/WebContentsView guest, or shipped in the guest's **preload** (strictly better than the extension's `document_idle` content script — preload runs before any page script, in an isolated world by default, with `contextIsolation` giving the same JS-world separation Chrome's isolated world gave). No chrome.* replacement needed.

Electron also offers a completely different implementation for the same visual: CDP `Overlay.highlightNode` / `Overlay.setInspectMode` via `webContents.debugger`, which draws the identical four-colour box model in the COMPOSITOR, outside the page DOM — no host div, no z-index war, no possibility of the page detecting or removing the overlay, and it works across iframes natively. Recommendation: use the DOM overlay when you need custom chrome (our HUD, our Arabic hint bar, our selection colours matching EXELMJ's design tokens), and use `Overlay.setInspectMode` as the zero-cost fallback for the mini-browser's plain "inspect" affordance.
mechanisms.port_notes: Two adjustments for EXELMJ: (1) the shadow stylesheet is a template string of hard-coded hex colours — replace with EXELMJ design tokens and mirror the light/dark palette, since the guest page's colour scheme is unknown; (2) the hint bar is `position: fixed; top: 12px; left: 50%` with LTR-authored content but Arabic text — in an RTL-first app set `direction: rtl` on `:host` and let the kbd chips flow naturally rather than the current hand-ordered `<kbd>↑</kbd><kbd>↓</kbd>` sequence.

mechanisms.name: Four-layer box-model visualisation from one rect + one computed style
mechanisms.problem: Show the developer where the element's margin, border, padding and content actually are — the thing DevTools' inspector draws — without any layout API that reports them directly. getBoundingClientRect returns only the BORDER box; the other three must be derived.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 220–267 (place / highlight / clearHighlight); layer CSS at lines 103–110
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker; the same four-rect math is directly reusable in (b) the vector designer for showing an artboard object's bounds/padding, and in (a) the builder for the drop-target indicator
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed. Runs unchanged in a preload/injected script. If you instead go the CDP route, `DOM.getBoxModel` returns `{content, padding, border, margin}` as four quad arrays (8 numbers each, already including transforms) computed by the renderer itself — more accurate than the arithmetic above for rotated/skewed elements, where getBoundingClientRect gives the axis-aligned bounding box and the arithmetic silently produces wrong padding rects.
mechanisms.port_notes: Two real weaknesses to fix rather than copy: (1) **transformed elements** — under `rotate()` or `skew()`, getBoundingClientRect returns the axis-aligned hull, so subtracting border/padding produces rectangles that do not correspond to anything. CDP `DOM.getBoxModel` quads solve this properly and should be used when the debugger is attached. (2) **`writing-mode` / logical properties** — the code reads physical `marginTop` etc., which is correct (getComputedStyle resolves logical to physical), so RTL is fine here; but verify against an Arabic RTL page since EXELMJ is RTL-first.

mechanisms.name: Hover tracking via capture-phase mousemove + composedPath()[0]
mechanisms.problem: Track whatever the cursor is over, including nodes inside web components, and do it without the page's own handlers interfering.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 801–812 (onMouseMove), 881–900 (listener registration in activate)
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed for the listener itself. But the environment changes the *targeting* story in our favour: with `webContents.debugger` attached, CDP `DOM.getDocument({ pierce: true })` and `DOM.getNodeForLocation({ x, y, includeUserAgentShadowDOM })` see through CLOSED shadow roots, which composedPath cannot. The extension had `chrome.dom.openOrClosedShadowRoot` for this (used in the extraction path, content.js 1212–1217) and there is NO plain-JS Electron equivalent — CDP is the replacement, and it is strictly more capable.
mechanisms.port_notes: Port the capture-phase + composedPath structure verbatim. Then add: (a) rAF coalescing — store the latest event, run `highlight()` once per animation frame; (b) short-circuit when `t === lastTarget` to skip the rect/style reads entirely on intra-element moves (this is the single biggest perf win and it is trivially safe); (c) for closed shadow roots and cross-origin frames, fall back to CDP `DOM.getNodeForLocation`.

mechanisms.name: How the overlay avoids picking itself (three independent defences)
mechanisms.problem: An overlay drawn on top of the page will, by default, be what the cursor is over — so the picker would highlight its own highlight rectangle, forever.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
Three layers of defence, deliberately redundant:

1. **`pointer-events: none` everywhere.** The host carries it inline, and the shadow stylesheet repeats it on `.layer`, `.hud`, `.hint`, `.toast`. Hit-testing passes straight through, so `composedPath()[0]` and `document.elementFromPoint` return the page element BENEATH the overlay. This alone is sufficient in normal operation.
2. **Explicit identity guard in both handlers.** `if (t === ui.root || ui.root?.contains(t)) return;` in `onMouseMove`, and in `onClick` the target selection is `const chosen = t && t !== ui.root && !ui.root?.contains(t) ? t : target;` — i.e. if the click somehow landed on the overlay, fall back to the last known good target rather than picking the overlay. Note `Node.contains()` does NOT cross shadow boundaries, so this guard only catches the host itself; the shadow-internal layers are covered by defence (1) instead. That asymmetry is fine but worth knowing.
3. **Exclusion from every tree walk and export.** The deep DOM walker skips it (`if (ui.root && (n === ui.root || ui.root.contains(n))) continue;`, content.js ~1224), keyboard navigation skips it when descending (`firstElementChildInViewport` does `if (child === ui.root) continue;`), and the page-clone exporter strips it by ID (`root.querySelectorAll("#__ai-picker-host, #__ai-picker-ruler").forEach(n => n.remove())`, content.js ~2047). The stable `__ai-picker-` ID prefix exists precisely so unrelated subsystems can excise the overlay by selector without importing a reference to it.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 83–96 (host pointer-events), 100–190 (per-class pointer-events in shadow CSS), 805–806 and 815 (handler guards), 1224 (deepAll skip), 795 (nav skip), 2047 (clone strip)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker, (d) mini-browser — and (a) builder, where the same problem appears as "the drop indicator must not be a drop target"
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed. If using CDP `Overlay.highlightNode` instead, the problem disappears entirely — the compositor overlay is not in the DOM and cannot be hit-tested or serialised.
mechanisms.port_notes: Keep all three. In EXELMJ, extend defence (3) to the code-emitting path of deliverable (a): any DOM→code serialiser must strip `[id^="__exelmj-"]` nodes, or generated projects will ship with picker chrome baked in. Make the prefix a single exported constant so the strip-selector and the create-selector can never drift apart.

mechanisms.name: HUD badge: content, generated selector, and flip/clamp positioning
mechanisms.problem: Show what is under the cursor — tag, id, classes, pixel dimensions, and a copy-ready CSS selector — in a floating label that never falls off screen and never covers the element it describes.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 269–306 (updateHUD), 310–313 (span/doc helpers), 110–124 (HUD CSS)
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed.
mechanisms.port_notes: Three fixes worth making in the port: (1) **no vertical clamp on the flipped case** — if the element's bottom is below the fold, the HUD is placed off-screen; add `top = Math.min(top, innerHeight - hudRect.height - 4)`. (2) **forced synchronous layout every mousemove** — `ui.hud.getBoundingClientRect()` after writing innerHTML triggers a second forced reflow per mouse event, on top of the one in `highlight()`; cache the HUD height (it only changes when the second line wraps, which `nowrap` prevents) and skip the measure. (3) **RTL** — `left: rect.left` left-aligns; in an Arabic RTL context the HUD should right-align with the element (`left = rect.right - hudWidth`) and the class/dim order should mirror. Also consider making `.sel` the primary line for EXELMJ, since deliverable (a) consumes selectors.

mechanisms.name: Selector generation (the string shown in the HUD and copied on pick)
mechanisms.problem: Produce a CSS selector that (a) uniquely identifies the element right now, (b) is as stable as possible against re-renders, and (c) is readable by a human and by an LLM. This is what the whole extension exists to hand to an AI.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
A strict priority cascade, each candidate verified for uniqueness against the live document before being accepted (`isUnique = s => document.querySelectorAll(s).length === 1`, wrapped in try/catch so a malformed selector is simply rejected rather than throwing):

1. **`#id`** — but only if `/^[a-zA-Z_][\w-]*$/` (framework-generated IDs like `:r7:` from React 18's useId, or `123-abc`, are rejected — they are neither valid identifiers nor stable), and only if unique (duplicate IDs are common in the wild). Escaped with `CSS.escape`.
2. **Test-automation attributes**, in order: `data-testid`, `data-test`, `data-cy`, `data-qa`, `data-test-id`, `data-automation-id` → `[data-testid="value"]`. Deliberately ranked above classes because these are the only attributes a team promises not to change.
3. **`tag[name="…"]`** for form controls.
4. **Semantic class combinations** — `tag.a`, then `tag.a.b`, then `tag.a.b.c`, stopping at the first unique one. Classes are pre-filtered by `semanticClasses()`, which strips utility-CSS noise with four rules: variant prefixes (`/^(sm|md|lg|xl|2xl|hover|focus|active|group|peer|dark|first|last|odd|even|disabled|aria|data|motion|print|rtl|ltr):/`), the utility shape `/^-?[a-z]{1,3}-[\dpxremvwh.\/-]+$/` (catches `p-4`, `mt-2`, `w-1/2`, `gap-x-4`), a literal blocklist of bare Tailwind words (`flex grid block inline hidden relative absolute fixed sticky static container truncate rounded shadow border uppercase … antialiased`), and a prefix blocklist (`/^(bg|text|from|via|to|ring|fill|stroke|w|h|min|max|top|left|right|bottom|inset|z|order|col|row|gap|space)-/`). Also drops anything failing `validIdent` or longer than 40 chars (CSS-modules hashes).
5. **`tag[aria-label="…"]`**.
6. **Structural fallback** — `structuralSelector()` walks UP from the element to `<html>`, unshifting one segment per level, and joins with ` > `. Each segment is the bare tag if it is the only child of its tagName (`Array.from(parent.children).filter(c => c.tagName === cur.tagName).length === 1`), otherwise `tag:nth-of-type(k)`. Crucially, the walk **terminates early** the moment it reaches an ancestor with a valid unique ID — it unshifts `#thatId` and returns immediately, so the selector is anchored rather than being a 15-level chain from `<html>`.

Attribute values are escaped for the quoted context by `cssAttr = v => v.replace(/\\/g, "\\\\").replace(/"/g, '\\"')`.

A parallel `buildXPath()` (content.js 437–453) emits `//*[@id="x"]` when possible, else a full `/html[1]/body[1]/div[3]/…` positional path counting same-tagName previous siblings.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 338–453 (isUnique, validIdent, semanticClasses, buildSelector, cssAttr, structuralSelector, buildXPath)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker primarily; (a) builder consumes these selectors to bind generated code back to the picked element; (e) MCP exposes them as the addressing scheme Claude uses to name elements
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed.
mechanisms.port_notes: Note the cascade is unbounded in depth — `structuralSelector` has NO level cap; on a deeply-nested React app with no IDs it can emit a 20-segment chain. Cap it (e.g. 6 levels, then prefix with the nearest identifiable ancestor) for readability and token cost, which matters for (e). Also: `isUnique` queries `document`, so it is blind to shadow roots — a selector for a node inside a shadow root will report zero matches and always fall through to the structural path, which then produces a selector that does not resolve from the document either. For the port, return a *scoped* selector object `{ hostPath: string[], selector: string }` where hostPath is the chain of shadow hosts, rather than a single string. Finally, the utility-class filter is a Tailwind-era heuristic with a maintenance cost — consider inverting it: prefer classes that appear FEW times in the document (compute `document.getElementsByClassName(c).length` and rank ascending), which is self-tuning and needs no blocklist.

mechanisms.name: Keyboard DOM-tree navigation (parent / child / sibling stepping)
mechanisms.problem: Hovering cannot reach an element that is fully covered by a child, or a wrapper that has no bare pixels of its own — which is most layout containers. Arrow keys let you climb out of the leaf you landed on.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 771–799 (navigate, firstElementChildInViewport); key dispatch at 826–878; NAV_KEY relay branch at 7355–7378
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker; (a) builder — the same up/down/left/right stepping is the natural keyboard model for selecting nodes in the builder's own tree
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed.
mechanisms.port_notes: Fix the shadow dead-end by using `target.parentElement ?? target.getRootNode()?.host ?? null` for UP, and by descending into `target.shadowRoot?.firstElementChild` for DOWN when the element has an open shadow root — that turns arrow navigation into a true composed-tree walk, which the extension never achieved. Rename `firstElementChildInViewport` to what it does. Consider adding Home/End (first/last sibling) and a visible breadcrumb of the ancestor chain, which the extension lacks entirely.

mechanisms.name: Event-blanket: making the page inert while picking
mechanisms.problem: While the picker is live, a click must SELECT, not navigate/submit/open-a-menu. Every interaction the page would normally react to has to be intercepted before the page sees it, and cleanly restored afterwards.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
Every listener is registered with `{ capture: true }` on `document` (or `window` for scroll/resize), so the picker runs first on the way down and can kill the event before it reaches any page handler. Nine event types are blanket-swallowed by a single three-call function:

```js
function swallow(e) {
  e.preventDefault();          // stop the default action (navigation, submit, menu)
  e.stopPropagation();         // stop it reaching other elements
  e.stopImmediatePropagation();// stop OTHER listeners on the SAME element
}
```
The third call is the one people forget: a page with three click handlers bound to the same node would still fire the other two after `stopPropagation()` alone.

Bound in `activate()`:
- `mousemove` → `onMouseMove` (tracks, does not swallow — swallowing mousemove would break the page's own scroll/hover in ways that alter what you are inspecting)
- `click` → `onClick` (swallows, then picks)
- `auxclick`, `mousedown`, `mouseup`, `dblclick`, `contextmenu`, `submit` → `swallow`
- `keydown` → `onKeyDown` (selective: swallows only Escape/Enter/Arrows/D/S; every other key passes through to the page)
- `window scroll` and `window resize` with capture → `onScrollOrResize`

`onClick` re-derives the target rather than trusting the stale hover state, with an overlay fallback:
```js
const t = (e.composedPath && e.composedPath()[0]) || e.target;
const chosen = t && t !== ui.root && !ui.root?.contains(t) ? t : target;
pick(chosen);
```

`deactivate()` removes all eleven with the identical `opts` object — passing the same `{capture:true}` reference is required for removeEventListener to match, and the code shares one module-level `const opts = { capture: true }` precisely so a fresh object literal can never cause a silent leak.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 813–824 (onClick, swallow), 880–905 (activate registration), 907–940 (deactivate removal), 880 (shared opts const)
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed for the listener code. But Electron adds a much stronger option the extension could not use: with the CDP debugger attached, `Input.setIgnoreInputEvents(true)` or `Emulation.setScriptExecutionDisabled` freezes the guest entirely at the browser level, and `Overlay.setInspectMode({mode:'searchForNode'})` puts the *browser* in pick mode with `Overlay.inspectNodeRequested` events coming back — the page never receives the events at all, so no swallow list can be incomplete.
mechanisms.port_notes: **The swallow list has a real hole: Pointer Events are not covered.** `pointerdown`, `pointerup`, `pointermove`, `pointercancel`, `gotpointercapture` all pass straight through, and modern drag/gesture libraries (dnd-kit, interact.js, Framer Motion's drag, every canvas app) listen on pointer events exclusively. Picking inside such a page will start a drag. Add `pointerdown`, `pointerup`, `pointercancel`, plus `touchstart`/`touchend` for the tablet/mobile modes of deliverable (d), plus `wheel` is deliberately left alone (you want to scroll while picking) but `dragstart` should be swallowed. Also add `focusin` swallow so the page cannot steal focus mid-pick.

mechanisms.name: Scroll/resize re-anchoring via capture-phase scroll on window
mechanisms.problem: The highlight is drawn in viewport coordinates. Any scroll — including a scroll inside a nested overflow container, not just the page — invalidates all four rectangles instantly.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
Two lines, one of which encodes a non-obvious DOM fact:

```js
window.addEventListener("scroll", onScrollOrResize, true);   // ← capture:true is load-bearing
window.addEventListener("resize", onScrollOrResize, true);

function onScrollOrResize() { if (target) highlight(target); }
```

**`scroll` events do not bubble.** A scroll inside `<div style="overflow:auto">` fires on that div and stops — a listener on `window` in the bubble phase never hears it, and the highlight would drift off the element the moment the user scrolls a sidebar, a modal body, or a virtualised list. But scroll events DO capture: registering on `window` with `capture: true` intercepts the scroll of ANY element in the document on the way down. That single boolean is what makes the highlight track inside nested scrollers.

`highlight()` is idempotent and cheap — it just re-reads `getBoundingClientRect()` and rewrites the four layers' `top/left/width/height` — so re-anchoring needs no special-casing. And because the layers carry the 50ms CSS transition, fast scrolling produces a smooth trailing motion rather than a jitter.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 876–878 (onScrollOrResize), 903–904 (registration), 938–939 (removal)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker, (d) mini-browser — and in (d) the viewport-size switcher (desktop/tablet/mobile) fires exactly this resize path
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed for the listener. In (d), the desktop/tablet/mobile icon switch should ALSO be wired to this: whether you implement the switch by resizing the WebContentsView bounds or by CDP `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride` (the better choice — it gives real DPR, touch emulation and a mobile UA), the guest fires `resize` and the highlight re-anchors for free.
mechanisms.port_notes: Three gaps to close in the port, all of which the extension has: (1) **no rAF coalescing** — a fast scroll fires this dozens of times per frame, each forcing a layout; wrap in a `requestAnimationFrame` guard. (2) **Nothing re-anchors on layout change with no scroll/resize** — a CSS animation, a font load, a lazy image landing, or a React re-render moves the element and the highlight goes stale with no event to catch it. Add a `ResizeObserver` on the target plus a low-frequency rAF re-check while active. (3) **No detach detection** — if the target is removed from the DOM, `getBoundingClientRect()` returns all zeros and a 0×0 highlight is painted at the origin instead of clearing; add `if (!target.isConnected) { clearHighlight(); target = null; return; }`.

mechanisms.name: Cursor override by injected light-DOM stylesheet
mechanisms.problem: Signal "you are in pick mode" globally, overriding every `cursor: pointer` / `cursor: text` / `cursor: grab` the page sets, and remove it perfectly on exit.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
One `<style>` element with one rule, appended to `document.documentElement` (NOT to the shadow root, and NOT to `<body>`):

```js
ui.cursorStyle = document.createElement("style");
ui.cursorStyle.id = "__ai-picker-cursor";
ui.cursorStyle.textContent = "*, *::before, *::after { cursor: crosshair !important; }";
document.documentElement.appendChild(ui.cursorStyle);
```
Removal is `ui.cursorStyle.remove(); ui.cursorStyle = null;` — a single node, no state to unwind, no per-element style to restore.

Three decisions:
- **Light DOM, not shadow** — a stylesheet inside the shadow root cannot style the page. This is the one piece of picker CSS that must leak.
- **`documentElement`, not `body`** — `<body>` may not exist yet at injection time on some pages, and appending to `<html>` also covers the case where the page replaces `document.body` wholesale.
- **`::before` and `::after` included** — pseudo-elements can carry their own cursor and would otherwise show the page's cursor over icon-font glyphs and decorative overlays.
- **`!important`** — required to beat page author rules; even so it loses to inline `style="cursor:…"` with `!important`, which is vanishingly rare.

The same function is reused by the ruler tool (`startRuler` calls `injectCursor()`), and `stopRuler` calls `removeCursor()` — hence the tools being made mutually exclusive (`if (active) deactivate()` at the top of `startRuler`), since a single nullable `ui.cursorStyle` cannot be owned by two tools.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 941–954 (injectCursor / removeCursor); reused at 2454 and 2471 by the ruler
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: `webContents.insertCSS(css, { cssOrigin: 'user' })` — and this is a genuine upgrade, not just a translation. It returns a key: `const k = await wc.insertCSS(css, {cssOrigin:'user'}); … await wc.removeInsertedCSS(k);`. Two concrete advantages over appending a style node: (1) **user-origin stylesheets apply inside shadow trees**, whereas an author-origin `*` selector does not match elements in shadow roots at all — so the extension's crosshair silently fails over every web component on the page, and `insertCSS` with `cssOrigin:'user'` fixes it; (2) user-origin declarations with `!important` beat author `!important`, so even the pathological inline case is covered; and Electron re-applies inserted CSS across navigations within the same webContents, so the crosshair survives the guest navigating.
mechanisms.port_notes: Use `insertCSS`/`removeInsertedCSS` rather than porting the style-node approach. Keep the pseudo-element selectors. Since EXELMJ owns both tools, keep the mutual-exclusion rule but replace the shared nullable with a small ref-counted "cursor owner" so a future third tool does not silently clobber it.

mechanisms.name: Toast notifications with retrigger-safe enter transition
mechanisms.problem: Confirm the pick (and report clipboard failure) without a dialog, without blocking, and without the animation failing to replay when two toasts fire in quick succession.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 314–336 (showToast), 202–228 (toast CSS)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker; the pattern generalises to all of EXELMJ Studio
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed.
mechanisms.port_notes: EXELMJ is RTL-first, so `right: 24px` should become `inset-inline-end: 24px` (or `left: 24px` under `direction: rtl`), and the icon/text order flips naturally with `direction: rtl` on the toast. The `.error` variant is the only variant — add `warning`/`info`. Replace the 3000ms hard-coded dismissal with a duration argument, since a selector string can be long enough to need longer than 3s to read. Also: this toast lives inside the guest page's overlay; for EXELMJ, most confirmations should surface in the HOST app's chrome (the Studio panel) instead, with the in-page toast reserved for things that only make sense in page context.

mechanisms.name: Activation / deactivation lifecycle, autoDeactivate, and the Alt+Shift+P command path
mechanisms.problem: Turn the picker on and off from three different places (a toolbar-driven side panel button, a global keyboard shortcut, and the page itself pressing Escape), keep all three views of the state in sync, and inject the machinery only when it is actually needed.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
**activate()** (idempotent via `if (active) return`):
1. `buildUI()` — lazy; the shadow host is created on first activation only.
2. `injectCursor()` — the crosshair stylesheet.
3. `ui.hint.style.display = "block"` — the Arabic hint bar (a pill at `top:12px; left:50%; translateX(-50%)`, `backdrop-filter: blur(4px)`, listing: click to copy · ↑↓←→ to navigate · D for an HTML file · S for a screenshot · Esc to cancel) with `<kbd>` chips.
4. **`try { window.focus(); } catch {}`** — the non-obvious one. When the user activates the picker from the side panel button, the SIDE PANEL holds keyboard focus, so arrow keys and Escape would go to the panel and the page's `keydown` listener would never fire. `window.focus()` pulls focus back to the page.
5. Registers the eleven capture-phase listeners.

**deactivate()** mirrors it exactly: clears `target`, `removeCursor()`, `clearHighlight()`, hides the hint, removes all eleven listeners with the same shared `opts` object, and posts `{ type: "PICKER_DEACTIVATED" }` so the service worker can flip the toolbar icon back to idle and the side panel can un-highlight its button. **It deliberately does NOT call `destroyUI()`** — the shadow host stays attached with all layers at `display:none`, so re-activation is a handful of style writes with zero allocation. (`destroyUI()` is defined at line 215 and is never called from anywhere — dead code.)

**autoDeactivate** (default `true`, a chrome.storage.sync setting): after a successful `pick()`, the picker turns itself off — one shot, one element, back to normal browsing. With it `false`, the picked element stays highlighted and `target` stays set, so you can keep arrow-navigating from where you picked.

**The three activation paths:**
- *Global shortcut*: manifest `commands.toggle-picker` with `suggested_key` Alt+Shift+P → `chrome.commands.onCommand` in the service worker → `togglePicker()` → `getActiveTab()` → `isInjectableUrl(tab.url)` check against a blocklist (`chrome://`, `chrome-extension://`, `edge://`, `about:`, the Web Store origins, `view-source:` — pages where content scripts are forbidden) → `ensureContentScript(tabId)` (the PING/version dance) → `chrome.tabs.sendMessage({type:"TOGGLE_PICKER", active: next})` → updates `pickerState: Map<tabId, boolean>` and swaps the toolbar icon to the "active" variant.
- *Side panel button*: `PANEL_TOGGLE_PICKER` → same `togglePicker()`.
- *Page-side Escape*: `onKeyDown` → `deactivate()` → `PICKER_DEACTIVATED` back up.

**Key-relay fallback**: because the side panel can re-take focus at any time, sidepanel.js registers its own capture-phase `keydown` listener over a whitelist `{ArrowUp, ArrowDown, ArrowLeft, ArrowRight, Enter, Escape, d, D, s, S}` and forwards each as `{type:"NAV_KEY", key}` to the content script, which re-dispatches it through the same navigate/pick/export branches. Two independent input paths converge on one handler body.

**State reconciliation**: the service worker's `pickerState` map is authoritative-ish but it re-verifies by asking the page directly on `PANEL_GET_STATE` (`chrome.tabs.sendMessage(tabId, {type:"GET_PICKER_STATE"})` returns `{active, rulerActive}`), and it invalidates aggressively — `chrome.tabs.onRemoved` deletes the entry, and `chrome.tabs.onUpdated` with `status === "loading"` deletes it and resets the icon, because a navigation destroys the content script and with it the picker.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 880–940 (activate/deactivate), 742–769 (pick + autoDeactivate), 826–878 (onKeyDown), 195–199 (hint bar content), 7245–7256 + 7355–7378 (TOGGLE_PICKER / GET_PICKER_STATE / NAV_KEY branches); background.js 19–33 (BLOCKED_PREFIXES/isInjectableUrl), 84–109 (togglePicker + onCommand), 415–430 (PANEL_TOGGLE_PICKER / PANEL_GET_STATE), 487–509 (PICKER_DEACTIVATED + cleanup); sidepanel.js 211–279 (renderPickerState, NAV_KEY relay, refreshState)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker end-to-end; (d) mini-browser owns the equivalent per-view state; (e) MCP needs exactly this activate/pick/deactivate surface as its tool boundary
mechanisms.electron_equivalent:
Every piece maps cleanly and most get simpler:
- **chrome.commands / Alt+Shift+P** → `globalShortcut.register('Alt+Shift+P', …)` for a true global hotkey, or better `Menu`/`MenuItem` accelerators (window-scoped, does not steal the shortcut system-wide) or `before-input-event` on the host webContents.
- **Side panel** → an ordinary DOM panel in the EXELMJ renderer. The entire `chrome.runtime.sendMessage` panel↔worker hop disappears — the panel and the picker controller are in the same process.
- **Service worker** → the Electron main process, which is not ephemeral: `pickerState` can be a plain `Map<viewId, boolean>` with no persistence concerns (MV3 service workers die after 30s idle; the extension's Map silently resets, which is part of why it re-verifies with GET_PICKER_STATE).
- **chrome.tabs.sendMessage** → `webContentsView.webContents.send(channel, payload)` + `ipcMain.handle` for the return path, or a MessageChannelMain port pair for a direct renderer↔guest channel.
- **chrome.scripting.executeScript** → `webContents.executeJavaScript`, or preferably a **preload** on the guest WebContentsView (`webPreferences.preload`), which is a strictly better `document_start` MAIN-world hook than the extension had.
- **isInjectableUrl / BLOCKED_PREFIXES** → still needed, with a different blocklist: block `devtools://`, `chrome://`, `file://` (unless the user opted in), and `about:blank` in deliverable (d); allow the `app://`/`file://` origin serving our own generated projects.
- **chrome.action.setIcon** → the Studio toolbar button's own CSS class.
- **chrome.storage.sync** → EXELMJ's existing settings store (electron-store / a JSON file), synchronous and typed.
- **`window.focus()`** → `webContentsView.webContents.focus()` from main, which is more reliable than the in-page call.
- **`tabs.onUpdated status===loading` invalidation** → `webContents.on('did-start-navigation')` / `'did-finish-load'`.
mechanisms.port_notes: Structural improvements available in the port: (1) with a preload, the picker code is present before the first paint, so there is no PING/inject dance in the hot path — activation is one IPC message. (2) The NAV_KEY relay exists ONLY because the extension had two focus-competing surfaces in separate processes; in Electron, keep it anyway — the Studio panel and the guest webview are still separate focus contexts — but implement it as `before-input-event` on the host, which sees keys without needing the guest to have focus at all, removing the `window.focus()` hack entirely. (3) Make `autoDeactivate` a per-invocation argument rather than a global setting, because (e) MCP will want one-shot picks while a human wants a sticky mode. (4) Add the missing `destroy()` (the extension's `destroyUI()` is dead code) and call it on guest navigation.

mechanisms.name: Iframe handling — what the picker actually does (and does not) do
mechanisms.problem: Pages embed content in iframes; an inspector that stops at the <iframe> boundary is useless on any page with an embedded editor, video player, ad, or payment widget.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 1209–1238 (shadowRootOf, deepAll); manifest.json content_scripts (no all_frames); background.js line 60 (executeScript with no allFrames)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker — required for real pages; (d) mini-browser — our own generated projects will use iframes for previews
mechanisms.electron_equivalent:
Three converging options, all better than what the extension had:
1. **Per-frame injection**: `webContents.mainFrame.framesInSubtree` gives every `WebFrameMain`, each with its own `.executeJavaScript()`. Inject the picker agent into every frame, have each frame report hits with its own viewport coordinates, and translate to host coordinates by walking the frame's `<iframe>` element rects up the chain. Works for cross-origin frames too, which no content-script approach can do without `all_frames` + host permissions.
2. **CDP, the clean route**: `webContents.debugger.attach('1.3')` then `DOM.getDocument({ depth: -1, pierce: true })` — `pierce: true` descends into BOTH iframes (including cross-origin, since CDP operates below the origin boundary) and **closed shadow roots**, which is the direct replacement for `chrome.dom.openOrClosedShadowRoot`. `DOM.getNodeForLocation({x, y})` hit-tests across frames and returns a backendNodeId; `Overlay.highlightNode` draws the box model in the right place automatically. `DOM.resolveNode` bridges back to a JS handle in the right frame's context.
3. **`Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride`** for (d)'s desktop/tablet/mobile switch, which also fixes coordinate mapping for you.
mechanisms.port_notes: Recommendation for EXELMJ: build the picker as DOM-overlay-first (portable, styleable, works with no debugger attached) but keep a CDP path behind a flag for the two things DOM cannot do — closed shadow roots and cross-origin frames. `webContents.debugger` and DevTools cannot both be attached at once, so make CDP opt-in per session and detach on error. The `depth`/`count` budget caps from `deepAll` should be ported as-is; they are the difference between a scan and a hang.

mechanisms.name: Pick payload assembly and clipboard write with execCommand fallback
mechanisms.problem: On pick, produce a self-contained description of the element for an LLM and get it onto the clipboard, from a context where the async Clipboard API may be blocked.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 720–740 (copy), 742–769 (pick), 621–643 (collect), 493–535 (getMetrics, cleanOuterHTML, sanitize)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker output; (a) builder consumes the collect() shape as its import format; (e) MCP returns exactly this object to Claude
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: `clipboard.writeText()` from the `electron` module in the main process — **no permissions, no secure-context requirement, no user-activation requirement, and it works from a background context**. The entire two-tier fallback becomes one line and can be deleted. The `PICK_RESULT` broadcast becomes `ipcMain`/`webContents.send` to the Studio panel, or is not needed at all if the picker controller lives in the same renderer as the panel.
mechanisms.port_notes: The clipboard is the wrong primary channel for EXELMJ. In the extension, clipboard-then-paste-into-ChatGPT WAS the product. Here, the pick result should flow structurally: straight into (a) the builder's node model, and straight out of (e) as an MCP tool result. Keep `copy()` as a convenience action, drop the execCommand fallback. Port `collect()`'s shape as a TypeScript interface — it is a well-considered schema and the `verbatim` distinction (readable vs. paste-and-it-works) is a real insight worth preserving as two explicit output modes.

mechanisms.name: Element screenshot by cropping a full-viewport capture
mechanisms.problem: Produce a PNG of just the picked element. There is no DOM API that renders an arbitrary element to a bitmap.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 2481–2509 (captureElementShot); background.js 463–470 (CAPTURE_TAB handler)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker; (b) vector designer — an element screenshot is an input to the existing raster→vector tracer; (d) mini-browser preview thumbnails
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: `webContents.capturePage(rect)` — takes the crop rectangle DIRECTLY, in CSS pixels, and returns a `NativeImage`. The entire canvas/DPR/drawImage dance collapses to `const img = await wc.capturePage({x, y, width, height})` and `fs.writeFileSync(path, img.toPNG())` with real filesystem access instead of a synthetic download. Even better for the scroll case: CDP `Page.captureScreenshot({ clip: { x, y, width, height, scale }, captureBeyondViewport: true })` captures regions OUTSIDE the viewport, removing the scrollIntoView step entirely, and `Page.captureScreenshot({format:'png'})` after `DOM.getBoxModel` gives an exact element shot.
mechanisms.port_notes: Keep exactly one idea from the original: **hide the overlay before capturing and restore it after.** That is not obvious and it is easy to ship a picker whose every screenshot has a blue outline in it. Everything else — the DPR math, the manual crop, the data-URL round-trip, the anchor-click download — is replaced by `capturePage(rect)` + `fs.writeFile`. Use `captureBeyondViewport` so tall elements do not need scrolling.

mechanisms.name: Ruler tool — full-viewport canvas overlay with rAF draw loop
mechanisms.problem: Measure arbitrary distances on the page by dragging a box, with a live crosshair and a pixel readout.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 2384–2479 (ruler state, rulerDraw, sizeRulerCanvas, startRuler, stopRuler)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (b) vector designer — EXELMJ's design module already has canvas artboards, and this is the measure/guide tool it lacks; (c) picker as a companion mode; (d) mini-browser for checking generated layouts
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed — pure canvas.
mechanisms.port_notes: This is the one subsystem whose implementation strategy EXELMJ should prefer over the picker's DOM-layer approach if the two are ever unified: a single canvas with a rAF loop is cheaper and more flexible than four transitioned divs once you want guides, snap lines, distance-to-neighbour arrows, or a spacing inspector (Alt-hover in DevTools). Since EXELMJ's design module is already canvas-based, the code style will feel native. Port the DPR pattern verbatim — it is correct. Replace the shared-nullable cursor ownership with a ref-count.

mechanisms.name: Message-hub protocol: one flat switch as the whole external API
mechanisms.problem: Expose ~40 page-side capabilities to a UI living in a different process, over an asynchronous single-channel transport, without a framework.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
A single `chrome.runtime.onMessage` listener with a flat `switch (message.type)`. The protocol convention is the load-bearing part:

- Synchronous handlers call `sendResponse(...)` and `break`; the listener returns `false` at the bottom, telling Chrome the port can close.
- **Asynchronous handlers `return true`** from inside the case — this keeps the message port open past the listener returning, which is the mandatory and easily-forgotten Chrome idiom. Every long-running case does `something().then(sendResponse).catch(e => sendResponse({ok:false, error:String(e)}))` and then `return true`.
- Every response is `{ok: boolean, ...}` — errors are values, never thrown across the boundary, and the error is always `String(err)` so it survives structured-clone.
- Picker-relevant messages: `PING` → `{ok, v: PICKER_VERSION}` (the version handshake), `TOGGLE_PICKER {active}` → `{active}`, `GET_PICKER_STATE` → `{active, rulerActive}`, `NAV_KEY {key}` (the focus-loss relay), `INSPECT_ANCESTOR` (walks `lastPicked.parentElement`, re-collects, re-copies, re-broadcasts — the mechanism that lets the panel climb the tree with the picker OFF), `EXPORT_ELEMENT_HTML`, `CAPTURE_ELEMENT_SHOT`, `TOGGLE_RULER`, `START_COLOR_PICKER`.
- Notably `EXTRACT_UI` carries a comment explaining WHY it became async: the scan scrolls the page first to mount lazily-rendered components, so a synchronous response is impossible.

The service worker is a pure relay for most of these: `relayToActiveTab(message)` resolves the active tab, checks `isInjectableUrl`, calls `ensureContentScript`, forwards, and wraps the result as `{ok, tabId, resp}`.
mechanisms.location: content.js lines 7239–7498 (the switch); background.js 68–82 (relayToActiveTab), 411–499 (message hub)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (e) MCP server — this switch IS the tool list, nearly one-to-one; (c) picker's control surface
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: `ipcMain.handle(channel, handler)` + `ipcRenderer.invoke(channel, args)`, which is promise-based natively — **the entire `return true` mechanism disappears**, along with the whole class of bugs where someone forgets it and the response silently never arrives. For the host↔guest hop, either `webContents.send` + `ipcRenderer.on` with a correlation id, or a `MessageChannelMain` port pair handed to the guest's preload for a direct duplex channel with no main-process relay.
mechanisms.port_notes: Do not port the flat switch. Port the *inventory* — the ~40 message types are a validated list of what a page-inspection agent needs to expose, and for deliverable (e) they map almost directly onto MCP tools. Replace the shape with a typed request/response registry: one TS interface per operation, `{ok, data} | {ok:false, error}` as a discriminated union, and a generated tool manifest so (e) does not hand-maintain a parallel list. Keep two conventions verbatim: errors-as-values (never throw across the boundary) and the `{ok, ...}` envelope.

gotchas: THE ORPHAN GUARD IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT LESSON. `if (window.__ALREADY__) return;` is the obvious guard and it is WRONG. After an extension reload (or, in Electron, a main-process restart / Vite HMR re-import), the previous script's JavaScript keeps running with all its listeners attached, but its bridge to the host is dead. It still owns the global marker, so a naive guard blocks reinjection forever and the page becomes permanently un-pickable. The fix is two-factor: version match AND a liveness probe (`chrome.runtime.id` in a try/catch; in Electron, a ping on the IPC/MessagePort channel or a generation counter). Register the marker at the END of setup so a script that crashed mid-init never claims to be alive.

THE EXTENSION'S OWN BUG, DO NOT COPY IT: when the fresh script displaces an orphan, it never tells the orphan to clean up. There is no `prev.dispose()`. If the orphan had the picker active, its capture-phase mousemove/click/keydown/contextmenu listeners keep swallowing events forever and two overlays fight. The marker must expose `dispose()` and the new instance must call it before taking over.

z-index 2147483640, not 2147483647. INT32_MAX leaves no headroom to stack the picker's own chrome above its own highlight. The extension reserves 7 units: layers at Z, HUD and hint at Z+2, ruler canvas at Z+3, toast at Z+4 — all still below the max, all still above any realistic page value.

`window.addEventListener('scroll', fn, true)` — the `true` is load-bearing and non-obvious. Scroll events DO NOT BUBBLE, so a window listener in the bubble phase never hears a scroll inside an `overflow:auto` div. Capture phase catches every element's scroll. Without it the highlight drifts off the target the instant the user scrolls a sidebar, modal body, or virtualised list.

`composedPath()[0]`, not `e.target`. Event retargeting rewrites `e.target` to the shadow HOST for anything inside an open shadow root, so a picker using `e.target` can never select inside a web component. composedPath()[0] is the true innermost node. Caveat: for CLOSED shadow roots composedPath is truncated at the host, so it degrades to the same answer as e.target — no worse, but no better.

`outline: 2px solid #2563eb; outline-offset: -1px` for the border-box stroke, NOT `border`. An outline adds no box (so it cannot disturb the layer's own geometry) and is drawn OUTSIDE by default — without the -1px offset the highlight reads 2px larger than the element on every side and misreports tight layouts.

All four highlight layers are `position: fixed` inside the shadow root, so `getBoundingClientRect()`'s viewport coordinates are used verbatim with ZERO scroll-offset arithmetic. There is no `window.scrollY` anywhere in the highlight path. This is the single biggest simplification in the overlay.

`transition: top .05s linear, left .05s linear, width .05s linear, height .05s linear` on the layers is what makes the highlight glide between elements instead of teleporting. 50ms. It is one CSS line and it is the entire difference between feeling like DevTools and feeling like a debug rectangle.

Toast replay needs a `requestAnimationFrame` between removing and re-adding the `.show` class. Both style changes in the same task get coalesced into one computed value and no transition runs. rAF forces a style recalculation between the two states.

`scrollIntoView({block:'nearest', inline:'nearest'})` for keyboard navigation — `nearest` scrolls only when needed and only minimally. `center` or `start` jerks the page on every arrow keypress even when the target is already visible.

BEFORE SCREENSHOTTING, HIDE YOUR OWN OVERLAY AND WAIT ~120ms, then restore it. The capture is of the real page; the highlight is in the real page. Easy to ship a picker whose every screenshot has a blue outline baked into it. 120ms covers ~2 frames plus the 50ms layer transition settling.

THE SWALLOW LIST HAS A REAL HOLE: no `pointerdown`/`pointerup`/`pointermove`/`pointercancel`, and no `touchstart`/`touchend`. Every modern drag and gesture library (dnd-kit, interact.js, Framer Motion drag, canvas apps) listens on pointer events exclusively, so picking inside them starts a drag. Add them in the port, and add touch events for deliverable (d)'s tablet/mobile modes.
`e.stopImmediatePropagation()` in addition to `stopPropagation()`. A page with three click handlers on the SAME node would still fire the other two after stopPropagation alone.

Always pass the SAME options object reference to addEventListener and removeEventListener. The extension shares one module-level `const opts = {capture:true}` for exactly this reason — a fresh `{capture:true}` literal at removal time still matches on the capture flag, but sharing the reference makes the invariant explicit and prevents silent leaks when options grow.

THE PICKER HAS NO IFRAME SUPPORT AT ALL. The manifest declares no `all_frames` and the re-injection passes no `allFrames: true`, so it lives in the top frame only; hovering iframe content highlights the opaque `<iframe>` rectangle. Iframes are only handled in the unrelated extraction walker (same-origin only, via `contentDocument` in a try/catch). Do not inherit this — Electron's `webContents.mainFrame.framesInSubtree` and CDP `pierce: true` both solve it, including cross-origin.

`chrome.dom.openOrClosedShadowRoot(el)` is the extension's superpower for closed shadow roots and has NO plain-JS Electron equivalent. The replacement is CDP: `DOM.getDocument({pierce: true})` via `webContents.debugger`, which descends into closed shadow roots AND cross-origin iframes. Note `webContents.debugger` and DevTools cannot both be attached — make CDP opt-in and detach on error.

`webContents.insertCSS(css, {cssOrigin: 'user'})` beats the extension's injected `<style>` for the crosshair cursor: an author-origin `*` selector DOES NOT MATCH elements inside shadow roots, so the extension's crosshair silently fails over every web component; user-origin stylesheets do apply inside shadow trees and beat author `!important`. `removeInsertedCSS(key)` for cleanup.

No rAF coalescing anywhere in the hover path. `highlight()` runs synchronously on every mousemove (one forced layout) and `updateHUD` adds a SECOND forced layout by measuring the HUD after writing its content. Two forced reflows per mouse event. Fix with: short-circuit when the target has not changed, coalesce to one rAF, and cache the HUD height.

Nothing re-anchors the highlight on a layout change with no scroll or resize event — CSS animation, font load, lazy image, React re-render. And if the target is removed from the DOM, `getBoundingClientRect()` returns all zeros and a 0×0 box is painted at the origin instead of clearing. Add a ResizeObserver on the target plus an `isConnected` check.

`structuralSelector` has NO depth cap; a deeply-nested app with no IDs produces a 20-segment `>` chain. It does terminate early on the first unique-ID ancestor, which is the good part. Cap the depth for readability and token cost — deliverable (e) pays for every one of those segments.

`isUnique` queries `document`, so it is blind to shadow roots: a node inside a shadow root always reports zero matches and falls through to the structural path, which then produces a selector that does not resolve either. For the port, return a scoped `{hostPath: string[], selector: string}` instead of a bare string.

`window.focus()` at the top of `activate()` exists because the side panel holds keyboard focus, so arrows and Escape would never reach the page. The port should not need this hack — use `before-input-event` on the host webContents, which sees keys regardless of which surface has focus. The parallel NAV_KEY relay in sidepanel.js exists for the same reason and can be simplified the same way.

`destroyUI()` (content.js:215) is defined and never called from anywhere. `deactivate()` deliberately leaves the shadow host attached with layers at `display:none` so re-activation is allocation-free — which is the right call — but it means there is no teardown path at all. Add a real `destroy()` and call it on guest navigation.

The clipboard fallback (`textarea` + `document.execCommand('copy')`) needs `position:fixed; opacity:0`, NOT `display:none` and NOT off-screen. A hidden or unrendered textarea cannot be selected, and off-screen positioning causes a visible scroll jump. In Electron this whole tier is deleted — `clipboard.writeText()` has no permission, secure-context, or user-activation requirement.

`cleanOuterHTML`'s `verbatim` flag encodes a real product insight worth keeping as two explicit output modes: the READABLE payload trims class lists past 8 and drops inline styles, but a component that will be pasted somewhere and expected to WORK dies if you drop its ninth utility class or its inline styles. `on*` attributes are stripped unconditionally in both modes, because the payload gets rendered in previews.

`deepAll` budget caps — `out.length >= 9000` and `depth > 14` — are not decoration. Shadow-root plus iframe recursion on a real application is unbounded; these caps are the difference between a scan and a hang. Port them.

`isInjectableUrl` / BLOCKED_PREFIXES (chrome://, chrome-extension://, edge://, about:, the Web Store origins, view-source:) still needs an Electron analogue with a different list: block devtools://, chrome://, about:blank, and file:// unless opted in; explicitly allow the origin serving our own generated projects in deliverable (d).

MV3 service workers die after ~30s idle, which is why background.js's `pickerState` Map is treated as advisory and re-verified with a live `GET_PICKER_STATE` query. Electron's main process is not ephemeral, so that reconciliation round-trip can be dropped — but keep the `did-start-navigation` invalidation, because a navigation still destroys the injected picker.

subsystem: content.js — element → portable data (selectors, XPath, a11y, attributes, computed-style subset, Tailwind inference, output formats) + the token-budget and redaction gaps
summary: This is the serialization layer of the picker: given one DOM element it produces a `data` object (selector, xpath, metrics, cleaned outerHTML, classes, attributes, a11y approximation, styleInfo with WCAG contrast, optional Tailwind inference, optional 24-property computed-style subset) and then renders that object into one of three text formats for the clipboard and the AI hand-off. The selector generator is a 6-tier priority cascade where every tier is verified with `document.querySelectorAll(sel).length === 1` before it is accepted, falling back to an `:nth-of-type` ancestor chain. Two things the prompt asked about did NOT ship: there is zero token accounting anywhere in the codebase (IDEAS.md #4 is still an idea — the real AI hand-off is a blind `outerHTML.slice(0, 1500)`), and there is no redaction choke point on the picker path (IDEAS.md #16 is unbuilt — `scrubPII` exists but is wired only to the Arabic-corpus harvester, and the `maskMatch` machinery is a security-report renderer, not an egress filter). Element picks therefore leave for the LLM completely unredacted.

mechanisms.name: buildSelector — six-tier priority cascade, uniqueness-verified at every tier
mechanisms.problem: Turn a hovered element into a CSS selector that (a) is unique now and (b) still resolves after the page is re-rendered by its framework. Naive `nth-child` chains break on every re-render; naive class chains break on every Tailwind edit.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
Six tiers, each candidate rejected unless `document.querySelectorAll(sel).length === 1` (helper `isUnique`, wrapped in try/catch so an invalid selector returns false instead of throwing):
1. `#${CSS.escape(id)}` — only if `validIdent(id)` passes `/^[a-zA-Z_][\w-]*$/`.
2. Test-automation attributes, in TEST_ATTRS order: `data-testid, data-test, data-cy, data-qa, data-test-id, data-automation-id` → emitted as a BARE attribute selector `[data-testid="v"]` with no tag prefix.
3. `${tag}[name="v"]` for form controls.
4. Semantic classes: takes `semanticClasses(elm)` (see separate entry) and tries progressively longer prefixes — `tag.c1`, then `tag.c1.c2`, then `tag.c1.c2.c3`, capped at `Math.min(classes.length, 3)`. First unique one wins; classes stay in DOM order, they are not reordered by specificity or rarity.
5. `${tag}[aria-label="v"]`.
6. Fall through to `structuralSelector(elm)`.
Attribute values go through `cssAttr(v)` = `v.replace(/\\/g,'\\\\').replace(/"/g,'\\"')` — backslash and double-quote only; newlines and control chars are not handled.

mechanisms.name: semanticClasses — the utility-CSS rejection filter (five stacked regexes)
mechanisms.problem: On a Tailwind/utility page an element carries 20+ classes, all of them presentational. `div.flex.items-center.gap-4` is not a selector, it is a coin flip. Meanwhile CSS-Modules/styled-components emit hashed classes that change on every build.

`Array.from(elm.classList).filter(...)` with five successive rejections, keep-if-all-pass:
1. `!validIdent(c)` → reject. `/^[a-zA-Z_][\w-]*$/` kills anything containing `:` `/` `[` `]` `.` `%` — i.e. every Tailwind variant (`hover:bg-blue-500`), every arbitrary value (`w-[calc(100%-2rem)]`), and — usefully by accident — React 18 `useId` output (`:r0:`) and Radix ids.
2. `c.length > 40` → reject. This is the hashed-class heuristic: CSS-Modules `Button_root__x7f2q` and emotion `css-1a2b3c4d-Foo` overrun 40 chars; genuinely semantic names rarely do. It is a LENGTH heuristic, not an entropy one — a short hash like `_a1b2c` survives.
3. Variant-prefix regex `/^(sm|md|lg|xl|2xl|hover|focus|active|group|peer|dark|first|last|odd|even|disabled|aria|data|motion|print|rtl|ltr):/` → reject (belt-and-braces; #1 already catches these because of the colon).
4. Shape regex `/^-?[a-z]{1,3}-[\dpxremvwh.\/-]+$/` → reject. This is the clever one: it matches "1–3 letters, dash, then only digits and unit letters" — `p-4`, `mt-2`, `w-1/2`, `gap-x-4`, `-ml-3`, `h-96` — without needing a Tailwind dictionary. It is purely structural, so it also catches Bootstrap-style `mb-3` and any custom utility scale.
5. Two literal keyword lists: exact-match on `flex|grid|block|inline|hidden|relative|absolute|fixed|sticky|static|container|truncate|rounded|shadow|border|uppercase|lowercase|capitalize|italic|font|leading|tracking|antialiased`, and prefix-match on `(bg|text|from|via|to|ring|fill|stroke|w|h|min|max|top|left|right|bottom|inset|z|order|col|row|gap|space)-`.

mechanisms.name: structuralSelector — nth-of-type ancestor chain with a unique-ID short circuit

- SHORT CIRCUIT: at each level, if `cur.id && validIdent(cur.id) && isUnique('#'+CSS.escape(cur.id))`, unshift `#id` and RETURN IMMEDIATELY. - Otherwise: count siblings of the same tagName under `cur.parentElement`. If there is exactly one, unshift the bare `tag` (no index at all). Otherwise unshift `${tag}:nth-of-type(${index+1})`.

Segments joined with ` > ` (direct-child combinator, so the path is exact and cannot accidentally match a deeper twin).
Deliberate choice of `:nth-of-type` over `:nth-child`: `nth-of-type` counts only same-tag siblings, so inserting a `<span>` between two `<div>`s does not shift the index — meaningfully more resilient to framework re-renders.
CRITICAL ABSENCES: there is NO depth cap (the loop runs to `documentElement`), and the final joined string is NEVER passed through `isUnique` — the function trusts that a full direct-child path with per-level type indices is unique by construction. It usually is, but a `parentElement === null` break (shadow-root child) produces a shadow-relative path that is not unique against `document`.

mechanisms.problem: `getComputedStyle` returns ~340 resolved properties. Dumping them is useless to a human and ruinous to a token budget; dumping none loses the design.

1. SHORTHAND ONLY where a shorthand exists — `margin`, `padding`, `border`, `border-radius` rather than the 4+4+12+4 longhands. That alone collapses ~24 declarations into 4. (Note the shorthand only serialises when all sides agree; asymmetric values still come back as the composed string, so nothing is lost.)
2. ONE PROPERTY PER LAYOUT DECISION, not per layout system: `display`, `position`, `box-sizing`, `width`, `height` (the box), then `flex-direction`/`justify-content`/`align-items`/`gap` (the only four flex properties that carry intent — `flex-wrap`, `align-content`, `order` are omitted), then a single `grid-template-columns` standing in for all of Grid, then `z-index`, `opacity`, `overflow`.
3. THE FULL TYPE RAMP, because type is what makes a copy look wrong: `color`, `background-color`, `font-size`, `font-family`, `font-weight`, `line-height`, `text-align`.

mechanisms.name: getStyleInfo + WCAG contrast with ancestor background resolution
mechanisms.problem: Report the typographic identity of an element and whether its text is legible, without the caller having to compute anything.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
Three parts.
`relLuminance(hex)`: strips `#`, parses the three byte pairs to 0..1, applies the sRGB inverse companding `v <= 0.03928 ? v/12.92 : ((v+0.055)/1.055)**2.4`, weights `0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B`. This is WCAG 2.x exactly.
`contrastRatio(h1,h2)`: `(hi + 0.05) / (lo + 0.05)` after ordering by luminance.
`effectiveBackground(elm)`: THE useful trick — `getComputedStyle(el).backgroundColor` on a text node's own element is almost always `rgba(0,0,0,0)`, which would compute a nonsense ratio. So it walks `parentElement` upward converting each `backgroundColor` through `rgbToHex` (which maps alpha===0 to the literal string `"transparent"`) and returns the first non-transparent hex, defaulting to `#ffffff` at `documentElement`.
`getStyleInfo(elm)` then returns `{fontFamily (first family only, quotes stripped), fontWeight, fontSize, lineHeight, letterSpacing (normalised: 'normal' → '0px'), color, background, padding, margin}` and, only when the element has non-whitespace `textContent` and its color is not transparent, `contrast: {ratio: round to 2dp, aa: ratio>=4.5, aaa: ratio>=7}`.
Limitations: the AA threshold is hardcoded at 4.5 with no large-text 3.0 branch (WCAG allows 3.0 at ≥18.66px bold / ≥24px), semi-transparent backgrounds are not alpha-composited (a `rgba(0,0,0,0.5)` overlay is skipped entirely as if it were fully transparent), and background IMAGES/gradients are ignored.

mechanisms.name: toTailwind — computed styles → utility classes (dictionary-free inference)
mechanisms.problem: Emit something the user can paste into a Tailwind project, from a page that may not use Tailwind at all, without shipping a Tailwind config parser.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
Reads `getComputedStyle` once and pushes class strings onto an array, joined with spaces. Two primitives do the heavy lifting:
- `twSpace(px)`: `const n = parseFloat(px); if (!n) return null; if (n % 4 === 0 && n/4 <= 96) return String(n/4); return '[' + n + 'px]';` — the whole Tailwind spacing scale is 'px/4' for multiples of 4 up to 384px, so no lookup table is needed; anything else degrades to arbitrary-value syntax rather than being dropped.
- `rgbToHex(rgb)`: regex-parses `rgb()`/`rgba()`, returns the literal `"transparent"` when alpha is exactly 0, else `#rrggbb`.
Then, in order: display via a 7-entry map (`none`→`hidden`); `position` emitted as-is when not `static` (Tailwind's position names ARE the CSS names); flex-only properties emitted only when `display.includes('flex')`, with `alignItems: 'stretch'` mapped to `null` because stretch is the default and emitting `items-stretch` is noise; `gap-${twSpace}`.
Padding uses a three-branch shorthand collapse: read all four sides as numbers, if `pads.every(v => v === pads[0])` emit `p-N`; else emit `py-N` when top===bottom (falling back to `pt-`/`pb-` when not) and `px-N` when left===right (falling back to `pr-`/`pl-`). Zero values are suppressed at every branch.
Font size uses an exact-match table of 10 entries (12→`text-xs` … 60→`text-6xl`) with `text-[Npx]` fallback; font weight a 6-entry table (400 deliberately absent — it is the default); text-align emitted only for center/right/justify.
Colors always emit arbitrary values (`text-[#1f2937]`, `bg-[#ffffff]`) — no attempt to reverse-map to `slate-800`. `#000000` text and transparent backgrounds are suppressed as defaults.
Borders read ONLY `borderTopWidth`/`borderTopStyle`/`borderTopColor` and assume uniformity; width 1 → bare `border`, else `border-[Npx]`. Radius uses a 7-entry table with `>= 9999 → rounded-full`.
Effects: any non-`none` box-shadow collapses to the single word `shadow` (the value is discarded); `opacity-${Math.round(op*100)}` (NOT snapped to Tailwind's step-5 scale, so `opacity-73` can be emitted); `overflow-hidden`.
NOT emitted at all: margin (any), width, height, and every variant (hover:/focus:/md:).

mechanisms.name: exportElementAsHtml + INLINE_PROPS — the fourth, undocumented output format
mechanisms.problem: Produce a standalone `.html` file that renders the element correctly with zero external CSS.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
`inlineStyles(src, dst, depth)` walks the original and the clone in lockstep (`src.children[i]` ↔ `dst.children[i]`), and for each pair reads `getComputedStyle(src)` and writes a single `style="..."` string onto `dst` built from the 46-property `INLINE_PROPS` list — skipping any value that is `none`, `normal` or `auto` (the three no-op defaults, which is what keeps the strings from tripling in size). It then `removeAttribute('class')` on the clone (styles are now self-contained, classes would only reference stylesheets that no longer exist) and strips `on*` handlers. Depth-capped at 400 via a threaded counter.
INLINE_PROPS (46) is the 'reproduce it' superset of KEY_STYLES (24): it adds top/left/right/bottom, flex-wrap, grid-template-rows, max-width/min-height, outline, box-shadow, font-style, letter-spacing, text-decoration, text-transform, white-space, vertical-align, list-style, cursor, transition, transform, object-fit, aspect-ratio — and uses `background` (shorthand, so gradients survive) where KEY_STYLES uses `background-color`.
`exportElementAsHtml` then wraps the clone in a full document with charset/viewport meta, a `<title>Export — {document.title}</title>`, a provenance comment `<!-- Exported by AI Element Picker from {location.href} -->`, and `<body style="margin:0;padding:24px;background:#fff;">`, removes all `<script>`, and downloads via `Blob` + `URL.createObjectURL` + a synthetic `<a download>` click, revoking the object URL after 5s.

mechanisms.name: ancestorContext + INHERITED_PROPS — recovering var() REFERENCES that getComputedStyle destroys
mechanisms.problem: A snipped element loses everything it inherited. Worse: you cannot recover its design tokens from computed styles, because `getComputedStyle` returns the RESOLVED value (`rgb(79,70,229)`) and never the `var(--brand)` reference that produced it — so the copy is hardcoded and detaches from the theme.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
Two halves.
(1) Inherited type context: read the 12 `INHERITED_PROPS` (`font-family, font-size, font-weight, font-style, line-height, letter-spacing, color, text-align, direction, white-space, text-transform, word-spacing, list-style`) off the element's own computed style — since they inherit, the element's resolved value IS what the ancestors contributed.
(2) Token recovery — the clever part. Since the references only exist in the AUTHORED rules, it reads the rules: build `subtree = [el, ...el.querySelectorAll('*').slice(0,60)]`, compute `have = subtreeTokens(subtree)` (a token set for fast rejection), then iterate a cached `ruleIndex(scopeOf(el))`; skip any rule that shares no token with the subtree, skip any whose `rule.style.cssText` lacks `var(`; then for each comma-separated selector run it through `matchableSelector(baseSelector(sel))` and test `subtree.some(n => n.matches(sel))`; on a hit, regex out every `var(\s*(--[\w-]+)` and add the name to `used`.
Then a second pass the author explicitly documents as a bug they hit: `@keyframes` are invisible to the style-rule walker, so a dot whose colour is only set at `66% { background: var(--wire) }` exported unresolved and animated to transparent. Fix: collect `getComputedStyle(n).animationName` across the subtree, split on commas, pull each block's text via `keyframesText(nm, scope)` and scrape its `var()` references too. Measured on one motion library: 12 of 94 keyframes referenced a variable.
Finally `resolve(name, depth)` reads each token's value back off the element (`getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue(name)`) and recurses up to depth 3 into nested `var()` references, so a token defined in terms of another token is captured too.

mechanisms.name: getCodeForReview — the ONLY budgeted exporter that actually shipped (byte budget + priority fill)
mechanisms.problem: A model cannot read a whole site; give it the highest-value-per-byte slice of the page's JavaScript within a hard ceiling.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
`getCodeForReview(budget = 60000)` — a BYTE budget, not a token budget, filled in strict priority order by a `push(label, code, lineOffset)` closure that: returns immediately if `used >= budget`; computes `room = budget - used`; slices the code to `room` if needed; increments `used`; and records `{label, code, lineOffset, truncated}` so the consumer knows a chunk was cut.
Priority order and the filters at each stage:
1. Inline `<script>:not([src])` — 'hand-written app logic, highest value per byte'. Rejects blocks under 40 trimmed chars, and rejects anything matching `/^\s*[\{\[]/` (JSON-LD / state blobs masquerading as scripts).
2. Same-origin `script[src]`, capped at 12 files. Each fetched with `credentials:'omit'` and an `AbortController` aborted after 8000ms; body capped at 400000 chars.
3. The fetched set is then SORTED before pushing: `(a.minified === b.minified) ? a.length - b.length : (a.minified ? 1 : -1)` — non-minified first, then shortest first, on the stated theory that app code is smaller than vendor bundles and small files fit a budget better. Minified files over 20000 chars are skipped entirely ('burns budget for almost no insight').
`isMinified(code)` is SHAPE-based, not filename-based: false if under 400 chars; true if the longest line exceeds 500 chars (bundlers strip newlines, so one enormous line is the tell); true if fewer than 5 lines and over 2000 chars.
Returns `{chunks, bytes: used, budget}` so the caller can report what fitted.

mechanisms.name: scrubPII — a real scrubber, wired to the WRONG path (idea #16 is unbuilt)
mechanisms.problem: IDEAS.md idea #16 ('نقطة تعقيم واحدة للبيانات الحسّاسة', scored 7.3) specifies ONE mandatory choke point that every output passes through before any LLM or network egress, with destination-dependent policy: on-screen values replaced by realistic same-LENGTH text so layout and measurements stay valid; in-data values replaced by stable pseudonyms that preserve TYPE not length, because the model needs data shape not content; anything high-entropy or matching a known key prefix blocked immediately; and anything unclassifiable blocked too — errors always fall toward safety.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
The choke point does not exist. `collect()` → `formatPayload()` → clipboard/`PICK_RESULT`/LLM carries raw text, raw attribute values and raw outerHTML with no redaction whatsoever.
What DOES exist is `scrubPII(raw, dropEmoji)`, wired ONLY into the Arabic-dialect corpus harvester (`corpusScan`/`corpusHarvest`/`corpusWatch`, call sites at 7061, 7107, 7165). Its transform chain, all replacements to a SPACE (destructive removal, the exact opposite of the length-preserving substitution idea #16 asks for):
1. Strip bidi control characters and zero-width joiners — noted as invisible but they break dedup and leak layout artefacts into the training file.
2. `https?:\/\/\S+|\bwww\.\S+` → space.
3. `[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]{2,}` → space (emails).
4. `@[\w.{AR_RANGE}-]{2,}` → space (social handles, Arabic-range aware).
5. Iraqi mobiles in both `(?:\+?964|00964)[\s.-]?{IQ_MOBILE}` and bare `\b{IQ_MOBILE}\b` forms.
6. `\b\d[\d\s.-]{5,}\d\b` → space, on the stated reasoning that seven or more digits is an ID, card, account or phone and never a word.
7. `[٠-٩][٠-٩\s.-]{5,}[٠-٩]` → space — a SEPARATE rule for Arabic-Indic digits with an explicit comment that `\b` is ASCII-only and never fires next to `٠-٩`, so the ASCII pattern silently skipped them. This is a genuinely non-obvious bug they hit and fixed, and it will bite EXELMJ identically given its Arabic-first brief.
8. Optional emoji strip via `\p{Extended_Pictographic}`, then whitespace collapse.
Also present but unrelated: `PII_RULES` (6 regexes: email, Iraqi phone, international phone, IBAN, card with Luhn-shaped prefixes, national-id) plus `maskMatch`/`maskContext`/`ALWAYS_MASK` — this is the SECURITY SCANNER's report renderer, not an egress filter. `maskMatch` is opt-in with `mask` defaulting to false ('on your own site you want to see the real value'), masks only when `ALWAYS_MASK.has(ruleId) || severity is critical|high`, skips anything ≤12 chars, and renders `first6…last4 (N حرفًا)`. Its design comment carries the one genuinely portable lesson: mask by WHAT the data is, never by how severe it was judged, because reclassifying a token as low-risk would silently print it in full into a report the user pastes into a chat.

mechanisms.name: deepAll / scopeOf / shadowRootOf — shadow and iframe piercing, and the uniqueness bug it causes
mechanisms.problem: Modern components live inside shadow roots and same-origin iframes; a `document.querySelectorAll('*')` walk misses them entirely.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
`shadowRootOf(el)` tries `chrome.dom.openOrClosedShadowRoot(el)` — an extension-only API that needs NO permission and returns CLOSED shadow roots — and falls back to `el.shadowRoot`.
`deepAll(root, out, depth)` recurses: hard caps at 9000 collected nodes and depth 14; skips the picker's own shadow host (`n === ui.root || ui.root.contains(n)`); for every node, descends into its shadow root, and for `IFRAME`/`FRAME` descends into `contentDocument.documentElement` inside a try/catch with the comment that cross-origin is unreachable by design.
`scopeOf(node)` returns `node.getRootNode()` when it is a DocumentFragment (11) or Document (9), else `document` — i.e. the correct query root for that node.
THE BUG: `buildSelector` is called on shadow-DOM elements (the component scanner does so at content.js 6450) but its `isUnique` helper hardcodes `document.querySelectorAll`. For an element inside a shadow root that always returns 0, so every tier fails uniqueness and the code falls through to `structuralSelector`, whose upward walk terminates when `parentElement` is null (a shadow root is a DocumentFragment, not an Element) — producing a shadow-RELATIVE path. The scanner then counts instances with `scopeOf(el).querySelectorAll(buildSelector(el))` (line 6455), i.e. it queries in the right scope with a selector that was validated in the wrong one. It happens to mostly work; it is not sound.
