mechanisms.chrome_apis_used: CustomEvent bridge between MAIN and isolated worlds
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: The whole handshake DISAPPEARS. In a preload you are either in the same world (contextIsolation:false — direct call) or you use contextBridge / webFrame.executeJavaScriptInIsolatedWorld, both of which pass structured data. No JSON-string smuggling, no nonce, no 500ms timeout. Shadow piercing: keep the manual sweep, or use CDP DOM.getDocument({pierce:true}) which returns closed roots too.
mechanisms.port_notes: Port the ALGORITHM (delegation hoisted out of the per-element loop; shadow sweep; inline on* counted; 40/12/4000 caps) and drop the transport. The delegated-attribution heuristic is weak and self-labelled as such — in our own builder we know the binding, so replace it with real data for generated projects and keep the heuristic only for imported pages.

mechanisms.name: queryListenerRegistry — the isolated-world side of the handshake (nonce is correlation, not trust)
mechanisms.problem: One round-trip for many components, and a stale reply from an earlier query must not be mistaken for the current one.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Tags each connected element with data-aiep-q=qN (skipping !isConnected), generates nonce = 'n'+random base36, subscribes to 'aiep:listeners:reply', dispatches the query, and arms a 500ms timeout. On reply: JSON.parse inside try/catch, DROP the reply unless parsed.nonce === nonce, then a single fin() that clears the timer, removes the listener, removes every data-aiep-q attribute, and resolves a Map<Element, info>. The comment is explicit that the nonce only distinguishes a stale answer from a current one and PROVES NOTHING ABOUT WHO SENT IT — the reply comes from the page's own world and is therefore untrusted input, sanitised at the point of use (see the SAFE_EVENT_RE mechanism).
mechanisms.location: content.js:6160-6202
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: ipcRenderer.invoke / MessageChannelMain — a real request/response channel with real identity, so the nonce becomes unnecessary. The 'the page's world is untrusted' rule still holds for anything the preload reads out of page objects.
mechanisms.port_notes: Keep the fin()-once + always-remove-the-attribute discipline: a thrown reply handler that leaves data-aiep-q on the page pollutes the next query and shows up in exported HTML.

mechanisms.name: Pass 3 orchestration — recordMotionPass: probe cap, JS-signal ORDERING (never filtering), budget, unique names
mechanisms.problem: Recording is expensive and slots are scarce; spend them where JavaScript is actually wired, without silently excluding whole classes of page.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Defaults: recordLimit 16, recordBudgetMs 90000, probeLimit 300. Only the first 300 components are asked about in the registry query (walking every tagged element's subtree in the page's world for 600 components in order to record 16 was work thrown away). Listener metadata is attached to EVERY probed component, not just recorded ones (it was previously discarded for everything the motion pass skipped). jsSignal(c) = +2 if any pointer/mouse move|enter|over listener, +1 if any pointer/mouse/touch down|start, +1 if any click/wheel/keydown. Components are sorted by (signal desc, original index asc) — CRITICALLY the signal decides ORDER ONLY, never admission: filtering on it silently excluded every component inside a shadow root and every page whose framework delegates from its own root rather than from document, on which the whole pass became a no-op. Zero-signal components still get a turn at the back of the queue, where the early-bail makes them cost a fraction of a second each. Loop: break on done>=16 or past deadline; skip !isConnected; scrollIntoView({block:'center', behavior:'instant'}) + 180ms; recordComponentBehavior; post UI_SCAN_PROGRESS {phase:'record', pct} so the panel can distinguish the sweep from the recording. Names are prefixed with a per-scan random tag (`aiep-${scanTag}-${i}`) because two components recorded in different scans both named `aiep-0-hover` collide in one stylesheet and the later one wins. Finally restores the original scrollY. Pass 3 is skipped entirely when document.visibilityState !== 'visible': rAF is frozen in hidden tabs, so the page's own engines cannot move and there is nothing to record.
mechanisms.location: content.js:6203-6290 (recordMotionPass), 6509-6520 (the call site and visibility gate)
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: Budgeting/ordering is plain JS and ports as-is. The visibility gate can be DELETED if the WebContentsView sets webPreferences.backgroundThrottling:false (and, for a truly hidden window, an offscreen window with paintWhenInitiallyHidden:true) — Electron lets us keep rAF running where a Chrome tab could not. Progress over webContents.send.
mechanisms.port_notes: The 'signal orders, never filters' rule is the most reusable line in the file — it is the fix for a class of bug where a heuristic quietly turns a feature into a no-op on a whole family of sites. Keep the per-scan name tag; our library will accumulate far more components than the extension's did.

mechanisms.name: recordComponentBehavior — the plan captured BEFORE any dispatch, and the phase ladder
mechanisms.problem: Indices and child paths measured after interaction are counted against a DOM the page mutated mid-interaction — one the exported markup does not have.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Before a single event is dispatched, build plan = {nodes, paths, cssAnimated}: nodes = watchNodes(el) — the root plus its first 32 descendants in document order (springs usually move a dedicated inner element, so children matter as much as the root); paths[i] = pathFromRoot(el, node) — a '> :nth-child(a) > :nth-child(b)' chain built by walking up to the root using Array.indexOf on parent.children, returning null if the chain breaks (resolvable inside the exported copy, which has the same structure but none of the page's unique ids); cssAnimated[i] = getComputedStyle(n).animationName !== 'none' — a node the stylesheet ALREADY animates moves on its own for the whole window, and recording it is transcription, not capture, and would fight the author's own @keyframes. Then the phase ladder is assembled: hover (1200ms) always; press (:active, 1100ms) unless pressUnsafe; click (:active, 2000ms) only if !clickUnsafe; drag (:active, 1600ms) only if the registry shows BOTH a *move and a *down/*start listener (a held pointer is only worth 1.6s where it is actually read). overlayCount() is snapshotted. covered/coveredActive are computed once. Per phase: samplePhase → attach paths/cssAnimated to the record → changedSeries → trim → phaseToBlocks; the first phase that yields keyframes breaks out of the aim loop.
mechanisms.location: content.js:6066-6158, watchNodes at 5747-5753, pathFromRoot at 5755-5768
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed; identical in a preload. In Electron the exported HTML can be snapshotted by the SAME code in the SAME tick as the plan, removing the class of mismatch entirely.
mechanisms.port_notes: The 'capture the plan before you perturb the system' discipline is the core lesson. In our builder we can go further: give every emitted node a stable data-studio-id so bindings never need nth-child at all — but keep pathFromRoot for imported pages.

mechanisms.name: runPhase — the four drive scripts (hover arc, press, click, drag) and elementFromPoint re-targeting
mechanisms.problem: Dispatching on the component root does the opposite of what a real pointer does: a listener wired to an inner element (a magnet zone inside a card) never hears it, and a single stationary hover records nothing from pointer-following physics.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Geometry: r = aim || root.getBoundingClientRect(); cx,cy = its centre. targetAt(x,y) = document.elementFromPoint(x,y), accepted only if it is the root or inside it, else fall back to root — this restores real hit-testing (a real pointer hits the DEEPEST element and the event bubbles up). enterAt(x,y) fires pointerover/mouseover/pointerenter/mouseenter at the deep target AND, because enter/over-enter do NOT bubble, a second pointerenter/mouseenter at the root, or root-level hover wiring stays deaf. fireAt() constructs PointerEvent for pointer* types and MouseEvent otherwise, with {bubbles:true, cancelable:true, composed:true, view:window, clientX/Y, pointerId:1, pointerType:'mouse', isPrimary:true, buttons: 1 for down}. HOVER: enterAt(centre), then 15 samples (i=0..14) around a full circle a = (i/14)*2π at radius (0.35*width, 0.35*height), firing pointermove+mousemove at the re-computed deep target, sleeping (durMs*0.55)/steps between them, then a final move back to the centre — the arc is what feeds magnetic pulls and tilt cards. PRESS/CLICK: enterAt, pointerdown+mousedown, wait 180ms, pointerup+mouseup; for CLICK only, set allowClickOn = the aimed target, fire 'click', then clear it. DRAG: enterAt at (cx - 0.28w, cy), pointerdown+mousedown there, then 12 moves sweeping to (cx + 0.28w) with a sinusoidal vertical bow of 0.18h and buttons:1 on every move, sleeping (durMs*0.45)/12, then pointerup at the far end — sliders, knobs and swipe-to-dismiss only move under a held pointer. Teardown always fires pointerout/mouseout/pointerleave/mouseleave at the inner target AND at the root when they differ, or its hover state stays stuck on.
mechanisms.location: content.js:5799-5916 (runPhase), 5732-5745 (fireAt)
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: webContents.sendInputEvent({type:'mouseMove'|'mouseDown'|'mouseUp', x, y, button, clickCount}) or CDP Input.dispatchMouseEvent via webContents.debugger. BOTH produce TRUSTED events, which is a categorical upgrade: real hit-testing, the real :hover pseudo actually applies (the extension can never make :hover true), real pointer capture, real drag. Coordinates must be translated from page coords to the WebContentsView's client coords (account for scroll and zoomFactor).
mechanisms.port_notes: Port the SCRIPTS (arc geometry 0.35r/14 steps, 180ms press, 0.28w→0.28w drag with a 0.18h sinusoidal bow, always release at both target and root) and replace the dispatch layer with sendInputEvent/Input.dispatchMouseEvent. WARNING: trusted events invalidate the entire isTrusted-based safety guard below — with real input, clicks really navigate and really submit, so safety MUST move to session.webRequest.onBeforeRequest(cancel), will-navigate preventDefault, and setWindowOpenHandler deny. Also: with trusted input the :hover state is real, so a whole class of motion the extension could never capture becomes recordable.

mechanisms.name: The sampling loop and its early bail (measured from the END of driving, not the start of the phase)
mechanisms.problem: An inert component cost the full window anyway, which is most of what made a scan of a static page take a minute — but bailing too early loses press motion, which only starts on pointerup.
mechanisms.how_it_works: drive is an async IIFE that runs the phase script; its completion time is recorded as driveDone = performance.now() - t0 via drive.then(fin, fin) (both branches, so a throw does not disable the bail). The sampler loop runs while performance.now() - t0 < durMs: await nextFrame(), then for each of the <=32 planned nodes call getComputedStyle(n) once and read all 22 RECORD_PROPS (transform, translate, scale, rotate, opacity, background-color, color, border-color, box-shadow, border-radius, filter, width, height, letter-spacing, clip-path, left, top, plus stroke-dashoffset, stroke-dasharray, stroke, fill, stroke-width — without the SVG five, a progress ring's whole animation reads as 'nothing moved'). Push {t, styles[]}. sawChange is computed incrementally by comparing the current frame against frames[0] on any node/prop. EARLY BAIL: if !sawChange && driveDone && t > driveDone + 450, break. The 450ms deadline is deliberately counted from the moment the driving events FINISHED, not from phase start: a press only acts on pointerup, so a deadline from phase start gave it a few dozen milliseconds to show a change before the sampler gave up. nextFrame() is requestAnimationFrame RACED against a 40ms setTimeout, both routed through a done flag — hidden tabs never fire rAF and the sampler would hang forever.
mechanisms.location: content.js:5877-5915, RECORD_PROPS at content.js:5610-5623, nextFrame at 5722-5730
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: Identical inside a preload. Alternative if you need the styles out-of-process: CDP CSS.getComputedStyleForNode per frame — DON'T, it is far slower than in-page getComputedStyle. Keep sampling in-page and stream the result over IPC once. Optionally pair it with Page.startScreencast for a visual ground truth the extension had no way to capture.
mechanisms.port_notes: Two numbers to keep: the rAF/40ms race (any rAF wait without a timeout fallback is a hang), and 'measure the idle deadline from when your stimulus finished, not from when you started'. Note the cost model: 22 props × 32 nodes × ~70 frames ≈ 50k getPropertyValue calls per phase, each forcing style recalc — this is the pass's whole budget.

mechanisms.name: changedSeries — turning a frame series into per-node changed properties (jitter floor, run-length, decimation)
mechanisms.problem: Sub-pixel layout jitter is not motion, 70 identical frames are not information, and a node the stylesheet already animates must not be re-recorded.
mechanisms.how_it_works: For each node index i: skip entirely if rec.cssAnimated[i] (authored animation — transcription, not capture). For each of the 22 props build series = [{t, v}] across all frames. Drop if fewer than 2 samples or if new Set(values).size <= 1. For NUMERIC_PROPS (width, height, letter-spacing, left, top) additionally parseFloat every value and drop if max-min <= 1 — a 1px floor kills layout jitter. Run-length compress: kept = [series[0]] then push only values that DIFFER from the last kept one, so a spring's plateau costs one entry. Drop if kept.length < 2. Decimate to at most maxFrames=26 by index sampling kept[floor(k*len/26)] for k in 0..24 and always appending the true last element (the settled value must survive decimation — it becomes the pinned 100% stop). Emit {nodeIndex, changed:{prop:[{t,v}]}} only for nodes with at least one surviving prop.
mechanisms.location: content.js:5926-5964, NUMERIC_PROPS at 5625
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed
mechanisms.port_notes: The 'always append the true last sample after decimation' detail is load-bearing — losing it breaks the 100% pin and the animation drifts back to base. Same compression is directly reusable for our vector designer's motion/keyframe timeline.

mechanisms.name: phaseToBlocks — settle-time duration, the pinned 100% stop, and HTML-verified child bindings
mechanisms.problem: Three separate bugs: a spring that settles in 400ms of a 1200ms window got stretched across the whole window; CSS synthesises a missing 100% frame from the element's RESTING style, so the motion then ran backwards to base and `both` held it there — the hover visibly UNDID itself while still hovered; and an nth-child path can point at a node the page injected mid-press that does not exist in the snapshotted HTML.
mechanisms.how_it_works: (1) The sampling window is a CEILING, not the duration. Scan every kept series for the largest final timestamp lastT, then effDur = max(200, min(durMs, round(lastT) + 60)). The +60ms is a tail; the 200ms floor stops a degenerate 2-sample series producing a 0s animation. (2) Each sample becomes a stop at pct = clamp(0, 99, round(t/effDur*100)) — note the clamp to 99, so no sampled frame can ever occupy 100%. (3) settled[prop] = the LAST kept value of that prop; then stops.set(100, {...existing100, ...settled}) explicitly PINS the resting-after-motion value at 100%, which is what stops CSS from synthesising a 100% from the element's base style and running the animation backwards. (4) Binding: suffix = '' for the root, else rec.paths[nodeIndex] (skip if null/undefined), and the binding SHIPS ONLY IF resolvesInHtml(comp.html, suffix) — parse the already-snapshotted export HTML into a <template>, take firstElementChild, and require rootEl.querySelector(':scope ' + suffix) to hit; if the HTML has no firstElementChild, keep the binding (nothing to check against, so don't drop it). (5) Emit `@keyframes NAME { pct% { prop: value; … } }` sorted by pct, requiring >= 2 stops, and a binding `${kfName} ${(effDur/1000).toFixed(2)}s linear both`. Note 'linear': the sampled points ALREADY encode the easing, so any other timing function would double-apply it.
mechanisms.location: content.js:6012-6064, resolvesInHtml at 6001-6010
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed — pure CSS synthesis. Optionally validate the result by replaying it in an offscreen window and comparing sampled frames, which Electron makes cheap and the extension could not do.
mechanisms.port_notes: The three tricks — settle-time duration, the 100% pin, and verifying the child path against the ACTUAL exported markup rather than the live DOM — are the whole reason the output replays correctly. `linear` + sampled points is the correct default and should be documented so nobody 'improves' it to ease-out.

mechanisms.name: cssCoveredProps / COVER_ALIASES / root-only trim — not re-emitting what the author already wrote
mechanisms.problem: A recorded property whose motion the author's own CSS already provides must not be re-emitted: the authored rule is the better artifact, and a duplicate animation with `both` fill freezes its end state over the live transition.
mechanisms.how_it_works: cssCoveredProps(comp, pseudo, root) walks comp.stateRules, splits each selector on commas, and for each part computes subjectCompound(sel) — the LAST compound after the last top-level combinator — and requires the PSEUDO to be on that subject. This is the sharp part: in `.card:hover .icon { transform }` the subject is `.icon`, and treating that as coverage threw away the card's own recorded transform; testing merely 'the pseudo appears somewhere' let any descendant's hover rule do the same. It then requires root.matches(matchableSelector(baseSelector(subject))). Covered property names are harvested with /(?:^|;)\s*([a-zA-Z-]+)\s*:/g. Coverage is tested through an explicit COVER_ALIASES table, NOT by comparing the first hyphen segment — that shortcut let `border-color` cover `border-radius` and `transform-origin` cover `transform`, deleting real motion. translate/scale/rotate each alias to themselves plus `transform`; background-color also accepts `background`; left/top also accept `inset`. Finally trim() applies coverage ONLY to nodeIndex 0: a card's `:hover { transform }` says nothing about the spring-driven button inside it, and filtering children on the root's rules silently discarded exactly the JS motion the recorder exists to catch.
mechanisms.location: content.js:5966-5999 (cssCoveredProps/isCovered), 5625-5647 (COVER_ALIASES), 6106-6120 (trim)
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed. CDP CSS.getMatchedStylesForNode would supply the matched-rule set more reliably than hand-rolled selector matching.
mechanisms.port_notes: Both bug histories are worth carrying as comments: 'subject of the selector, not any part of it' and 'alias table, not prefix matching'. The root-only rule is the one that decides whether the recorder produces anything at all.

mechanisms.name: SAFETY 1 — clickUnsafe(): whole-subtree vetting against real handler SOURCE
mechanisms.problem: Click is the event that deletes, buys and submits. It is also what drives most demos — refusing to click at all cost about two thirds of everything worth recording.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Fail-CLOSED at every step (any throw returns true = unsafe). (1) el.closest('form') → unsafe, period. (2) Scan [el, ...el.querySelectorAll('*')].slice(0,60) — the WHOLE SUBTREE, because the event is aimed at whatever elementFromPoint returns, which is almost always a descendant and not the vetted root. Within it: any <A href> → unsafe; any BUTTON/INPUT with type submit|reset → unsafe; any on* ATTRIBUTE whose value matches EFFECT_RE → unsafe. (3) pressUnsafe(el): the concatenation of aria-label + textContent (first 160 chars) tested against DESTRUCTIVE_RE, a bilingual list — delete|remove|discard|clear|reset|logout|sign out|buy|purchase|checkout|pay|order|subscribe|unsubscribe|confirm|submit|publish|archive plus Arabic احذف|حذف|إزالة|شراء|ادفع|إرسال|أرسل|تأكيد|اشتراك|إلغاء|خروج. (4) THE KEY STEP: take behavior.handlers (from hook.js, i.e. the page's REAL registered functions) and filter OUT on==='delegated'; if nothing readable remains → UNSAFE (no handler to clear it with; a delegated framework handler is a whole bundle and says nothing about this element in particular). Otherwise every remaining handler's SOURCE TEXT is tested against EFFECT_RE = /\bfetch\s*\(|XMLHttpRequest|sendBeacon|window\.open|location\s*\.\s*(href|assign|replace)|location\s*=|\.submit\s*\(|\.click\s*\(|history\s*\.\s*(pushState|replaceState)|localStorage|sessionStorage|indexedDB|document\.cookie|navigator\.clipboard/ — any hit → unsafe. The stated principle: a handler whose source contains none of these calls cannot delete, buy, navigate or persist anything, however it is written.
mechanisms.location: content.js:5687-5712 (clickUnsafe), 5672-5685 (pressUnsafe), 5651 (DESTRUCTIVE_RE), 5668 (EFFECT_RE)
mechanisms.chrome_apis_used: none directly; depends entirely on hook.js handler source
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: Keep the vetting AND add real enforcement, which Electron can do and Chrome extensions cannot: session.webRequest.onBeforeRequest cancelling non-GET during the window; webContents.on('will-navigate'/'will-redirect', e=>e.preventDefault()); setWindowOpenHandler(()=>({action:'deny'})); optionally a session partition with a throwaway cookie jar. With trusted input events the source-scan alone is NOT sufficient.
mechanisms.port_notes: Port the algorithm exactly for imported third-party pages; it is a genuinely thoughtful static check. For OUR OWN generated projects in the mini-browser, most of it can be relaxed — we own the code and can reload from a known state — but keep 'no readable handler means unsafe' as the default posture. NOTE a doc/code drift in the source: the section banner at content.js:5599 still states 'click is NEVER dispatched', which the shipped phase ladder contradicts. Anyone porting from the banner will build the wrong safety model.

mechanisms.name: SAFETY 2 — the window guard: preventDefault only OUR events, stopImmediatePropagation any unaimed untrusted click
mechanisms.problem: The first version cancelled EVERY click on the page for the whole pass, so a user clicking a link mid-scan silently got nothing. And preventDefault alone does not stop the page's own listeners from running.
mechanisms.how_it_works: samplePhase installs one capture-phase listener on window for both 'click' and 'submit': `const guard = (e) => { if (e.isTrusted) return; e.preventDefault(); const aimed = allowClickOn && (e.target === allowClickOn || allowClickOn.contains(e.target)); if (!aimed) e.stopImmediatePropagation(); }`. Two distinct rules: (a) a TRUSTED event is the user's own and passes through completely untouched; (b) an UNTRUSTED event loses its default action, and if it is not the one click we are currently aiming (module-scoped allowClickOn, set immediately before fireAt('click') and cleared immediately after) it is killed with stopImmediatePropagation — an untrusted click we did not aim is one the PAGE synthesised out of our pointerdown/pointerup, and preventDefault would not stop the page's own listeners from acting on it. Both listeners are added with capture=true so they run before page handlers.
mechanisms.location: content.js:5772-5798 (guard inside samplePhase), allowClickOn declared at 5663, set/cleared at 5852-5856
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: THIS MECHANISM DOES NOT SURVIVE. sendInputEvent/Input.dispatchMouseEvent produce isTrusted===true, so there is no way to tell our clicks from the user's inside the page. Replacement: the user cannot click at all during a recording because we drive the view — gate input at the Electron layer instead (webContents.setIgnoreMenuShortcuts / an input-blocking overlay in the host renderer over the WebContentsView, plus 'before-input-event' to swallow real user input for the duration), and enforce side-effect safety at the network/navigation layer (webRequest cancel, will-navigate preventDefault, setWindowOpenHandler deny) rather than at the event layer.
mechanisms.port_notes: The DESIGN GOAL — 'the user's own interaction must remain completely untouched while ours is fully controlled' — is what to carry over; the isTrusted implementation is an artifact of being unable to synthesise trusted input. In Electron, invert it: our input is real, so block the USER's input for the recording window and show a visible 'recording' state.

mechanisms.name: SAFETY 3 — hook.js quiet mode: mutating requests, beacons, popups and SPA navigation held for the window
mechanisms.problem: The recorder clicks demo controls, and a click is exactly what sends a POST, fires an analytics beacon, opens a popup, or routes an SPA to another view mid-scan.
mechanisms.how_it_works: content.js quietPage(on) dispatches CustomEvent('aiep:quiet', {detail:'on'|'off'}); hook.js listens through the ORIGINAL addEventListener (routing it through the patched one would file it in the registry it is about to read back) and flips a module flag. Blocks, all installed with mask() so they look native: navigator.sendBeacon → returns true without sending; window.open → returns null; history.pushState/replaceState → return undefined without navigating (a single-page router navigates without ever touching location, so this is the only place that kind of navigation can be stopped); fetch → the METHOD is read from init.method || input.method || 'GET' and, if it matches /^(POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE)$/i, returns held() = `new Promise(() => {})`, a promise that NEVER SETTLES so no error surfaces to the page; XMLHttpRequest → open() records this.__aiepMutating from the method and send() silently returns when quiet. GET/HEAD are deliberately let through untouched: silencing all requests could break the page mid-session, which is a worse bug than the one being avoided. Quiet mode also SELF-EXPIRES after 8000ms on every 'on' (clearTimeout+setTimeout) — if the content script is torn down mid-recording by a navigation or an extension reload, the 'off' never arrives, and a page left permanently unable to send a beacon or open a window would be far worse than the bug being avoided.
mechanisms.location: hook.js:88-170 (quiet mode block), content.js:5656-5659 (quietPage), 5788/5794 (on/off around the phase)
mechanisms.chrome_apis_used: none — pure monkeypatching in the page world
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: MUCH better and out of the page's reach: session.webRequest.onBeforeRequest((details, cb) => cb({cancel: quiet && details.method !== 'GET'})) blocks fetch, XHR, sendBeacon (resourceType 'ping'), form posts and service-worker requests in one place, cannot be un-patched by the page, and covers code paths the monkeypatch misses. window.open → setWindowOpenHandler(()=>({action:'deny'})). Navigation → will-navigate/will-redirect preventDefault. history.pushState is the ONE case with no main-process equivalent (it never hits the network) — keep the preload patch for that, or detect it via 'did-navigate-in-page' and treat it as an abort signal.
mechanisms.port_notes: Keep two design decisions verbatim: (1) draw the line at the HTTP METHOD, not at 'all requests' — reads must go through or the page breaks mid-session; (2) ALWAYS give a global mute a self-expiring timer, because the process that turned it on may never come back to turn it off. In Electron, put the timer in the main process where a renderer crash cannot orphan it. Caveat on held(): a never-settling promise means a page awaiting its own POST hangs that code path for the window — acceptable for 2s, but it is a silent stall, not a clean rejection.

mechanisms.name: SAFETY 4 — samplePhase try/finally teardown and the Escape-only-if-an-overlay-opened rule
mechanisms.problem: A throw anywhere inside the recording must never leave the page carrying our click guard or stuck in quiet mode — either would go on silently breaking the page (programmatic clicks swallowed, beacons dropped) for as long as the tab stays open. And an unconditional Escape closed dialogs the USER had open, leaving the rest of the scan reading a different page.
mechanisms.how_it_works: samplePhase's entire body is `addEventListener×2; quietPage(true); try { return await runPhase(...) } finally { removeEventListener×2; quietPage(false); await waitMs(350) }` — setup and teardown bracket the work, and the 350ms tail lets the spring settle before the next phase. Separately, recordComponentBehavior snapshots overlaysBefore = overlayCount() before the phase ladder, where overlayCount = document.querySelectorAll('dialog[open], [role="dialog"], [role="alertdialog"], [aria-modal="true"]').length, and only if overlayCount() > overlaysBefore afterwards does it dispatch keydown+keyup Escape (key/code 'Escape', keyCode 27, bubbles, cancelable) at document.body. The same try/finally discipline appears at the outer level too: extractUiComponents wraps the whole scan so revealDisclosures() is always undone (leaving a reader's menus hanging open would be worse than the bug the setting fixes).
mechanisms.location: content.js:5772-5798 (try/finally), 5714-5721 (overlayCount), 6146-6155 (Escape rule), 6292-6312 (outer restore)
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: Identical in a preload, plus a main-process backstop: because the main process owns the WebContentsView it can force-clear quiet mode on 'did-navigate', 'render-process-gone' and window close — the extension had to rely on hook.js's 8s timer for exactly this.
mechanisms.port_notes: Generalise the rule to the whole Studio: any global page mutation (quiet mode, input blocking, forced pseudo-states via CSS.forcePseudoState, revealed disclosures) gets (a) a try/finally, (b) a self-expiring timer, and (c) a main-process backstop on renderer death. The 'count before, compare after, only undo what YOU caused' pattern applies verbatim to forced pseudo-states.

mechanisms.name: SAFETY 5 — treating everything from the page's world as hostile input (SAFE_EVENT_RE, source caps, inert())
mechanisms.problem: Handler sources and event names come from the page and end up inside a ` as a listener type would otherwise have that string emitted into the bundle.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Three layers. (1) At the point of crossing: event names must match SAFE_EVENT_RE = /^[A-Za-z][\w.:-]{0,39}$/ — anything else is DROPPED, not escaped, because there is no legitimate `</style>` in an event type; events capped at 20, handlers at 6, each source sliced to 1500 chars, and `on` coerced to one of self|descendant|inline|delegated. (2) At CSS emission: the events comment strips [<>] and neutralises '*/' so the comment cannot be closed. (3) At bundle emission, sidepanel.js componentBundle applies inert(s) = s.replace(/<\/(script|style)/gi,'<\\/$1').replace(/<!--/g,'<\\!--') to the WHOLE style block and the WHOLE handler-reference block — the handlers are shipped as `<script type="text/plain" data-aiep-behavior-reference>` so a developer or an AI porting the component gets the real handlers rather than a guess, and type="text/plain" only stays inert as long as nothing in the body can close the tag, which is why the entire body including event names is escaped. The library-persistence path stores only a SUMMARY of a recording ({key, trigger, count}) because the keyframes already live in `css` and keeping the raw sample series made every saved component several times larger against a 10MB quota.

mechanisms.electron_equivalent: Same escaping is required — more so, since our output goes to real files on disk and into an editor. Storage: Node fs / SQLite in the main process instead of chrome.storage.local, so the 10MB pressure that forced the summary-only persistence disappears and the raw sample series CAN be kept for re-derivation.
mechanisms.port_notes: This is the boundary rule the whole design rests on: the MAIN world is shared with the page, is explicitly NOT a trust boundary, and everything crossing back is validated at the point of USE, not at the point of transfer. Keep it in Electron even though preload feels safer — the page can still patch anything the preload reads out of page objects.

mechanisms.name: Emission — componentCss recorded block and the authored-animation clash guard
mechanisms.problem: The `animation` shorthand RESETS every sub-property it omits. Binding a recorded animation to an element the author already animates stops that animation dead for as long as the state is held, and turns `forwards` into `none` so an element written opacity:0 and revealed by its animation stays invisible.
mechanisms.how_it_works: componentCss assembles, in order: :root variables, a .parent wrapper reproducing the parent's layout, base rules, state rules (with `data-state=open` style triggers rewritten as attribute selectors `[k="v"]` rather than pseudo-classes), then every needed @keyframes emitted exactly once via a seen-Set (both the ones a STATE reaches for — a wave a button plays on hover never runs at rest, so nothing else would collect them — and the ones already running). authoredAnimation(trigger) returns true if any BASE rule declares `animation` OR any STATE rule whose selector contains that trigger declares it — checking only baseRules let a recorded :hover animation replace an authored `.btn:hover { animation: pulse … infinite }`, and the shorthand reset turned the infinite pulse into a single pass frozen on its last frame. Then, for each recorded phase: bindings where b.root is true are DROPPED if authoredAnimation(ph.trigger); only the @keyframes actually referenced by surviving bindings are emitted (used-Set on the first token of the animation shorthand); each binding becomes `${sel}${ph.trigger}${suffix ? ' ' + suffix : ''} { animation: NAME Xs linear both; }`, i.e. the recorded motion is re-attached to the SAME pseudo-class that produced it, so it replays on real hover/press with none of the page's JavaScript. The block is prefixed with an Arabic comment marking it as motion recorded from actually running the page's JS.
mechanisms.location: content.js:6646-6712 (emission), 6542+ (componentCss overall)
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed — this is our own output format.
mechanisms.port_notes: The 'animation shorthand resets what it omits' hazard shows up three separate times in this file and will show up in our builder's style writer too. Prefer emitting longhands (animation-name/-duration/-timing-function/-fill-mode) in generated code so a later rule cannot silently clobber an earlier one.

mechanisms.name: revealDisclosures — opening collapsed widgets WITHOUT clicking (and the class-guessing experiment that failed)
mechanisms.problem: A collapsed dropdown or accordion has no measurable open geometry, so a copied dropdown could never be opened in the user's project.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Off by default (settings.revealCollapsed) because it mutates a page the reader is looking at. Uses only the two switches the platform itself defines: set d.open = true on every `details:not([open])`, and setAttribute('aria-expanded','true') on every `[aria-expanded="false"]` — both are what the site's own CSS keys off and what a screen reader would toggle, so the geometry that comes back is the geometry the site really shows. It NEVER clicks (a click runs the site's handlers, which can navigate, submit or fire analytics). Every mutation pushes an undo closure; the returned restore function replays them in REVERSE. Settling waits on a race between double-rAF and a 120ms setTimeout, whichever lands first, because a background tab never paints and rAF alone would hang the scan with the reader's menus left open. Measured on MDN: 111 collapsed <details> plus 9 aria toggles opened, one element measured 112→400→112px, page returned byte-identical. TRIED AND REJECTED: guessing open classes (adding open/show/active to ancestors) — measured live it opened 3 of 5 panels, failed on one hidden behind a media query that no class can override, and falsely claimed credit for two that were already open. Class-toggled widgets are served instead by ANY_STATE_RE, which captures their open-state CSS without touching the page at all.

The media-query case is a real capability gain in Electron via setEmulatedMedia, and it ties directly to deliverable (d): the desktop/tablet/mobile switcher is the same primitive.

gotchas: MEASURED HEADLINE (kinetics.colorion.co, the recorder's reference page): of 80 components, only 6 record EXPORTABLE motion, while 77 carry real listener metadata. The recorder is a low-yield/high-value pass — budget for a ~7% hit rate on a motion-heavy showcase, and note that the listener metadata (which is nearly universal) is arguably the more valuable output.

FAILED EXPERIMENT #1 — aiming at inner controls instead of the component centre: recorded motion went 6 → 0. FAILED EXPERIMENT #2 — centre first, then retry aimed at the inner trigger: 6 → 1, and this was re-run with a 900-SECOND budget specifically to rule out starvation as the explanation. Root cause: every extra press leaves the page in a state that components recorded AFTER it no longer animate from. Interacting in MORE places per component measurably records LESS. The code therefore hardcodes `aimsFor = () => [null]` (component centre only) with the retry machinery left in place but disabled. Missing coverage must come from recording the trigger elements themselves — they are already separate entries in the component list — not from poking around inside their cards.

GROUND-TRUTH CORRECTION (the most important negative result): the widely-quoted 'hover alone reaches 17 of 26 demos, hover+click reaches 24 of 26' figure — still present as a comment at content.js:6085 justifying the click phase — was measured on whole `.card` UNITS, NOT on the exported component. Much of that motion happens in SIBLINGS outside the pressed element's subtree (e.g. confetti particles appended elsewhere in the DOM) and is therefore not expressible in an exported component at all. Any future coverage work must FIRST re-measure the ceiling on the exported unit. Do not carry 24/26 into the Studio as a target.

DOC/CODE DRIFT in the source: the recorder's section banner at content.js:5599 states rule 1 as "`click` is NEVER dispatched", but the shipped phase ladder DOES dispatch click whenever clickUnsafe() clears the component (justified at content.js:5850 as 'refusing to click at all cost about two thirds of everything worth recording'). Anyone porting from the banner will build the wrong safety model.

In Electron, webContents.sendInputEvent and CDP Input.dispatchMouseEvent produce TRUSTED events. This is a capability upgrade (real hit-testing, real :hover, real drag) but it DESTROYS the isTrusted-based window guard: there is no longer any way to tell our clicks from the user's inside the page, and a trusted click really navigates and really submits. Safety must move to session.webRequest.onBeforeRequest (cancel non-GET), will-navigate/will-redirect preventDefault, setWindowOpenHandler deny, and blocking real user input for the recording window via 'before-input-event'.

Any wait on requestAnimationFrame alone hangs forever in a non-painting context. The file races rAF against setTimeout in THREE places (nextFrame 40ms, revealDisclosures 120ms, drive completion) and each one was added after a real hang. In Electron this is mitigated by webPreferences.backgroundThrottling:false and paintWhenInitiallyHidden:true, but keep the races.

Any global page mutation needs a self-expiring timer, because the process that turned it on may never come back to turn it off. hook.js quiet mode auto-clears after 8000ms specifically for the case where the content script is torn down mid-recording by a navigation or extension reload — a page permanently unable to send a beacon or open a window would be far worse than the bug being avoided.

Budgets and caps, all measured: pass2Ms 8000 (then degrade with truncated=true, never hang); recordBudgetMs 90000; recordLimit 16 components; probeLimit 300 for the registry query; registry reply timeout 500ms; phase durations hover 1200 / press 1100 / click 2000 / drag 1600 ms; 180ms hold between pointerdown and pointerup; 350ms inter-phase settle; 180ms after scrollIntoView; early bail at driveDone+450ms with no observed change; effDur = clamp(200, durMs, lastSampleT+60); 32 watched nodes; 26 decimated frames; 22 recorded properties; 60 nodes scanned by clickUnsafe; 30 listeners per (target,type) in hook.js; 12 handlers per element; 40 descendants per element in the registry; handler source 4000 chars in-page, 1500 crossing, 1200 persisted.

Sampling cost: 22 properties × up to 32 nodes × ~70 frames ≈ 50,000 getPropertyValue calls per phase, each forcing style recalculation. That is the entire budget of the pass. Do NOT move sampling out-of-process to CDP CSS.getComputedStyleForNode — it is far slower. Sample in-page, stream once over IPC.

Dedup signature tuning is a minefield with hard numbers attached: motion-only signature grows MDN 0% and recovers kinetics 7→144 cards; adding structure UNCONDITIONALLY inflates MDN by 62-74%; adding descendant COUNT to the key inflates MDN by 61%. Only escalate to the structural key for a group already proven (>=3 distinct motion signatures) to be a gallery of effects.

paintScore's furniture penalty is measured against the VIEWPORT, and the viewport shrinks when a panel opens — a gallery card then clears 40% of it, takes -8, and fails the score gate, while the buttons inside it score 16 and fill the list (kinetics: 8 of 144 cards survived before the fix; after adding the repeatedItem exemption, 144 of 144, and the list grew 161→249, while MDN as a control stayed at 4→4). Any threshold built on viewport area is inherently unstable — in Electron, hold the WebContentsView bounds constant during a scan.

Ordering accepted components by a pairwise 'is-an-ancestor' comparator is NOT transitive and Array.sort mangles it. Precompute __depth = number of other accepted components above the element, then sort by (depth asc, rank desc). Measured effect of doing it properly: the XY Pad card moved 159→48 and its 26px puck 1→174; the first non-card fell to position 144.

A signal used as a FILTER instead of as an ORDERING silently turns a whole feature into a no-op for entire families of pages: filtering the record queue by JS-signal excluded every component inside a shadow root and every framework that delegates from its own root rather than from document. Signals order; they never gate admission.

The `animation` CSS shorthand resets every sub-property it omits. This caused three separate shipped bugs: an authored `infinite` pulse became a single frozen pass; an element written `opacity:0` and revealed by its animation stayed invisible when `forwards` was reset to `none`; and a recorded animation bound via a structural selector killed the authored animation on that one element while its siblings kept it (one letter of a word disappeared and the rest did not). Emit longhands in generated code.

CSS synthesises a MISSING 100% keyframe from the element's resting style. Without the explicit pinned 100% stop (settled values), a recorded hover animation with `both` fill runs backwards to base and holds there — the hover visibly undoes itself while still hovered.

A shorthand declaration containing a var() (`border: 4px solid var(--line)`) returns 15 EMPTY longhands from the CSSOM and cssText emits invalid `border-top-width: ;` — and no shorthand recovers the value (border, border-width, border-style, border-color all return ""). The fix fills gaps from getComputedStyle of a matching element — but you must NOT pass a sample element for STATE rules, because reading a :hover rule off an element that is not hovered yields resting values and corrupts the export.

Coverage aliasing must be an explicit table, not first-hyphen-segment matching: the prefix shortcut let `border-color` cover `border-radius` and `transform-origin` cover `transform`, deleting real recorded motion from the export.

Selector-subject matters: in `.card:hover .icon { transform }` the SUBJECT is `.icon`, so treating that rule as covering the card's own recorded transform threw away real motion; and testing merely 'the pseudo appears somewhere in the selector' let any descendant's hover rule do the same. Coverage suppression must additionally apply to the ROOT NODE ONLY — filtering child nodes on the root's state rules discarded exactly the JS-driven motion the recorder exists to catch.
Class matching must be on WORDS, never substrings: substring matching read the 'item' inside Tailwind's `items-center` and filed every flex wrapper on the page as a card.
Dedup signatures must exclude analytics/utility classes (e.g. `plausible-event-effect=Card+Resize`) — they are unique per instance and defeat deduplication entirely, flooding the list with copies.

REJECTED experiment: guessing open-state class names (adding .open/.show/.active to ancestors) to reveal collapsed widgets. Measured live it opened 3 of 5 panels, failed entirely on one hidden behind a media query that no class can override, and falsely claimed credit for two panels that were already open. Use only platform-defined switches (details.open, aria-expanded) and let ANY_STATE_RE capture class-toggled open states from CSS without touching the page.

State-detection regexes must EXCLUDE bare `.open`, `.active`, `.show`, `.selected`: half the web uses them for the current tab or nav link, and moving those rules out of the resting set leaves ordinary elements previewing unstyled. Only compounded markers (`.nav-dropdown.open`) count. Measured widening was 1.95% of rules on kinetics and 1.68% on MDN, all genuine, zero false positives.

hook.js registry memory rules, each learned from a leak: `once:true` listeners must NOT be stored (the browser removes them without calling removeEventListener, so they pin dead closures AND the per-type cap then rejects live listeners); AbortSignal cleanup must hold a WeakRef to the target (a long-lived signal otherwise retains every element it ever saw, detached nodes included); cap each (target,type) Set at 30 against pages that re-bind in a loop.

Delegated handlers must be collected ONCE per query from document/window/body/documentElement, not rebuilt per element — rebuilding turned a scan of a delegation-heavy SPA into a multi-second freeze. Also filter out your own listener types from the reply: attributing them to the page as its 'real JavaScript' poisons the click-safety check, since the delegated-attribution test is a substring match and this codebase contains words like 'list', 'data' and 'name' that half the web uses as class names.

The MAIN world is explicitly NOT a trust boundary — a hostile page can read, patch or impersonate anything in it, and the query nonce is for correlation (spotting a stale reply), not for trust. Everything crossing back must be validated at the point of USE: event names are DROPPED unless they match /^[A-Za-z][\w.:-]{0,39}$/ rather than escaped, because there is no legitimate `</style>` in an event type, and the whole style block plus the whole handler-reference block get a `</script`/`</style`/`<!--` escape before landing in an artifact the user pastes.

hook.js's native-function masking (redefining name/length/toString to report '[native code]') defeats the common `.toString().includes('[native code]')` probe but Function.prototype.toString.call() still sees through it — the file says so plainly rather than papering over it. Do not oversell it as stealth.

Blocked fetch returns `new Promise(() => {})` — a promise that never settles, so no error surfaces to the page. The trade-off is a silent stall: a page awaiting its own POST hangs that code path for the whole recording window. Acceptable at ~2s, but it is a hang, not a clean rejection.

A never-audited audit is worse than none: an earlier verification harness extracted `.card` elements directly instead of going through the real extraction pipeline, so it reported 120/144 passing while the user was looking at empty previews. Any Studio verification must run the ACTUAL pipeline (all three passes plus the ordering), not a hand-picked element set. That same harness also reported 144 phantom defects on its first run because the site's styles had not loaded in headless Chrome — it now waits for the rule count to stabilise across 4 identical reads, does a sanity check before starting, and uses a real user-agent. And comparing a moving page against a fresh preview requires freezing animations on BOTH sides via getAnimations().forEach(a => { a.currentTime = 0; a.pause() }) — TWICE (after 60ms then 40ms); a single freeze left 5 phantom differences.

subsystem: hook.js — MAIN-world listener registry, quiet-mode side-effect suppressor, and the cross-world bridge (E:\exten Picker\hook.js, 281 lines / 12 KB), plus its isolated-world consumers in content.js
summary: hook.js is a single IIFE injected at document_start into the page's OWN JavaScript world. It monkey-patches EventTarget.prototype.addEventListener/removeEventListener so every listener the page ever registers is recorded in a WeakMap registry keyed by target, capturing each handler's SOURCE TEXT via String(fn). On demand it answers a nonce-correlated CustomEvent query from the isolated content script with a JSON string describing which events and which handler sources are wired to a set of DOM-tagged elements — including a heuristic resolution of framework event delegation. It additionally installs a "quiet mode" that, for a bounded window, suppresses only the calls whose whole purpose is an outward side effect (sendBeacon, window.open, mutating fetch/XHR, history.pushState) so the motion recorder can safely synthesise clicks. The author explicitly documents that this file is NOT a trust boundary — it shares a world with the page, so everything crossing to the isolated world is treated as untrusted and re-sanitised at point of use.

mechanisms.name: The world-split premise — why the bridge exists at all
mechanisms.problem: An extension content script runs in an ISOLATED world: it shares the DOM (same C++ Node objects) but has a completely separate JavaScript heap, separate globals, and separate function identities from the page. Listener registration lives in Blink's internal EventTarget listener table, which is NOT exposed to any JS API. There is no `getEventListeners()` outside DevTools. So from the isolated world, `document.querySelector('button')` returns the same element the page has, but there is literally no expression that can ask 'what handlers are on this?' — every naive inventory reports zero listeners on every element, on every site.
mechanisms.how_it_works: The only way to observe registration from JS is to be present in the page's own world BEFORE the page registers anything, and to intercept the registration API itself. manifest.json declares TWO content_scripts entries against <all_urls>: hook.js at {run_at:'document_start', world:'MAIN'} and content.js at {run_at:'document_idle'} (default ISOLATED world). Chrome guarantees the MAIN-world document_start script is evaluated before the first page <script> executes, which is the entire load-bearing property: a patch installed one tick later misses every listener a framework binds during hydration.
mechanisms.location: E:\exten Picker\hook.js:1-21 (header + install); E:\exten Picker\manifest.json content_scripts block
mechanisms.chrome_apis_used: manifest content_scripts with world:'MAIN' + run_at:'document_start'; the isolated-world default for the second entry
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: Three options, all strictly better than the extension's: (1) `webPreferences.preload` on the WebContentsView/<webview> — the preload module is evaluated before ANY page script AND has Node.js require available, which no content script ever had; with contextIsolation:true the preload itself is in an isolated world, so it calls `webFrame.executeJavaScript(src, false)` to land code in the page's MAIN world. (2) CDP `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument({source})` via `webContents.debugger` — this is the exact 1:1 semantic of world:'MAIN' + document_start, applied automatically to every future navigation and every frame, driven from the main process with zero preload file. (3) `contextIsolation:false` on the guest webContents, making the preload itself main-world (only acceptable for our own generated localhost projects, never for arbitrary remote pages).
mechanisms.port_notes: The premise survives but the constraint that forced it does not. In Electron we ALSO have webContents.debugger → DOMDebugger.getEventListeners, which reads Blink's listener table directly from OUTSIDE the renderer — the thing that did not exist for the extension. See the PORT DECISION mechanism. Recommendation: keep a main-world injected script for the things only in-page code can do, but stop using it as the listener inventory source.

mechanisms.name: document_start install with a cross-realm re-entry guard
mechanisms.problem: The same script can be evaluated more than once in one document — same-document navigations, an extension reload, a manual re-injection, or (in Electron) both a preload and a CDP addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument firing. Patching addEventListener twice creates a wrapper-of-a-wrapper: every listener is then double-registered in the registry, and the 30-per-type cap silently starts rejecting real listeners.
mechanisms.how_it_works: `const MARK = Symbol.for('aiep.hook'); if (window[MARK]) return;` then `Object.defineProperty(window, MARK, {value:true, enumerable:false})` with a plain-assignment fallback in a try/catch. Two deliberate choices: Symbol.for (the GLOBAL symbol registry) rather than a private Symbol, so a second evaluation in the same realm resolves the identical symbol; and enumerable:false so the marker never shows up in a page's `for…in` / `Object.keys(window)` enumeration or in the extension's own window-property scans.

mechanisms.port_notes: Note: in Electron, if you inject via webFrame.executeJavaScript from a context-isolated preload, `window` inside the injected code is the PAGE's window, which is the realm you want to mark. mechanisms.name: The addEventListener / removeEventListener monkey-patch with native-toString masking
mechanisms.problem: Two problems at once. (1) Capture every listener registration without changing observable behaviour. (2) Not get caught: a page (or an anti-bot script, or a framework's own feature detection) that sees `EventTarget.prototype.addEventListener.toString()` return something other than native code may take a different code path, refuse to boot, or fingerprint the visitor.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Two closures replace the prototype methods. `patchedAdd(type, fn, opts)` does its bookkeeping inside a try/catch that swallows everything, then unconditionally `return origAdd.call(this, type, fn, opts)` — the patch can never change the page's behaviour even if the bookkeeping throws. `patchedRemove` calls `forget(this, type, fn)` then delegates identically. Before installation both wrappers go through `mask(fn, name, arity)`, which redefines three own-properties: `name` (so `patchedAdd.name === 'addEventListener'`), `length` (arity 2 — the number of declared params differs from the rest arg / actual signature), and an own `toString` returning the literal string `"function addEventListener() { [native code] }"`. This defeats the standard probe `String(el.addEventListener).includes('[native code]')` and `.toString()` calls. The author documents in a comment (lines 23-26) that `Function.prototype.toString.call(patchedAdd)` still sees through it, and states this plainly rather than papering over it — there is no way to fake a native function's Function.prototype.toString result from JS.

mechanisms.electron_equivalent: Identical JS, injected via preload+webFrame.executeJavaScript or CDP Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument. BUT: in Electron the masking is largely unnecessary for deliverable (d), because the pages the mini-browser runs are OUR OWN generated projects on localhost — there is no adversary fingerprinting us. Keep the mask only for the (c) picker path if it is ever pointed at arbitrary remote sites.
mechanisms.port_notes: For the mini-browser (d) I would DROP the mask entirely (it is pure defensive complexity against a threat we removed) and keep the try/catch-then-always-delegate discipline, which is real robustness, not stealth. For the picker (c) on remote pages, prefer CDP getEventListeners — which requires NO patch at all and therefore no mask and no detectability, since it reads Blink's table from another process.

mechanisms.name: The registry data structure and the CAP LADDER (the mis-documented 'cap type')
mechanisms.problem: A registry that holds strong references to DOM nodes and closures for the life of a page is a guaranteed memory leak on any long-lived SPA. A page that re-binds listeners in a render loop (React re-rendering, a mousemove handler rebound per frame) would grow one Set unboundedly. And a query that walks an unbounded subtree with unbounded source strings turns a scan of a large SPA into a multi-second main-thread freeze.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
Structure is `WeakMap<EventTarget, Map<string type, Set<Function handler>>>` — the outer WeakMap means a detached node's entire listener record is collectable with the node; the inner Map/Set are strongly held only as long as the target is. Then a ladder of hard numeric caps, each with a stated reason:
  • 30 handlers per (target, type) — `if (set.size < 30) set.add(fn)`; a re-binding loop is capped, and the FIRST 30 are kept (not the last), so the initial framework wiring survives.
  • 4000 chars per handler source string.
  • 12 handlers total reported per queried element.
  • 40 nodes walked per queried element (self + first 39 descendants).
  • shadow-root sweep depth 6.
  • 300 elements probed per scan (content.js `opts.probeLimit`).
  • 500 ms reply timeout on the isolated side.
Then the isolated world RE-clamps everything it receives: 20 events, 6 handlers, 1500 chars per source.
IMPORTANT: Tree-Project.md line 25 says hook.js 'Defines: cap type' — that is a doc-generator mis-parse of the prose comment 'the 30-per-type cap' at hook.js:52. There is no symbol or type named `cap` in the file. The real 'cap type' is this numeric ladder.

mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed. The caps are MORE important in Electron, not less: the mini-browser keeps one webContents alive across many navigations of a generated project, so a leaking registry accumulates for the whole session rather than until the next tab close.
mechanisms.port_notes: Port the ladder verbatim but re-tune two numbers for the CDP route: `DOMDebugger.getEventListeners({depth:-1, pierce:true})` returns the WHOLE subtree in one call, so the 40-node walk cap becomes a post-filter on the returned array rather than a walk limit, and the 12-handler cap should be applied per-node not per-component (CDP gives you backendNodeId per listener, so you can attribute precisely).

mechanisms.name: once-listener exclusion and AbortSignal cleanup via WeakRef
mechanisms.problem: Listeners registered with `{once:true}` and listeners bound to an AbortSignal are removed by the browser WITHOUT ever calling removeEventListener. The registry's only eviction path is patchedRemove, so those records would be pinned forever: dead closures held for the life of the page, and — worse — they consume slots in the 30-per-type cap, so a page that binds many one-shot listeners would start REJECTING its live ones. Naively fixing this by keeping a strong reference to the target inside the abort handler is itself the leak: a long-lived AbortSignal (an app-lifetime controller) would hold every element it ever saw a listener added to, detached nodes included.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
Two separate fixes.
  • `once` is detected as `!!(opts && typeof opts === 'object' && opts.once)` and the listener is NOT registered at all — it is skipped outright, not registered-then-evicted.
  • For `opts.signal`, the hook attaches its own abort handler THROUGH THE ORIGINAL `origAdd.call(signal, 'abort', …, {once:true})`, and captures the target through a WeakRef: `const ref = typeof WeakRef === 'function' ? new WeakRef(this) : {deref: () => this}` — the object-literal fallback preserves the API shape on engines without WeakRef while accepting the leak there. On abort it does `const t = ref.deref(); if (t) forget(t, type, fn);` — if the element is already collected there is nothing to clean and nothing was pinned.
mechanisms.location: E:\exten Picker\hook.js:50-73
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed — identical.
mechanisms.port_notes: This is where the monkey-patch has a REAL, measurable blind spot the port should fix: a component whose entire behaviour is a `{once:true}` listener reports ZERO listeners, which downstream causes clickUnsafe() to return true (no readable handlers → refuse to click) and the component is silently never recorded. CDP `DOMDebugger.getEventListeners` returns once-listeners with an explicit `once: true` boolean and does NOT have this blind spot. In the hybrid design, CDP supplies the inventory (once included) and the injected patch is no longer the source of truth, so the exclusion becomes harmless bookkeeping.

mechanisms.name: Handler SOURCE capture via String(fn) with a WeakMap memo — and why minification does not defeat it
mechanisms.problem: Knowing THAT a button has a click listener is nearly useless. The downstream recorder needs to decide 'is it safe to synthetically click this?' and the code generator needs to know what the handler DOES. Both need the handler's text. On real sites that text is minified — variable names are mangled to single letters.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
`handlerSource(fn)` = `String(fn).slice(0, 4000)` (i.e. Function.prototype.toString on the page's own closure — which the isolated world could never call, because it never holds a reference to that function object), memoised in a `WeakMap<Function,string>` so a handler shared across 200 delegated bindings is stringified once. Unreadable functions (native/bound) fall back to the literal `'[unreadable]'`.
The non-obvious insight — stated as the 'hidden advantage' in IDEAS.md #13 — is that MINIFICATION CANNOT MANGLE THE THINGS THAT MATTER. A bundler renames locals, but it can never rename `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `sendBeacon`, `localStorage`, `document.cookie`, `classList`, `aria-expanded`, `preventDefault` — those are global identifiers, property names and string literals, and renaming them would break the program. So a regex over minified handler source that matches PROPERTY and GLOBAL names is robust on production sites, while any approach based on identifier names collapses. That is why the whole safety gate is built on this and not on AST analysis.

And `Debugger.scriptParsed` events carry `sourceMapURL` — with the source map you recover the ORIGINAL unminified TypeScript/JSX, not the mangled output.

mechanisms.name: The cross-world transport: DOM-attribute tagging + nonce-correlated CustomEvent carrying a JSON STRING
mechanisms.problem: MAIN world and isolated world share the DOM but not the JS heap. The isolated script cannot pass an element reference into the MAIN world, cannot receive an object back, and has no callback channel. Worse: a structured `detail` on a CustomEvent constructed in the MAIN world does NOT survive being read from the isolated world (the detail reads as null / is not cloned across worlds). Only primitives — in practice, strings — cross reliably.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
A four-step handshake, batched to exactly ONE roundtrip per scan:
  1. Isolated side (`queryListenerRegistry(els)`, content.js:6144) walks the candidate elements, skips `!el.isConnected`, and stamps each with `el.setAttribute('data-aiep-q', 'q' + i)` — the DOM attribute IS the shared address space, since the DOM is the only thing both worlds see.
  2. It generates `nonce = 'n' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2,10)`, registers a `aiep:listeners:reply` listener, arms a 500 ms `setTimeout` that resolves the promise EMPTY (never hangs), and dispatches `new CustomEvent('aiep:listeners:query', {detail: nonce})`.
  3. MAIN side finds all `[data-aiep-q]` elements, builds the report keyed by that attribute value, and replies with `document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('aiep:listeners:reply', {detail: JSON.stringify({nonce, data})}))` — a STRING, explicitly because a structured detail does not survive the boundary (comment at hook.js:188-191).
  4. Isolated side JSON.parses, discards any reply whose `parsed.nonce !== nonce` (a stale answer from an earlier query), then in a `finished`-guarded `fin()` removes every `data-aiep-q` attribute and resolves a `Map<Element, info>` — re-associating string IDs back to live element references on its own side.
The nonce is explicitly documented as CORRELATION, NOT TRUST (hook.js:190-191): it discriminates stale replies, it proves nothing about who sent the reply, since the page can read the query nonce and forge a reply.
Note also that hook.js registers its own two listeners through `origAdd.call(document, …)` (lines 103, 192) — routing them through the patched method would file them into the very registry it is about to read back.
A SECOND, different channel exists for the network capture: background.js's NET_INTERCEPTOR uses `window.postMessage({__aiPickerNet:true, rec}, '*')` and content.js filters on `e.source !== window` (content.js:2518). Two channels, two shapes, both string/structured-clone-limited — evidence of how awkward this boundary is.

mechanisms.name: Shadow-DOM-piercing sweep for tagged elements
mechanisms.problem: `document.querySelectorAll('[data-aiep-q]')` stops dead at every shadow boundary. Any component inside a shadow root (every web-component-based design system) was never found by the query, reported zero listeners, and was consequently skipped by the recorder entirely.

mechanisms.name: Event-delegation resolution by class-token substring match (IDEAS.md #13)
mechanisms.problem: THE central problem of listener inventory on the modern web. React, Vue, Svelte, jQuery and every design system bind ONE listener at the app root (document, window, body, or their own container) and dispatch internally by matching the event target. So a naive inventory says 'this button has no listeners' in essentially 100% of cases on framework sites. Without solving this, the whole subsystem reports nothing useful.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
A two-phase heuristic.
  Phase 1 — collect delegated handlers ONCE per query, not once per element. It reads the registry for exactly four targets — `document`, `window`, `document.body`, `document.documentElement` — and flattens them into a `delegated[]` array of `{type, source}`. The comment records the reason this is hoisted out of the per-element loop: rebuilding it per element 'turned a scan of a delegation-heavy SPA into a multi-second freeze'. It also skips any `type.startsWith('aiep:')` so the extension's OWN two listeners on document are not attributed to the page as its real JavaScript — and the stated reason is that the class-token test below is a SUBSTRING match, and hook.js's own source contains common words like `list`, `data` and `name` that half the web uses as class names, so self-attribution would produce a flood of false positives.
  Phase 2 — link a delegated handler back to a specific element. The only usable evidence available is the element's own class names appearing as literals inside the handler's source. It extracts tokens matching `/^[a-zA-Z_][\w-]{2,}$/` from `el.classList` (identifier-like, at least 3 chars — filters out `a`, `p1`, numeric utility noise), then for each delegated handler tests `classTokens.some(c => d.source.includes(c))`. A match adds the event type to the element's event set and pushes the handler with `on: 'delegated'`.
The author labels this a heuristic in-comment (lines 257-259) and the label propagates into the data as the `on` field, which is what makes the downstream safety gate able to distrust it specifically.
IDEAS.md #13 proposes the STRONGER version that was NOT built: dispatch a synthetic event at the element and observe which registered handler actually EXECUTES (by wrapping each handler function), giving a definitive answer instead of an inference — then classify what the handler did into known primitive actions (class toggle, aria-expanded flip, preventDefault, form submit) and emit working code for those.
mechanisms.location: E:\exten Picker\hook.js:198-212 (collection), 257-269 (resolution); E:\exten Picker\IDEAS.md:306-324
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: CDP does NOT solve this either — `getEventListeners` on a button correctly reports zero listeners when the framework delegates from the root, because that is the truth. CDP tells you the delegated root listener exists and gives you its exact scriptId/line, which is strictly more than the extension had, but the ATTRIBUTION problem is unchanged. The definitive route in Electron: inject a main-world wrapper that instruments handler invocation (IDEAS #13's 'direct testing'), OR use CDP `DOMDebugger.setEventListenerBreakpoint({eventName:'click'})` + `Debugger.paused` to see exactly which handler frame is entered — authoritative, but it pauses the page, so it is only usable inside a controlled recorder window.
mechanisms.port_notes: Port the class-token heuristic as the cheap fallback, but BUILD IDEAS #13's execution-witness as the primary. In Electron it is far easier than it was in the extension: from a preload-injected main-world shim, wrap every registered handler in a proxy that reports `{handlerId, eventTargetPath, tookTime}` over ipcRenderer when it fires, then dispatch a synthetic event and read the witness list. For deliverable (d) — running OUR generated projects — this is near-perfect because we control the code and can even emit stable handler IDs at build time. Also worth doing: `getEventListeners` on document/window in Electron gives us the delegated root handler's scriptId, so with a source map we can recover the framework's actual dispatch table rather than substring-matching class names.

mechanisms.name: Quiet mode — bounded side-effect suppression with a dead-man timer
mechanisms.problem: The motion recorder needs to synthesise real clicks on real page controls to capture JS-driven animation that no stylesheet contains. A real click on a real site sends analytics beacons, opens popups, POSTs form data, and navigates a SPA router. All of those are outward side effects performed on the user's behalf without the user's intent. Blocking EVERYTHING instead is worse: a page starved of its reads breaks mid-session, which is a more damaging bug than the one being avoided.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
A boolean `quiet` toggled by a `aiep:quiet` CustomEvent with detail 'on'/'off' (dispatched by content.js `quietPage()` at content.js:5656), registered via `origAdd` so it is not filed into the registry. Then five surgical patches, each chosen by a stated rule — patch ONLY calls whose entire purpose is an effect outside this page:
  • `navigator.sendBeacon` → returns `true` (the success value) while quiet, so the caller sees no failure.
  • `window.open` → returns `null` while quiet.
  • `window.fetch` → reads the method from `init.method || input.method || 'GET'`, tests it against `/^(POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE)$/i`, and if quiet+mutating returns `held()` = `new Promise(() => {})`, a promise that NEVER SETTLES. This is the sharpest trick in the file: rejecting would surface an error the page might display to the user or retry; a never-settling promise makes the request simply not happen, with no error path taken. GET/HEAD pass through untouched, so page reads keep working.
  • `XMLHttpRequest.prototype.open` stamps `this.__aiepMutating` from the same regex; `send` silently returns without calling through when quiet+mutating.
  • `history.pushState` / `replaceState` → no-op while quiet, because a single-page router navigates without ever touching `location`, so this is the ONLY place that kind of navigation can be stopped.
The dead-man timer is the safety property: `if (quiet) quietTimer = setTimeout(() => { quiet = false; }, 8000)`. If the content script is torn down mid-recording — navigation, extension reload — the 'off' event never arrives, and a page left permanently unable to send a beacon or open a window would be a far worse bug than the one being avoided. The isolated side reinforces this with a try/finally in `samplePhase` (content.js:5788-5796) that always calls `quietPage(false)`.

(2) `window.open` → `contents.setWindowOpenHandler(() => ({action:'deny'}))` — a first-class Electron API, page-proof. (3) `history.pushState`/`replaceState` → NO out-of-page equivalent exists; `webContents.on('did-navigate-in-page')` detects it but cannot prevent it, so this ONE patch must stay in the injected main-world script.

Also keep the never-settling-promise trick if you do keep any in-page fetch patch; it is the correct choice over reject() and is not obvious.

mechanisms.name: The payoff: clickUnsafe() — a safety gate that reads handler source before allowing a synthetic click
mechanisms.problem: The recorder must click things to capture motion, but a click is what deletes accounts, submits forms, buys things and logs users out. Label heuristics alone are not enough — a button labelled 'Try it' can fire a DELETE. This is the single mechanism that justifies hook.js's entire existence: the handler SOURCE is the evidence that lets an automated system prove a control is inert.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
`clickUnsafe(el, behavior)` returns true (refuse) unless every check clears, and the try/catch's catch returns TRUE — fail-closed by construction. Order:
  1. `el.closest('form')` → unsafe. Any ancestor form at all.
  2. Walk `[el, ...el.querySelectorAll('*')].slice(0,60)` — the whole subtree, because the synthetic event is aimed at whatever `elementFromPoint` returns, which is almost always a descendant, not the vetted root. Within it: any `<A href>` → unsafe; any BUTTON/INPUT with type submit|reset → unsafe; any inline `on*` ATTRIBUTE whose value matches EFFECT_RE → unsafe.
  3. `pressUnsafe(el)` — tests the first 160 chars of aria-label + textContent against a bilingual DESTRUCTIVE_RE covering delete/remove/discard/clear/reset/logout/buy/purchase/checkout/pay/order/subscribe/confirm/submit/publish/archive AND their Arabic equivalents (احذف، حذف، إزالة، شراء، ادفع، إرسال، تأكيد، اشتراك، خروج).
  4. THE HOOK.JS-DEPENDENT STEP: `const readable = (behavior?.handlers || []).filter(h => h.on !== 'delegated')`. If `readable.length === 0` → UNSAFE. No handler to read means nothing to clear it with. Delegated handlers are excluded specifically because they are a whole framework bundle and say nothing about THIS element — the heuristic that was good enough to rank a component is explicitly not good enough to authorise a click.
  5. Any readable handler source matching EFFECT_RE → unsafe. EFFECT_RE = /\bfetch\s*\(|XMLHttpRequest|sendBeacon|window\.open|location\s*\.\s*(href|assign|replace)|location\s*=|\.submit\s*\(|\.click\s*\(|history\s*\.\s*(pushState|replaceState)|localStorage|sessionStorage|indexedDB|document\.cookie|navigator\.clipboard/ — every token in it is a global or property name that a minifier CANNOT rename, which is why this survives on production sites.
The stated principle: 'A handler whose source contains none of them cannot delete, buy, navigate or persist anything, however it is written.'

But the INPUT gets much better: with CDP + source maps the gate reads the original authored source instead of minified text, so EFFECT_RE can be replaced by a real AST/import analysis for our own projects. That string would then flow into the extension's generated CSS/@keyframes and into the HTML bundle the user copies out and pastes into their own project — an injection whose payload traverses from a scanned website into the developer's codebase.

The isolated side never trusts a field. `SAFE_EVENT_RE = /^[A-Za-z][\w.:-]{0,39}$/` — 'Event names are identifiers.
