mechanisms.name: PORT DECISION — preload monkey-patch vs CDP getEventListeners vs hybrid
mechanisms.problem: Deciding which of the three routes deliverable (d) the mini-browser (and (c) the picker behind it) should use to know what JavaScript is wired to an element in a page it is hosting.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
WHAT CDP GIVES THAT THE MONKEY-PATCH CANNOT:
  1. It reads Blink's actual listener table from OUTSIDE the renderer process. The page cannot detect it, cannot un-patch it, cannot poison it. The monkey-patch is defeatable — the author documents that `Function.prototype.toString.call()` sees through the mask (hook.js:23-26), and a page that re-assigns `EventTarget.prototype.addEventListener` after us silently blinds the whole registry.
  2. IDL property handlers. `el.onclick = fn` never calls addEventListener, so hook.js is completely blind to it — it only scans inline `on*` ATTRIBUTES (hook.js:249-254), a different thing. CDP reports property handlers.
  3. `once:true` listeners, which hook.js deliberately does not record at all (hook.js:55-56) and which therefore make a component read as 'no listeners' → clickUnsafe refuses → never recorded. CDP returns them with an explicit `once` flag.
  4. `useCapture` and `passive` flags per listener — hook.js discards them entirely.
  5. `scriptId` + `lineNumber` + `columnNumber` per listener. With `Debugger.getScriptSource` this yields the enclosing scope and sibling helpers, not just the function text; with `Debugger.scriptParsed`'s `sourceMapURL` it yields the ORIGINAL TypeScript/JSX. String(fn) can never do this.
  6. Listeners registered BEFORE we were present, and listeners from any source (including framework internals that hold their own reference to the native addEventListener).
  7. `depth:-1, pierce:true` walks the whole subtree including open shadow roots in ONE command, replacing the hand-rolled depth-6 sweep and the 40-node cap.
  8. `backendNodeId` per listener — precise attribution of which node each listener sits on, across the process boundary, replacing the `data-aiep-q` attribute-stamping hack entirely.
WHAT THE MONKEY-PATCH GIVES THAT CDP CANNOT:
  1. Suppression. CDP cannot make `history.pushState` a no-op. (sendBeacon/fetch/window.open all have better out-of-page Electron answers, but pushState does not.)
  2. Execution witness. CDP cannot observe which handler actually RAN without pausing the page (`DOMDebugger.setEventListenerBreakpoint` + `Debugger.paused` works but stops the world). An in-page wrapper reports 'this handler fired for this target' with zero pause — which is precisely IDEAS #13's definitive answer to delegation.
  3. Zero attach cost and no client conflict. Only ONE debugger client may attach to a webContents; `webContents.debugger.attach()` throws if DevTools is open on that guest, and the reverse also bites. An injected script has no such exclusivity.
  4. Synchronous in-page availability during a recording tick, with no async main↔renderer roundtrip per sample.
THE DECISION — HYBRID, with a clean split of duties:
  • CDP (`webContents.debugger.attach('1.3')` → `DOM.enable`, `Runtime.enable`, `Debugger.enable`; then `DOM.getDocument` → `DOM.querySelectorAll` → `DOM.resolveNode` → `DOMDebugger.getEventListeners({objectId, depth:-1, pierce:true})`, and `Debugger.getScriptSource({scriptId})` for source) is the SOURCE OF TRUTH for the listener inventory and for handler source. Nothing else can see once/passive/capture/IDL handlers or reach the original unminified source.
  • A preload-injected main-world script (via `webFrame.executeJavaScript(src, false)` from a contextIsolation:true preload, or CDP `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` which needs no preload file at all) keeps EXACTLY TWO jobs: the history.pushState/replaceState suppression, and the handler-execution witness that resolves delegation definitively. Nothing else.
  • The main process owns the rest of quiet mode out-of-page: `session.webRequest.onBeforeRequest` cancelling non-GET (and resourceType 'ping') while recording, and `contents.setWindowOpenHandler(() => ({action:'deny'}))`.
  • The whole CustomEvent/JSON-string/nonce/data-aiep-q transport is deleted; results come back as structured values from `webContents.executeJavaScript`, `ipcRenderer.invoke`, or CDP command replies.
WHY HYBRID AND NOT PURE CDP: because IDEAS #13's core insight — that only direct observation of execution definitively resolves delegation — is the highest-value idea in the whole prior art, and CDP cannot do it without pausing. WHY NOT PURE MONKEY-PATCH: because for deliverable (d) we own the pages, we ship the source maps, and CDP hands us back the authored TypeScript of every handler — which is exactly what deliverable (a) the builder needs to emit code we own.

gotchas: Tree-Project.md line 25 claims hook.js 'Defines: cap type'. That is a doc-generator mis-parse of the prose comment 'the 30-per-type cap' at hook.js:52. There is NO symbol, type, or function named `cap` anywhere in the file. Do not go looking for it. The real 'cap type' is a ladder of hard numeric limits: 30 handlers per (target,type); 4000 chars per handler source; 12 handlers reported per element; 40 nodes walked per element; shadow sweep depth 6; 300 elements probed per scan; 500 ms reply timeout; then re-clamped on the isolated side to 20 events / 6 handlers / 1500 chars.

MEASURED BLIND SPOT #1 — `{once:true}` listeners are deliberately never registered (hook.js:55-56, to avoid pinning dead closures and starving the 30-cap). Consequence: a component whose behaviour is entirely a one-shot listener reports zero handlers, `clickUnsafe()` hits its 'no readable handlers → unsafe' rule (content.js:5704-5705), and the component is silently never recorded. CDP `DOMDebugger.getEventListeners` returns once-listeners with an explicit `once` flag and closes this hole.

MEASURED BLIND SPOT #2 — IDL property handlers (`el.onclick = fn`) never pass through addEventListener and are invisible to the registry. hook.js only scans inline `on*` ATTRIBUTES (hook.js:249-254), which is a different mechanism. CDP sees both.

The toString mask is explicitly, knowingly incomplete: `Function.prototype.toString.call(patchedAdd)` defeats it. The author states this in-comment (hook.js:23-26) rather than papering over it. Do not port the mask believing it is stealth.

WHY THE SOURCE-TEXT APPROACH SURVIVES MINIFICATION (the single most important insight, IDEAS.md #13): a bundler renames locals but can NEVER rename `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `sendBeacon`, `localStorage`, `document.cookie`, `classList`, `aria-expanded`. EFFECT_RE matches only globals and property names, which is why the safety gate works on production sites while identifier-based analysis collapses.

Delegated handlers are matched to elements by SUBSTRING-searching the element's class tokens in the handler source — a heuristic, labelled as such in-comment. It is trusted enough to RANK a component (jsSignal) but explicitly NOT trusted to authorise a synthetic click: `clickUnsafe` filters `h.on !== 'delegated'` before evaluating. Preserve that distinction on the port.

hook.js must skip its own listeners (`if (type.startsWith('aiep:')) continue`, line 209) because the class-token test is a substring match and hook.js's own source contains generic words like `list`, `data` and `name` — self-attribution would flood every element with false delegated matches.

hook.js registers its own two document listeners through `origAdd.call(...)` (lines 103, 192), NOT the patched method, because routing them through the patch would file them into the registry it is about to read back.

A structured `detail` on a CustomEvent does NOT survive MAIN → isolated world. The reply must be `JSON.stringify`'d into a string (hook.js:188-191, 276-278). This is the single reason the whole bridge is string-encoded, and it disappears entirely in Electron.

The nonce is CORRELATION, NOT TRUST — documented at hook.js:190-191. It discriminates a stale reply from an earlier query; it proves nothing about the sender, since the page can read the query nonce and forge a reply.

`held() = new Promise(() => {})` — a NEVER-SETTLING promise — is used to suppress mutating fetch instead of rejecting. Rejecting surfaces an error the page may display to the user or retry-loop on. This is the correct choice and is not obvious.

Quiet mode is bounded by an 8-second dead-man timer (hook.js:106) AND a try/finally teardown on the isolated side (content.js:5788-5796). Reason: if the content script is torn down mid-recording the 'off' never arrives, and a page left permanently unable to send a beacon or open a window is a worse bug than the one being avoided. KEEP THIS in Electron for the session.webRequest filter — an armed filter left on by a skipped teardown silently breaks the user's mini-browser for the rest of the session.

fetch/XHR are suppressed BY METHOD (`/^(POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE)$/i`), never blanket-blocked. Reads pass through untouched, deliberately, because silencing a page's reads breaks it mid-session — a worse bug than the one being avoided.

PATCH LAYERING IS ORDER-DEPENDENT: background.js's NET_INTERCEPTOR (background.js:112-165) patches window.fetch and XMLHttpRequest.prototype.open/send ON TOP OF hook.js's already-patched versions, and its `this.addEventListener('load', ...)` inside `send` goes through hook.js's patched addEventListener. The composition happens to be correct (NET wraps hook wraps native), but it is load-bearing and undocumented. In Electron both collapse into session.webRequest and the layering problem disappears.

Only ONE CDP client may attach to a webContents. `webContents.debugger.attach()` throws 'Another debugger is already attached' if DevTools is open on that guest, and opening DevTools while attached is blocked. Plan the mini-browser's dev-tools affordance around this — either proxy DevTools through your own CDP client or detach on demand.

In Electron with `contextIsolation: true`, the preload runs in an ISOLATED world — the same problem the extension had. To reach the page's main world from a context-isolated preload use `webFrame.executeJavaScript(code, false)`; `webFrame.executeJavaScriptInIsolatedWorld` is the opposite of what you want. Alternatively skip the preload and use CDP `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument`, which is the exact semantic equivalent of world:'MAIN' + run_at:'document_start' and survives navigations automatically.

Only OPEN shadow roots are reachable by the DOM sweep (hook.js:224). A `{mode:'closed'}` shadowRoot is null from outside and permanently invisible to any in-page technique — but CDP's `pierce: true` reaches closed roots too, because it operates below the JS boundary. That is another concrete CDP-only capability.

Real measured numbers from the project's own log (Tree-Project.md, site kinetics.colorion.co): 77 of 80 scanned components carried REAL listener metadata via hook.js, but only 6 of 80 produced exportable motion. The listener registry works far better than the motion recorder built on top of it — port the registry's ideas with confidence, treat the recorder's coverage claims with suspicion. The log also records that an earlier '24/26 demos' ground truth was measured on whole `.card` units, not on the exported component subtree, and is therefore not a valid ceiling.

`clickUnsafe` is fail-closed: its `catch (_) { return true; }` means any exception during vetting refuses the click. Preserve this inversion on the port — the default answer to 'is this safe?' must be no.

DESTRUCTIVE_RE (content.js:5671) is already bilingual and includes the Arabic terms احذف، حذف، إزالة، شراء، ادفع، إرسال، أرسل، تأكيد، اشتراك، إلغاء، خروج. Directly reusable in Arabic-first EXELMJ; extend rather than rewrite.

subsystem: background.js — the MV3 service worker (AI Element Picker v3.2.0, 509 lines / 19 KB)
summary: background.js is the extension's single privileged process. It does five distinct jobs that MV3 forces into one file: (1) lifecycle/plumbing — side-panel opening, per-tab picker on/off state, toolbar icon swapping, URL injectability gating, on-demand content-script injection with a version handshake, and a generic panel→page message relay; (2) privileged browser calls the content script is not allowed to make — captureVisibleTab for element screenshots and chrome.downloads for asset saving; (3) arming a MAIN-world fetch/XHR monkey-patch that streams the page's own JSON responses back to the content script over window.postMessage; (4) a three-shape AI provider proxy (OpenAI-compatible / Anthropic / Gemini) whose key lives only in chrome.storage.local; (5) a serialised, deduplicating append-only store for the Arabic-dialect text corpus, guarded by a promise chain so two tabs writing at once cannot clobber each other. Almost every line of it exists because of an MV3 restriction rather than because of the problem domain — which is exactly what makes it a high-signal port target: the *policies* encoded here are worth keeping, the *mechanisms* are almost all replaceable by something strictly better in Electron.

mechanisms.name: Per-tab picker state + toolbar icon, with the page as the authority
mechanisms.problem: The panel must show whether the picker is currently armed on the tab the user is looking at. The worker holds a Map from tabId→boolean, but MV3 kills the worker after ~30s idle and the Map evaporates; also the picker can turn itself off (Esc, or auto-deactivate after a pick) without the worker knowing.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Three cooperating pieces. (1) `const pickerState = new Map()` tabId→boolean, written only by togglePicker and by the PICKER_DEACTIVATED message the content script sends when it self-disarms; chrome.action.setIcon({tabId, path}) swaps between ACTIVE_ICONS and IDLE_ICONS so the toolbar reflects per-tab, not global, state. (2) Invalidation: `chrome.tabs.onRemoved` deletes the entry; `chrome.tabs.onUpdated` deletes it and resets the icon the moment changeInfo.status === 'loading' — a navigation destroys the content script, so any cached 'active' is a lie from that instant. (3) The trick that makes it survive worker death: PANEL_GET_STATE does NOT trust the Map. It queries the active tab, and if injectable it sends GET_PICKER_STATE straight to the content script and prefers that answer (`if (st) { pickerActive = st.active; rulerActive = st.rulerActive }`), falling back to the Map only when the page does not answer. The DOM is the source of truth; the Map is a cache.
mechanisms.location: E:\exten Picker\background.js lines ~6–47 (icon tables, pickerState, setIcon, getActiveTab), ~83–101 (togglePicker), ~412–428 (PANEL_GET_STATE), ~502–509 (cleanup listeners)
mechanisms.chrome_apis_used: chrome.action.setIcon, chrome.tabs.query, chrome.tabs.sendMessage, chrome.tabs.onRemoved, chrome.tabs.onUpdated, chrome.sidePanel.setPanelBehavior
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: A plain module-scope Map<number /* WebContentsView id */, PickerState> in the main process — it never dies, so the whole invalidation-anxiety layer becomes optional. Icon state → your own toolbar button in the renderer. `chrome.tabs.onUpdated({status:'loading'})` → `webContents.on('did-start-navigation')` / `'did-start-loading'`. `chrome.tabs.onRemoved` → `webContents.on('destroyed')`.
mechanisms.port_notes: Keep the POLICY (reset picker state on navigation start; ask the page rather than trusting the cache) and drop the reason it was needed. In Electron the main-process object is authoritative and permanent, but the 'ask the page' fallback is still worth keeping for one reason the extension didn't have: hot module reload. When Vite swaps our injected picker bundle, the main process's belief about picker state is stale in exactly the same way. Model it as `getPickerState(viewId)` that races a 200 ms IPC round-trip to the view against the cached value.

mechanisms.name: isInjectableUrl — the refusal list, and why each entry is on it
mechanisms.problem: Attempting chrome.scripting.executeScript on a page the browser protects throws an ugly async error and leaves the UI in a half-armed state. The user needs one clear message instead of a stack trace.
mechanisms.how_it_works: A flat prefix blocklist checked with `url.startsWith(p)`, wrapped in `!!url && !BLOCKED_PREFIXES.some(...)`. The list is: `chrome://`, `chrome-extension://`, `edge://`, `extension://`, `about:`, `https://chrome.google.com/webstore`, `https://chromewebstore.google.com`, `https://microsoftedge.microsoft.com/addons`, `view-source:`. The reasons differ per entry and matter: the `chrome://`/`edge://`/`about:` schemes are browser-internal WebUI and Chrome hard-refuses injection there at the process level; the web-store URLs are a *special-cased policy block* (Chrome forbids extensions from scripting the store so an extension cannot silently uninstall its competitors or fake reviews); `chrome-extension://`/`extension://` blocks cross-extension injection; `view-source:` has no live DOM to pick from. Note what is NOT on the list: `file://` is allowed by the code, but in practice it fails anyway unless the user ticks 'Allow access to file URLs' — the author let that one fail naturally rather than pre-refusing it. `about:blank` is caught by the `about:` prefix. Every call site funnels the failure into a single sentinel `{ok:false, error:'restricted'}` that the panel maps to one Arabic sentence; the worker never surfaces the raw Chrome error for this class.
mechanisms.location: E:\exten Picker\background.js lines ~19–32; used at ~69, ~85, ~167, ~415
mechanisms.chrome_apis_used: none — pure string test over tab.url
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: Same shape, different list. Guard `webContents.getURL()` against: `devtools://`, `chrome://`, `about:blank` (nothing to pick), `chrome-error://` (our own error pages), and — the one that is new and important for us — any URL outside the project sandbox when the user is running a generated project.
mechanisms.port_notes: Two changes. First, invert the polarity: the extension had to work on the whole web so a blocklist was right; Studio's mini-browser mostly hosts *our own* dev server and *our own* file:// output, so an allowlist (`http://localhost:*`, `file://<projectRoot>/**`, plus explicitly user-approved external origins) is both safer and easier to reason about. Second — and this is the part worth copying verbatim — keep the single typed sentinel. One `{ok:false, code:'RESTRICTED'}` that the UI renders as one sentence beats leaking Electron's `Script failed to execute` text to the user. Also add `about:blank` handling explicitly, because in Electron a freshly created WebContentsView legitimately sits at about:blank before first navigation and the picker UI should say 'load a page first', not 'restricted'.

mechanisms.name: ensureContentScript — the PING/version handshake and the orphaned-script problem
mechanisms.problem: Three races at once: (a) the manifest declares content.js at document_idle, but the panel may act before that fires, or on a tab that existed before the extension was installed; (b) after an extension update or a manual reload, the tab still hosts the OLD content.js, whose `chrome.runtime` is now dead — messages to it hang or reject with 'Extension context invalidated'; (c) blind re-injection would double-install listeners and overlays.
mechanisms.how_it_works: A three-stage protocol split across both files. Worker side: `await chrome.tabs.sendMessage(tabId, {type:'PING'})`; if the reply's `r.v === CONTENT_VERSION` (currently 35) return true — a live script of the right version is already there. If the reply exists but the version differs, DELIBERATELY fall through and re-inject (stale build). If sendMessage throws, no script or an orphaned one — also inject. Injection is `chrome.scripting.executeScript({target:{tabId}, files:['content.js']})` wrapped in try/catch returning false on failure, which the caller converts to the 'restricted' sentinel. Page side, and this is the clever half: content.js opens with `const prev = window.__AI_PICKER_STATE__; if (prev && prev.version === PICKER_VERSION && prev.isAlive()) return;` where the previously-installed instance published `{version, isAlive(){ try { return !!chrome.runtime?.id } catch { return false } }}` on window. So the guard is not 'am I already installed' but 'is an installed instance of my exact version STILL CONNECTED TO A LIVE EXTENSION'. An orphan's `chrome.runtime.id` throws or is undefined, isAlive() returns false, and the fresh injection is allowed to replace it. Version numbers must be kept in lockstep in two files (background.js CONTENT_VERSION = 35, content.js PICKER_VERSION = 35).
mechanisms.location: E:\exten Picker\background.js lines ~49–65; paired guard at E:\exten Picker\content.js lines 1–8 and 7505–7518; PING handler at content.js 7242–7244
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: `webPreferences.preload` on the WebContentsView (or `session.setPreloads()` for all frames). A preload runs before ANY page script at document_start, in every navigation automatically, with Node `require()` available and a real `contextBridge` — it is strictly better than the extension's document_idle content script AND better than its MAIN-world hook. For the on-demand path there is `webContents.executeJavaScript(sourceString)` which returns a Promise of the evaluated value.
mechanisms.port_notes: The entire ensureContentScript dance can be deleted. A preload is guaranteed present before the page's first line runs, on every navigation, with zero races and zero double-install risk — there is no 'is it there yet' question to ask. What to carry over: (1) KEEP the version handshake, but only for dev-mode HMR — during development our picker bundle will be swapped under a running view and we need the same 'is this the current build' check. Expose it as one IPC `picker:ping` returning a build hash. (2) KEEP the isAlive() *idea* in a new form: an Electron renderer can be torn down while main still holds a reference, so any main→view IPC should be timeout-raced, not awaited forever. The extension's implicit 'sendMessage rejects if nothing is listening' is a freebie we lose; `webContents.send` is fire-and-forget and will silently succeed into the void. Use `ipcMain.handle` + a `Promise.race` with a 2 s timeout, or MessageChannelMain ports whose `close` event tells you the peer died. (3) DROP the two-file version constant — derive it from one build-time define so it cannot drift.

mechanisms.name: relayToActiveTab — the panel⇄page relay and how responses are correlated
mechanisms.problem: The side panel is a separate document with no reference to the page's DOM and no way to message a content script directly (chrome.tabs.* is worker-only). Every panel action — extract colors, list captures, get a table — has to travel panel → worker → content script and bring an answer back.
mechanisms.how_it_works: There is NO correlation table and no request ids — and that is the point worth understanding. Correlation rides entirely on Chrome's one-shot promise-returning sendMessage: each `chrome.runtime.sendMessage(msg)` opens its own single-use port, and the promise resolves with exactly whatever that receiver's `sendResponse` passed. The author adds only an *envelope*: the panel sends `{type:'PANEL_RELAY', payload}`; the worker's hub matches it, calls `relayToActiveTab(message.payload).then(sendResponse)` and — critically — `return true` to tell Chrome to keep the message channel open for an async reply (omit that `return true` and the port closes and the panel's promise rejects). relayToActiveTab then: query the active tab of the current window → isInjectableUrl guard → ensureContentScript → `await chrome.tabs.sendMessage(tab.id, message)` → wrap as `{ok:true, tabId, resp}`, or `{ok:false, error}` on throw. The result is a deliberate TWO-LEVEL ok: the outer `ok` means 'the transport worked / the page was reachable', the inner `resp.ok` means 'the operation succeeded'. Panel code reads `r?.ok && r.resp?.ok` everywhere. The content script's own listener mirrors the rule — it `return true`s per-case for async handlers (e.g. CAPTURE_ELEMENT_SHOT, CODE_FOR_REVIEW) and falls through to `return false` at the end of the switch.

mechanisms.electron_equivalent: `ipcRenderer.invoke(channel, args)` ⇄ `ipcMain.handle(channel, fn)` for renderer→main (correlation is built into invoke/handle, ids are generated for you). For main→page-content, `webContents.executeJavaScript('...')` already returns a Promise resolving to the evaluated expression's value — correlation free. For a long-lived typed channel to a preload, `MessageChannelMain` + `port.postMessage` with your own id, or simply `ipcRenderer.invoke` from the preload upward.
mechanisms.port_notes: Collapse three hops into one. In the extension the chain is panel→worker→content→worker→panel because the panel has no privileges and the content script has no privileges; in Electron the Studio UI renderer talks to main once (`invoke`), and main talks to the hosted page once (`executeJavaScript` or a preload port). What to KEEP: (1) the two-level ok envelope — genuinely useful, because 'the view navigated away mid-call' and 'the selector matched nothing' are different failures the UI must word differently; formalise it as a discriminated union `{ok:true, data} | {ok:false, code, detail}`. (2) the 'active target' indirection — relayToActiveTab resolves *which* tab at call time rather than the panel tracking a tabId; in Studio the same applies once the mini-browser has tabs, and it prevents a stale id from addressing a recycled view. What to DROP: the `return true` protocol entirely — it is pure MV3 tax and the single most common source of silent 'message port closed' bugs; `ipcMain.handle` returning a promise has no equivalent footgun.

mechanisms.name: togglePicker with forceState — idempotent arm/disarm
mechanisms.problem: Three different inputs can toggle the picker (panel button, Alt+Shift+P global command, the page self-disarming) and they must not fight. The panel button in particular sometimes needs 'set to exactly off' rather than 'flip'.
mechanisms.how_it_works: `togglePicker(forceState)` — `const next = typeof forceState === 'boolean' ? forceState : !current`. The same function serves both the idempotent set and the flip, so there is exactly one code path that can change picker state. Order of operations matters and is correct here: the message is sent to the page FIRST and only if `chrome.tabs.sendMessage` did not throw are `pickerState` and the icon updated — so the worker's belief can never get ahead of the page's reality. The keyboard command handler calls `togglePicker()` with no argument (flip); the panel calls it with `message.forceState`.

mechanisms.name: CAPTURE_TAB — visible-only screenshot, and the crop-from-one-shot batching it forces
mechanisms.problem: Element screenshots and the eyedropper both need pixels. A content script cannot screenshot; only the worker can, and only what is currently on screen.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Worker side is four lines: on CAPTURE_TAB it reads `sender.tab.windowId` (note: the *sender's* window, not the active one — correct, because the requester is the content script itself) and calls `chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab(windowId, {format:'png'})`, replying `{ok, dataUrl}`. Format is PNG with no quality parameter (quality only applies to jpeg; the author chose lossless because the output feeds a color eyedropper where JPEG chroma subsampling would literally give wrong hex values). Everything hard is on the content side, driven by the visible-only limitation: (1) single-element shot — `elm.scrollIntoView({block:'center', behavior:'instant'})`, clear the picker highlight, wait 120 ms for the browser to settle, capture, then crop with `ctx.drawImage(img, r.left*dpr, r.top*dpr, r.width*dpr, r.height*dpr, 0,0, w,h)` using getBoundingClientRect (viewport-relative, which is exactly the capture's coordinate space) scaled by devicePixelRatio, then re-apply the highlight. (2) batch shots — the code hides its OWN overlay (`ui.root.style.display='none'`, 60 ms settle), takes ONE capture, and crops up to 40 element rects out of that single PNG with a 2 px pad, clamping sx/sy to ≥0 and sw/sh to the image bounds. That batching exists because captureVisibleTab is rate-limited (MAX_CAPTURE_VISIBLE_TAB_CALLS_PER_SECOND) — one capture, many crops. All capture calls are wrapped in a 5 s `Promise.race` timeout because a hung worker would otherwise freeze the picker. A full-page capture is NOT implemented and would have required: scroll to 0, capture, scroll by innerHeight, wait for lazy-load + sticky headers to re-settle, capture again, and stitch — with sticky/fixed elements duplicated in every tile and scroll-linked animations differing between tiles. The author correctly did not attempt it.
mechanisms.location: E:\exten Picker\background.js lines ~465–474 (CAPTURE_TAB case); crop logic at E:\exten Picker\content.js 2482–2508 (captureElementShot), 1331–1370 (batch crop), 2292–2318 (eyedropper)
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: `webContents.capturePage(rect?)` returns a NativeImage of a given region — and for off-screen content, `webContents.debugger` + CDP `Page.captureScreenshot({clip:{x,y,width,height,scale}, captureBeyondViewport:true})`, which renders content below the fold WITHOUT scrolling. Full-page is the same call with the clip set from `Page.getLayoutMetrics().cssContentSize`. What SURVIVES from the original: (1) the devicePixelRatio math — CDP's `clip.scale` plays the same role and you still must decide whether the caller wants CSS pixels or device pixels; expose it explicitly. (2) hiding our own picker overlay before capture — still necessary, and still needs a settle frame (use `requestAnimationFrame` twice via executeJavaScript rather than a fixed sleep). (3) PNG-not-JPEG for anything feeding color extraction — keep this rule, it is a real correctness constraint, not a preference. (4) the 5 s timeout race — keep; CDP calls can hang on a busy renderer. NEW capability worth exploiting for deliverable (d): capturePage on a hidden/offscreen WebContentsView lets us render the SAME generated project at desktop/tablet/mobile widths and screenshot all three without the user seeing any flicker — the extension could never do this.

mechanisms.name: NETWORK INTERCEPTION — MAIN-world fetch/XHR monkey-patch with a postMessage bridge
mechanisms.problem: The extension wants to see the JSON the page fetches (to know what data drives the UI, to export it as CSV, to scan responses for leaked secrets). A content script lives in an isolated JS world: it shares the DOM but has a different `window.fetch`, so patching fetch there sees nothing. chrome.webRequest in MV3 cannot read response bodies at all.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Armed on demand, not always-on. START_NET_CAPTURE → `chrome.scripting.executeScript({target:{tabId}, world:'MAIN', func: NET_INTERCEPTOR})` — note `func`, not `files`: Chrome serialises the function to source and evals it in the page's own world, which means NET_INTERCEPTOR can close over NOTHING; every constant it needs is redeclared inside it. Inside: a re-entry guard `if (window.__AI_NET_CAPTURE__) return; window.__AI_NET_CAPTURE__ = true`. Then two patches. fetch: `const origFetch = window.fetch; window.fetch = function(...args){ const p = origFetch.apply(this,args); p.then(resp => { ... }); return p }` — the ORIGINAL promise is returned synchronously so the page's timing and error handling are untouched; the tap is a separate `.then` on the same promise. Body reading is `resp.clone().text()` — cloning is mandatory, reading the original would consume the page's own body and break the site. XHR: `open` is patched only to stash `this.__aiUrl` and `this.__aiMethod` on the instance (the send-time listener otherwise has no URL); `send` attaches a `load` listener before delegating, and reads `this.responseText` ONLY when `responseType` is '' or 'text' — for blob/arraybuffer/json responseTypes responseText throws, so those are silently skipped. Filtering is identical on both paths: capture only if `/json|text\/csv|application\/xml|text\/xml|graphql/i` matches the content-type header, OR the URL matches `/\.json(\?|$)/i` (the fallback for servers that mislabel JSON as text/plain). Size cap `MAX_BYTES = 3_000_000` characters, dropped silently above that. The MAIN→isolated bridge is `window.postMessage({__aiPickerNet:true, rec}, '*')` — the only channel between the two worlds. The content script listens on window 'message' and validates `e.source !== window` (rejects messages posted from iframes/other origins) plus the `__aiPickerNet === true` marker before accepting. Every function body is individually wrapped in try/catch so a malformed response cannot break the page's own fetch.

mechanisms.problem: An extracted component is a corpse: it contains literal strings and literal numbers with no indication of which came from a database and which are design copy. Whoever rebuilds it cannot tell '١٢٬٥٠٠ ر.س' (a bound price field) from 'اشترِ الآن' (a hardcoded label), so the rebuilt component is frozen and unbindable.
mechanisms.how_it_works: This is a specification in IDEAS.md, scored 8.1 (novelty 10/10, impact 8/10, feasibility 6/10 — the lowest feasibility in the top tier), with dependency listed as 'network interception (MAIN-world bus, arm+reload) + inline payload harvesting'. NOTHING in content.js/background.js implements it; the raw materials (netCaptures + extractRepeats + extractTables) exist and are wired to the panel for export only. The designed algorithm, per IDEAS.md §6: (1) Gather both sides of the join — the network responses AND, explicitly called out as the larger and usually-forgotten case, the SSR payload injected inline into the first HTML document (`__NEXT_DATA__`, `__NUXT__`, `window.__INITIAL_STATE__`, `<script type="application/json">`), which needs no permission at all. (2) Flatten the payload to leaf paths. (3) For every visible text node, attempt a match. Strings match directly. Numbers are the hard case, because the DOM shows a FORMATTED number ('١٢٬٢٥٠٠ ر.س') and the payload holds a raw one (12500) — so INVERT the formatting: strip currency symbols/separators/Arabic-Indic digits, coerce to a Number, and look it up in a numeric index built once over the payload. This narrows to a handful of candidates; only THEN do you replay standard format patterns (Intl.NumberFormat locale/currency/grouping variants) against those few candidates to confirm and, importantly, to RECOVER the format spec. The author's stated payoff for this ordering: 'a process that takes minutes becomes fractions of a second' — index-first, format-replay-second, never format-replay over the whole payload. (4) The strongest evidence is ORDINAL correspondence: if DOM list item #3 matches payload record #3 across three or more consecutive items, the binding is effectively proven, and you have learned the repeater's array path, not just one field. (5) The NEGATIVE result is a first-class output: text that matches nothing in any payload is provably static design copy — 'these four words matched no data' is as valuable to the rebuilder as a positive binding.

mechanisms.name: corpusAppend — the serialised write chain, dedup key, and minimal provenance
mechanisms.problem: chrome.storage.local is read-modify-write with no transactions. The continuous collector runs in EVERY tab simultaneously; two tabs finishing a sweep in the same tick would each `get` the same array, each `set` their own version, and the later write silently erases the earlier tab's rows. Additionally the panel may be closed, so the store — not the panel — must be the sink.
mechanisms.how_it_works: A single-slot promise mutex, 4 lines: `let corpusChain = Promise.resolve(); function corpusEnqueue(job){ const next = corpusChain.then(job, job); corpusChain = next.catch(()=>{}); return next }`. Note `.then(job, job)` — the job is passed as BOTH the fulfil and reject handler, so a previous job that threw does not poison the chain and still lets the next one run; and `corpusChain` is assigned the `.catch`-swallowed version so an unhandled rejection can never propagate, while the CALLER still receives the un-swallowed `next` and can see its own error. Every write to the store goes through it. Inside the critical section: get the array, build `new Set(store.map(r=>r.k))` of existing keys, compute `const day = new Date().toISOString().slice(0,10)`, then for each incoming item skip falsy/keyless/already-seen (adding to the Set as it goes, so duplicates WITHIN one batch are also caught), and push `{t,s,m,w,k, src: msg.host || '', d: day}`. Only `set()` if something was actually added — a no-op batch does zero writes. The dedup key `k` is computed in the CONTENT script, not here (content.js 7045: `normArabic(clean).replace(AR_NON_LETTER,'')` — Arabic normalisation then strip everything that is not a letter), and travels with the record specifically so the worker and the panel both dedup by the identical rule without reimplementing it. PROVENANCE IS DELIBERATELY LOSSY: the stored fields are the text, its dialect score, matched markers, word count, the dedup key, the bare HOST (`location.hostname` minus `www.`), and the DAY — with an explicit comment that the URL, author and timestamp are omitted 'because that is what would turn a text back into a person'. Finally, if anything was added, `chrome.runtime.sendMessage({type:'CORPUS_STORE_CHANGED', added, total}).catch(()=>{})` broadcasts to whoever is listening; the `.catch` is mandatory because with no panel open there is no receiver and the promise rejects. The panel listens and simply reloads + re-renders.

PNG, not JPEG, for any capture that feeds color extraction. The eyedropper (content.js 2292–2318) samples pixels from the captured dataURL; JPEG chroma subsampling would return literally wrong hex values. `captureVisibleTab(windowId, {format:'png'})` has no quality param because quality only applies to jpeg. This is a correctness constraint, not a preference — carry it into `Page.captureScreenshot({format:'png'})`.

`resp.clone().text()` is mandatory in the fetch tap, not optional. Reading the original response body consumes it and breaks the page's own code. The cost is doubled peak memory on a 3 MB body — hence MAX_BYTES = 3_000_000 chars and a silent drop above it. CDP's getResponseBody has neither problem.

The network interceptor only sees calls made AFTER it is armed. IDEAS.md literally lists the dependency as 'arm+reload' — the first page load, which carries the SSR payload and the most important XHRs, is always missed. This is the single largest functional limitation in the whole extension and it evaporates the moment we attach webContents.debugger before first navigation.

CDP counterpart footgun to plan for: `Network.getResponseBody` fails once the body is evicted from the renderer's buffer (typically after navigation). Fetch bodies EAGERLY on responseReceived/loadingFinished into our own store — do not copy the extension's lazy 'fetch the body when the user clicks' pattern, it will not translate.

The XHR tap can only read `responseText` when `responseType` is '' or 'text'; for blob/arraybuffer/json it would throw, so those responses are silently skipped. The fetch tap has no such hole. So today, a site using `xhr.responseType='json'` is invisible to the tool — a real coverage gap, invisible in the UI.

Content-type filtering has a deliberate escape hatch: `CAPTURABLE.test(ct) || /\.json(\?|$)/i.test(url)`. The URL fallback exists because real servers mislabel JSON as text/plain. Keep it; it is field knowledge.

The content-script injection guard is NOT 'am I installed' but 'is a live instance of my exact version installed'. `isAlive()` reads `chrome.runtime?.id` inside try/catch — an orphaned script (post extension-reload) has an invalidated context, so the guard correctly lets the fresh injection replace it. CONTENT_VERSION (background.js) and PICKER_VERSION (content.js) are both 35 and MUST be kept in lockstep by hand — a drift bug waiting to happen; derive from one build define in the port.

corpusEnqueue uses `chain.then(job, job)` — job passed as BOTH handlers — so a job that threw does not stall the queue; and `corpusChain = next.catch(()=>{})` while the CALLER gets the un-swallowed `next`. Four lines, and every part of them is load-bearing. Worth keeping for any JSON-file store in Studio: `await fs.readFile` yields, so read-modify-write clobbering is reproducible in Electron main despite it being single-threaded.

Provenance policy, quoted from the source comment and worth adopting as a hard rule: only the HOST and the DAY are stored — 'never the URL, author or time, which is what would turn a text back into a person'. Electron's real filesystem makes over-collection easier, so this discipline gets MORE important, not less.

`chrome.runtime.sendMessage` for a broadcast (CORPUS_STORE_CHANGED) REJECTS when no context is listening — the `.catch(()=>{})` is mandatory, not defensive style. Electron's `webContents.send` is fire-and-forget and will silently succeed into the void instead; we lose the 'nobody is listening' signal and must not assume delivery.

Gemini's API key is placed in the URL QUERY STRING (`?key=…`) — query strings end up in proxy logs, crash dumps and referrer headers. Do not replicate this if we ever build an optional provider layer; and note the key is stored in chrome.storage.local in plaintext. Electron equivalent should be `safeStorage.encryptString`.

`anthropic-dangerous-direct-browser-access: true` is required ONLY because the request originates from a browser context. In Electron main there is no origin and no CORS — the header becomes unnecessary. This is a good litmus test for the whole port: every header, permission and workaround that exists 'because browser' should be re-examined rather than translated.

No streaming anywhere: runAi is a single non-streaming fetch with a 60 s AbortController timeout, so a long generation shows nothing for a minute and then may just time out. Defaults are maxTokens 4000 / temperature 0.2, with the comment that reasoning models need budget for BOTH thinking and answer.

Empty answers are triaged, not just reported: aiEmptyReason distinguishes finish_reason=length ('spent the whole budget thinking') from content_filter ('blocked'), because they need different fixes. Generalise the discipline even after dropping runAi — every empty result our MCP tools return should carry a reason code (no match vs. page still loading vs. view navigated away).

IDEAS.md #6 (data-binding inference, score 8.1, novelty 10/10, feasibility 6/10 — the lowest in the top tier) is a DESIGN ONLY. Nothing implements it. What exists is capture + summariseJson + export. Its stated performance trick is index-first / format-replay-second: strip formatting from the DOM text, coerce to Number, look up in a prebuilt numeric index, and only replay Intl format patterns against the few survivors — 'minutes become fractions of a second'. And its strongest signal is ordinal correspondence (DOM item #3 ↔ record #3 across ≥3 items ≈ proof), which also yields the repeater's array path. The negative result is a first-class output: text matching no payload is provably static design copy.

summariseJson's heuristic — first array at depth ≤ 4 whose length ≥ 2 and whose [0] is an object — is deliberately dumb and works because nearly every API nests its list one or two wrapper keys deep. It is a pure function with zero chrome dependency: lift it to TypeScript unchanged.

netCaptures is a ring buffer capped at 300 records that silently shifts off the oldest, with monotonically increasing ids so ids stay stable as entries fall off. A long capture session loses data with no warning. In Electron, spill to an NDJSON log on disk and keep only metadata in memory.

chrome.downloads sanitises filenames for you; fs.writeFile does not. When porting DOWNLOAD_ASSET, keep the `^https?:` scheme guard AND add path-traversal sanitising ('..', absolute paths, drive letters, Windows reserved names CON/NUL/COM1) plus a `path.relative(projectRoot, target)` containment check — a Windows-specific risk the extension never had.

Prefer a Menu accelerator over globalShortcut for the picker hotkey: globalShortcut steals the combination from every app system-wide even when EXELMJ is minimised, and will collide with Illustrator/Photoshop — likely open simultaneously given the COM bridge. Also note keystrokes inside the hosted WebContentsView do not reach our menu; intercept with `webContents.on('before-input-event')` + preventDefault so the page cannot swallow the hotkey.

The worker is a hub for request/response but a BYSTANDER for events — PICK_RESULT and RULER_STOPPED are broadcast by the content script straight past it to the side panel, because chrome.runtime.sendMessage fans out to every extension context. Preserve that split explicitly in Studio (ipcMain.handle for commands, webContents.send for events); it is what lets MCP tools map 1:1 onto the command set and MCP notifications onto the event set.

The default AI endpoint ships pointing at a free Chinese tier (open.bigmodel.cn, glm-4-flash) and error parsing includes a `data.msg` fallback specifically for Chinese providers. Evidence the author optimised for zero-cost-to-start — relevant only as a reminder of who the tool was for, and further evidence that the whole provider layer exists to serve a human clicking a button, not an agent.

Every function inside NET_INTERCEPTOR is individually try/catch-wrapped, and the postMessage receiver validates BOTH `e.source === window` (rejects iframe/cross-origin posts) AND the `__aiPickerNet === true` marker before accepting a record. Both are non-negotiable when you are running inside someone else's page — the first because a thrown exception in a patched fetch breaks the host site, the second because the bridge is a public channel any script on the page can post to.

subsystem: The Side Panel — sidepanel.html (821 lines) + sidepanel.js (4099 lines) + sidepanel.css (1332 lines)
summary: A 9-tab, Arabic-RTL, hand-rolled (no framework, no build step) tool panel that renders everything the content script extracts and owns all persistence, export and settings UI. It is a thin, stateless-per-tab shell: each tab lazily pulls its data via one relay() round-trip on first activation, caches it in a module-level variable, and nulls every cache when the inspected page's URL changes. Its two genuinely hard-won subsystems are (1) the UI-component library — a persisted gallery of live-rendering sandboxed-iframe previews, whose JSON schema was deliberately made lossy to fit a 10 MB store, and (2) the RTL CSS system, which is RTL-by-default with ~22 explicit `direction: ltr` islands for machine text. Roughly a third of the file by volume (bulk fetch, security scanner, dialect corpus, AI provider config, site clone) is extension-specific and irrelevant to EXELMJ Studio.

mechanisms.name: Tab shell with lazy per-tab fetch and URL-change cache invalidation
mechanisms.problem: Nine heavy tabs, each needing an expensive page round-trip; eager-loading all of them freezes the panel, and stale data after navigation silently lies to the user.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Tabs are plain `<button class="tab" data-tab="styles">` in a `<nav role="tablist">`; panes are `<main id="tab-styles" class="tabpane">`. `activateTab(name)` toggles `.is-active` on every `.tab` where `t.dataset.tab === name` and on every `.tabpane` where `p.id === 'tab-'+name` (CSS: `.tabpane{display:none} .tabpane.is-active{display:block}`), sets `currentTab`, then calls `autoFetchForTab()`. `autoFetchForTab()` is a flat if-chain keyed on `currentTab` that fetches ONLY when the module-level cache for that tab is null (`if (currentTab==="styles" && !stylesData) loadStyles()`), so switching back is instant. Expensive scans are deliberately excluded from auto-fetch — the UI-component scan walks every stylesheet and is behind an explicit button ("فحص المكوّنات"). Freshness: `refreshState()` polls the worker for the active tab's URL; if `resp.url !== panelUrl` it nulls EVERY cache (`stylesData=assetsData=designSystem=lastPick=null; dataScanned=false`), hides the result card, and re-runs `autoFetchForTab()`. It is wired to `chrome.tabs.onActivated` and `chrome.tabs.onUpdated` (status==="complete"). The 9 tabs are: الأنماط (colors/fonts/page meta), الأصول (UI components + images + SVG + icons + video + audio + font files + other files, with a filter-chip row), الفحص (picker toggle, shortcut table, result card, settings <details>), التصميم (color ramps, type scale, suggested components, tokens, multi-format export), البيانات (auto-extract, network monitor, bulk fetch, tables/repeating lists/structured data), اللهجة (Arabic-dialect corpus collector), الذكاء (AI provider config + data assistant + free question), الأمان (security scanner), استنساخ (site clone).
mechanisms.location: sidepanel.html:74-84 (nav), 89-760 (panes); sidepanel.js:150-188 (activateTab/autoFetchForTab), 232-258 (refreshState invalidation); sidepanel.css:104-138
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker panel shell, reused by (a) builder and (d) mini-browser
mechanisms.chrome_apis_used: chrome.tabs.query / onActivated / onUpdated (for URL change detection); chrome.runtime.sendMessage for the state poll
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: Cache invalidation becomes event-driven instead of polled: listen on the hosted view's webContents for `did-navigate`, `did-navigate-in-page` and `did-finish-load`, and `webContents.send('studio:page-changed', url)` to the panel renderer. The tab/pane DOM toggling needs no change at all — it is vanilla DOM and drops straight into EXELMJ's TypeScript design module.
mechanisms.port_notes: The pattern is the valuable part, not the tab list. EXELMJ Studio's tabs should be: Elements (picker), Components (library), Tokens (design system), Preview (mini-browser device switcher), Code (emitted output). Drop البيانات / اللهجة / الأمان / الذكاء / استنساخ entirely — those are the extension's separate product ambitions, not panel craft.

mechanisms.name: Component library persistence with a hard 10 MB budget and a pre-emptive warning
mechanisms.problem: Saved UI components must survive across sessions, must dedupe reliably, and must not silently start failing to save when the store fills up.
mechanisms.how_it_works: Key `"uiLibrary"` in chrome.storage.local holds an array of `{id, savedAt, host, component}`. `libId(c)` builds the dedup identity by joining with `|`: `[name, kind, size.w, size.h, css.length, html.length, text.length, text.slice(0,40)]`. The first six fields alone were the original identity and were adequate while a page yielded a handful of components; 144 same-sized cards scanned from one page collided on all six, so the component's own TEXT had to become part of the identity — both its length and its first 40 characters. `libAdd` refuses duplicates (`libHas` = `uiLibrary.some(e => e.id === id)`), records the hostname it came from (derived from `c.source.url` falling back to the last pick's URL), and stores `componentJson(c)` — not the live object. Critically, after every successful save it calls `chrome.storage.local.getBytesInUse(LIB_KEY, bytes => { if (bytes > 8*1024*1024) showStatus("المكتبة تقترب من حدّ المساحة — احذف بعض المكوّنات.", false, true) })` — i.e. it warns at 80% of the 10 MB ceiling, BEFORE writes begin to throw, because a quota failure in chrome.storage is reported asynchronously and reads as "the save button does nothing". The gallery has a two-view toggle (`.ui-tab` buttons, `uiView` = "scan" | "lib") and `shownComponents()` returns either the live scan array or `uiLibrary.map(e => e.component)` — so every downstream renderer, exporter and index lookup is view-agnostic.
mechanisms.location: sidepanel.js:651-714 (LIB_KEY, libId, libLoad/libSave/libHas/libAdd/libRemove), 716-722 (view toggle), 1093 (libLoad on boot)
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: Node `fs` under `app.getPath('userData')/studio/library/`, or better-sqlite3 with one row per component and the HTML/CSS as TEXT columns. There is NO 10 MB ceiling, so `getBytesInUse` becomes an fs.stat on the library directory (still worth surfacing — a 400 MB library is a different failure but still a failure). Main-process ownership via IPC (`ipcMain.handle('library:add' | 'library:list' | 'library:remove')`) so two windows can't race the file, mirroring how this extension routes corpus writes through the worker for exactly that reason.
mechanisms.port_notes: Port `libId` verbatim including the text-length + first-40-chars fields — that collision was found the hard way against a real 144-component page. In EXELMJ, prefer one file per component (`<hash>.json`) over one big array: it removes the read-modify-write of the whole store on every save and makes deletion O(1).

mechanisms.name: componentJson — a deliberately LOSSY persistence schema, and what was cut to fit
mechanisms.problem: A live scanned component object is several megabytes when it carries raw motion sample series and unbounded handler source. Storing it whole blew the 10 MB library after a handful of saves.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
`componentJson(c)` is the single serialisation function used by save-to-library, download-single-JSON, download-all-JSON and the AI payload — so nothing can be lost in one path and present in another. Three explicit reductions:
(1) RECORDED MOTION — the live recorder produces `c.recorded.phases[i].keyframes`, an array of sampled computed-style snapshots. Only `{key, trigger, count}` is stored; the actual keyframes are dropped because they have ALREADY been compiled into `c.css` as @keyframes. `count` falls back to `p.count ?? (p.keyframes||[]).length` precisely so a component round-tripped OUT of the library and saved again does not lose its count once the raw list is gone.
(2) BEHAVIOR — `events` capped at 20 entries; `handlers` capped at 6 entries, each with `source` truncated to 1200 characters.
(3) STATES — normalised on read as well as write: `s.key || s.state` accepts both the live shape (`key`) and the stored shape (`state`), so re-serialising a library component is idempotent.
Things that had been accidentally omitted and were added back after being found missing from exports, library AND AI payload: `text`, `dataset`, `labels`, `codeBlocks`. Things kept in full because they are what makes a copy actually behave: `stateRules`, `stateKeyframes`, `baseRules`, `css`, `html`, `tailwind`, `motion`, `context`.
mechanisms.location: sidepanel.js:992-1067
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (a) builder — this IS the shape of the component asset the builder emits code from
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed — pure JS. In EXELMJ it becomes a TypeScript interface `StudioComponent` with the same fields, written by fs.
mechanisms.port_notes: The 10 MB constraint disappears in Electron, so raw keyframe samples COULD be kept — but keep the summary anyway and store raw samples in a sidecar file loaded on demand. Reason: the panel deserialises the whole library on boot, and JSON.parse of megabytes of numeric sample arrays is the same freeze by a different route. The 'accept both live and stored shape' idempotence rule is the single most portable lesson here — make it a typed union in TS rather than a `||`.

mechanisms.name: inert() — neutralising page-authored strings before they are pasted into someone's project
mechanisms.problem: `componentBundle` concatenates page-authored CSS and page-authored JS handler source into a single HTML string that will be pasted into a real project. Anything in that text that can close the enclosing `<style>` or `<script>` tag turns the paste into an injection.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
One tiny function applied to the WHOLE of each embedded block, not to selected fields:
```js
const inert = (s) => String(s)
  .replace(/<\/(script|style)/gi, "<\\/$1")
  .replace(/<!--/g, "<\\!--");
```
It is applied to (a) the entire CSS payload inside `<style>…</style>`, and (b) the entire body of the handler-reference block. The handler block is emitted as `<script type="text/plain" data-aiep-behavior-reference>` — `type="text/plain"` is what stops the browser executing it, but the comment on the code is explicit that this only holds *as long as nothing in the body can close the tag*, and that the body includes the EVENT NAMES, which also come from the page. So the escaping covers the entire joined string (`/* الأحداث الحقيقية: … */` header plus every `/* N. حدث <type> (<on>) */` label plus every handler source), not just the source bodies. The `<!--` replacement covers the second way to break out of a script/style context (HTML comment start inside a script is parsed specially in legacy HTML parsing).
mechanisms.location: sidepanel.js:1096-1136 (componentBundle + inert)
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (a) builder code emission, (e) MCP tool output
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: none needed — but the threat model gets WORSE in Electron, not better: EXELMJ writes emitted code to disk and the mini-browser may load it. Every path that concatenates page-derived text into markup must go through this, including the builder's HTML emitter and any MCP tool that returns a component bundle to Claude.
mechanisms.port_notes: Copy the function verbatim into EXELMJ as a shared util and route ALL page-derived string embedding through it. Consider adding `</textarea` and `</title` for completeness if the builder ever emits those containers. Note this is escaping-for-embedding, not sanitisation — the handler source is still attacker-controlled text; keeping it non-executing (`type="text/plain"`) is the actual safety property.

mechanisms.name: Two-phase scan progress reported onto the trigger button itself
mechanisms.problem: The component scan does two long, structurally different things — a scroll sweep that mounts lazy content, then a live motion-recording pass — and both look identical to the user: a frozen panel. Rendering a modal progress bar for a 12-second operation is heavier than the operation deserves.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
There is no progress widget. The panel sets a `uiScanning` flag, disables the scan button, and writes the percentage into the BUTTON'S OWN LABEL. A single `chrome.runtime.onMessage` listener filters `message.type === "UI_SCAN_PROGRESS"` and gates on `uiScanning` (so a stale message from a previous scan cannot repaint the button), then branches on `message.phase`:
```js
$("btnUiScan").textContent = message.phase === "record"
  ? `جارٍ تسجيل الحركة… ${message.pct}%`
  : `جارٍ التمرير… ${message.pct}%`;
```
The two producers in content.js compute pct differently and honestly:
- SWEEP (content.js ~5409-5432, `materializeLazyContent`): scrolls `y` from 0 to `min(scrollHeight, 60000)` in steps of `max(400, 0.9*innerHeight)`, waits 45 ms per stop, emits `pct = min(99, round(y/h*100))`. It is TIME-BOXED at a 12 000 ms budget rather than run to the page end (each stop costs whatever the page spends mounting what appeared — near a second per screen on a heavy showcase), returns `{truncated: true}` when the deadline hit, restores `startY` and waits 250 ms for the last mounts to settle.
- RECORD (content.js ~6255-6288): sorts candidates by a `jsSignal(c)` heuristic descending (components with a JS signal first, ties by original index), plans `planned = min(maxN, order.length)`, and emits `pct = min(99, round(done/planned*100))` with `phase: "record"` after each one; also honours a wall-clock deadline.
Both cap at 99 — the button is reset to "إعادة الفحص" by the awaiting caller, so 100% is never displayed by the progress path.
On completion the panel ALWAYS reports the tally, never silently: `showStatus("${n} من ${scanned} مرشحًا · مستبعَد: ${dropped.dupe} مكرر، ${dropped.hidden} مخفي، ${dropped.size} صغير")` — the comment says outright that a silent "(7)" beside a page holding 144 cards is exactly how a dedup bug went unnoticed.
mechanisms.location: sidepanel.js:536-545 (listener), 547-583 (loadUiComponents); content.js:5409-5432 and 6255-6288 (producers)
mechanisms.chrome_apis_used: chrome.runtime.sendMessage from the content script → chrome.runtime.onMessage in the panel
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: The injected script (via `webContents.executeJavaScript`) cannot sendMessage. Two options: (1) expose a callback on the injected side through a preload-defined bridge — preload runs at document_start in the MAIN world's isolated context and can `ipcRenderer.send('studio:scan-progress', {phase, pct})`, which main forwards to the panel window with `panelWin.webContents.send(...)`; or (2) drive the sweep from the MAIN process via CDP (`webContents.debugger` → `Input.dispatchMouseEvent`/`Runtime.evaluate`), in which case the main process owns the loop and emits progress natively — no in-page messaging at all. Option (2) is cleaner and lets you cancel a runaway sweep from outside the page.
mechanisms.port_notes: Port the two ideas, not the plumbing: (i) progress belongs on the control that started the work when the work is <30s; (ii) report the rejection breakdown, always. Keep the time-box — the reason it exists (unbounded sweeps on long pages hang for minutes) applies identically in a WebContentsView.

mechanisms.name: The long-operation progress bar pattern (clone / auto-extract / bulk / corpus)
mechanisms.problem: Four unrelated multi-minute operations each need a progress display, a live stage label, and a stop button, without four bespoke widgets.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
One markup shape reused four times: `
…
`. CSS is 20 lines: `.clone-bar` is a 6 px pill with `overflow:hidden`, and `.clone-bar i` is a block whose `width` transitions `.2s ease`. Each consumer installs a `chrome.runtime.onMessage` listener for its own message type and — importantly — bails immediately if its box is hidden (`if (box.hidden) return`), which prevents a background operation from repainting a panel the user has navigated away from. Percentage strategy differs by whether a total is known: - Clone knows totals: `pct = round(done/total*100)`, floored at 4% so the bar is visible at the start; stage label is a lookup table `{css:'الأنماط', images:'الصور', fonts:'الخطوط', media:'الوسائط', scripts:'السكربتات', zip:'الضغط'}` rendered as `"الصور: 12/47"`. - Auto-extract and corpus do NOT know the total (pagination depth is unknown), so they use a monotonic asymptote: `width = min(96, 8 + page*4)%` / `min(96, 8 + round*6)%`. Never reaches 100 until `message.done` arrives, so it can never lie by finishing early. Every flow follows the identical lifecycle: disable button → stash `oldText` → set button to a gerund → unhide progress at 8% → await the relay → restore button → hide progress → render a result box with counts. Failures render into a `.probe-box` with `` rather than replacing the whole pane.
mechanisms.location: sidepanel.js:2060-2090 (auto), 2134-2230 (bulk), 3545-3596 (clone), 3718-3760 (corpus); sidepanel.css:1244-1268
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (a) builder code-gen progress, (c) picker scan, (d) mini-browser project build/run
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: `ipcRenderer.on('studio:progress', (_, {op, stage, done, total})=>…)` with a single `op` discriminator instead of four message types; main process emits via `win.webContents.send`. The `if (box.hidden) return` guard survives unchanged and is still needed.
mechanisms.port_notes: Collapse the four near-duplicates into one `<studio-progress data-op="…">` element in EXELMJ. Keep BOTH percentage strategies — the `min(96, base + n*step)` asymptote for unknown-total work is the honest choice and is worth having as a named helper.

mechanisms.name: DEFAULT_SETTINGS duplicated in both processes + live push on change
mechanisms.problem: The panel writes settings; the injected page code reads them. A settings change made while a scan is mid-flight must reach the page code without a reload, and a fresh injection must start from the same defaults the panel shows.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
The SAME literal `DEFAULT_SETTINGS` object is declared twice — sidepanel.js:4-14 and content.js:27-37 — with identical keys and values (`format:'markdown'`, `includeAttributes:true`, `includeAccessibility:true`, `includeComputedStyles:false`, `includeXPath:true`, `includeTailwind:true`, `autoDeactivate:true`, `revealCollapsed:false`, `recordMotion:true`). It is NOT imported; it is copied, because the content script is a plain IIFE with no module system. A parallel `CHECKBOXES` array lists the 8 boolean ids, and the panel drives everything off that array — hydration (`chrome.storage.sync.get(DEFAULT_SETTINGS, s => CHECKBOXES.forEach(id => $(id).checked = Boolean({...DEFAULT_SETTINGS, ...s}[id])))`) and persistence (`CHECKBOXES.forEach(id => $(id).addEventListener('change', () => chrome.storage.sync.set({[id]: $(id).checked})))`). Passing DEFAULT_SETTINGS as the argument to `.get()` is what makes unset keys come back with the default rather than undefined. The content script does the same `.get()`, then installs `chrome.storage.onChanged` filtered to `area === 'sync'` and merges only keys it already knows: `for (const [k,v] of Object.entries(changes)) if (k in settings) settings[k] = v.newValue` — the `k in settings` guard is what keeps unrelated storage keys (the library, the corpus, the watch flag) from polluting the settings object. The radio group (`format`) is handled separately since it is one value across three inputs. The corpus tab repeats the entire pattern with its own `CORPUS_DEFAULTS` (7 keys, including number inputs coerced with `Number(v) || CORPUS_DEFAULTS[id]`).
Two of the switches carry a `.option__hint` sentence explaining the side effect, because they modify the live page: `revealCollapsed` ("opens details/aria-expanded widgets to measure them open, then puts them back — leave it off unless needed") and `recordMotion` ("hovers and presses JS-bound components to record their real motion as CSS; does not press links, delete or buy buttons, and sends no click").
mechanisms.location: sidepanel.js:4-20 (DEFAULT_SETTINGS + CHECKBOXES), 189-210 (hydrate/persist), 3605-3682 (corpus mirror); content.js:27-76 (mirror + onChanged); sidepanel.html:230-258
mechanisms.which_deliverable: (c) picker settings, shared by all five
mechanisms.electron_equivalent: The duplication exists ONLY because the extension has no shared module across the extension/page boundary — Electron does not have that problem. Put the defaults in one `src/studio/settings.ts`, import it in both the panel renderer and the preload script. Persist to a JSON file under `app.getPath('userData')`; broadcast changes with `webContents.send('studio:settings-changed', patch)` to every renderer AND to the hosted view's preload, which keeps its own live copy. The `k in settings` merge guard is still worth keeping as a runtime type gate.
mechanisms.port_notes: The CHECKBOXES-array-drives-hydration-and-persistence pattern is genuinely good and should survive: it makes adding a setting a one-line change in one array instead of three edits. In TypeScript make it `const BOOLEAN_SETTINGS = [...] as const` so the ids are type-checked against the settings interface. Also port the `.option__hint` convention — any toggle that mutates the user's live page must carry a sentence saying what it touches and how it restores.

mechanisms.name: Live component previews in sandboxed iframes, lazily mounted, with two different scale policies

mechanisms.how_it_works: Each card's preview is an `

mechanisms.name: The enlarged detail sheet and its evidence chips
mechanisms.problem: A thumbnail cannot tell you whether a component's behaviour was actually captured. The user needs, in one glance, (a) whether motion was recorded LIVE versus merely read from CSS, and (b) what JavaScript events the component really listens to.
mechanisms.how_it_works: `openUiSheet(c)` builds a full-panel `position:fixed; inset:0` flex column: a `.sheet__bar` (title + close icon button), a `.sheet__stage` (`height:46vh; min-height:190px`, checkerboard, holds the scaled iframe), a wrapping `.sheet__acts` chip row, and a scrolling `.sheet__body`. The title is not the component name alone — it is `` `${c.name} — مرّر وانقر لتجربته` `` ("hover AND click to try it"), because many components only reveal themselves on `:focus`/`:active`, and without saying so half the interaction goes unnoticed. The EVIDENCE CHIP is a non-interactive `.chip` with `pointerEvents:'none'`, rendered only if `c.behavior?.events?.length || c.recorded?.phases?.length`, whose text joins up to two facts with " — ": `"✦ حركة مسجّلة حيّة"` when `c.recorded.phases.length` (motion was recorded by actually driving the element), and `` `الأحداث: ${c.behavior.events.slice(0,6).join("، ")}` `` — the first six real listener types harvested from the MAIN-world hook registry. This is the panel's answer to "looks right vs behaves right". Action chips: نسخ الكود (`componentBundle`, the pasteable HTML+CSS+inert JS reference), نسخ HTML, نسخ CSS, تنزيل JSON, then a context-dependent library chip — delete if viewing the library, a DISABLED "محفوظ" chip if already saved (shown rather than omitted, because an absent button reads as a bug), else "حفظ في المكتبة" which mutates itself to a checkmark in place. `renderUiDetails` fills the body: dataset keys, extracted labels, then per state (`:hover`, `:focus`, …) per target a row reading `"تلمس ← يتغيّر "` with up to 12 property changes as `propvalue` chips; then up to 20 transitions and 12 animations; then any `codeBlocks` the page shipped beside its demo, in a `max-height:220px; white-space:pre; overflow:auto` block truncated at 4000 chars. Every truncation is VISIBLE via `more(shown,total)` which appends `+N` — the limits were originally 3/2/6 with no hint the rest existed, which hid data.

mechanisms.name: Arabic-RTL CSS architecture: RTL by default, LTR islands for machine text
mechanisms.problem: An Arabic-first tool panel is full of machine text — CSS selectors, hex colours, URLs, font names, filenames, numbers, keyboard shortcuts — that is inherently left-to-right and becomes unreadable or reordered if it inherits the document's RTL direction.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
The direction is declared THREE times, at three layers, and never fought again: ``, plus `body { direction: rtl }` in CSS. Everything else is RTL by inheritance. Layout is then built almost entirely from direction-agnostic primitives — flexbox with `justify-content: space-between`, `gap`, and CSS grid — so the vast majority of the 1332-line stylesheet contains no directional properties at all and mirrors for free. Where a directional offset IS needed, LOGICAL properties are used: `margin-inline-start` (brand badge, status chip, icon-font tag, `.fchip.dl{margin-inline-start:auto}` which pushes the download chip to the far end of the filter row), `padding-inline-end` (`.option__text`, keeping the hint clear of the switch), `border-inline-start` (severity stripes on `.sec-item.critical/.high/.medium/.low`, the purple `.ui-state-row`, the amber `.ui-motion-row`, `.bounty-note`), `inset-inline-end` (the `.ui-badges` overlay), and `text-align: start` (hint lines, `.clone-facts`, `.ai-usage`, `.finfo b`). The key move is the LTR ISLAND: 22 separate `direction: ltr` declarations, each scoped to exactly the run of machine text it protects, never to a container. They cover — `.field__code` and `.field__pre` (selector / HTML dumps, with `text-align:left` as well and `word-break:break-all; white-space:pre-wrap`), `.result__tag` (`
#id`), `.sinfo > div span:last-child` (computed style values), `.color-card__meta` (hex), `.snippet` and `.font-item .fname` (font names / @import lines), `.meta-row .val`, `.ramp__head code`, `.sem code`, `.gradient-item code`, `.trow .lbl/.demo/.val` (token rows), `.vsrc` and `.finfo b` (URLs and filenames, with ellipsis), `.ui-chg` (property/value pairs), `.field-input` (URL and number inputs), `.ai-usage`, and `.components-card` (a whole LTR island, because it renders sample Latin UI components). Two details that only show up in practice: (1) `.font-item .fname { direction: ltr; text-align: right }` — direction LTR keeps the Latin glyph order correct, while `text-align: right` pins the run to the RTL side of the card so it lines up with the Arabic around it. This is the correct combination for a Latin token inside an Arabic layout and is not obvious. (2) form controls carry `dir="ltr"` in the HTML, not CSS: every one of the ~20 `

mechanisms.name: Status toast with a contextual repair affordance, and self-disarming destructive buttons
mechanisms.problem: Errors in a tool panel are usually recoverable by one specific action (reload the page); a toast that only states the problem makes the user hunt for the fix. Conversely, a destructive button that acts on first click can wipe the user's whole store.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
`showStatus(msg, ok=false, offerReload=false)` writes into a single `

`, swaps `.status` / `.status ok` (red-bg vs green-bg token pairs), unhides it, and — when `offerReload` is true — APPENDS a live `.chip` button labelled "إعادة تحميل الصفحة" that reloads the inspected tab and hides the toast. The auto-hide timer is duration-differentiated: `setTimeout(..., offerReload ? 8000 : 3200)` — a toast the user is expected to ACT on gets more than twice the dwell time. The previous timer is always cleared via a function-property (`clearTimeout(showStatus._t)`), so rapid successive messages don't cut each other short. Every failing relay path passes `offerReload: true`, because "the content script isn't there" is the dominant failure and reloading is the fix. Destructive actions use a two-step ARMED pattern with no dialog: `btnCorpusClear` checks `btn.dataset.armed !== '1'` → sets `armed='1'`, retitles itself `` `اضغط للتأكيد (${n})` `` (showing the count at risk), and schedules a 4000 ms disarm that restores both `dataset.armed` and the label. Only a second click within that window performs the delete. Cheaper than a modal, and it cannot be muscle-memoried through. Copy feedback is in-place on the button that was pressed: `copyText(text, btn)` swaps `btn.textContent` to "✓ تم", adds `.done` (green background + green border), and restores both after 1400 ms — the caller passes `e.target`/`e.currentTarget`, so one function serves every copy button in the panel. Clipboard failure falls through to `showStatus`.

mechanisms.name: Multi-format design-token export from one in-memory model
mechanisms.problem: Extracted colours/type/spacing are only useful if they land in whatever the consumer's stack actually reads — CSS vars, Tailwind v3 config, Tailwind v4 @theme, SCSS, shadcn HSL triples, W3C DTCG JSON.
mechanisms.how_it_works:
`genExport(fmt)` is a single switch over one `designSystem` object `{ramps, typeScale, spacing, radii, shadows, bodyFont}` where `ramps` is `{role: {50..950: hex}}` built by `buildRamp(baseHex)`. `buildRamp` keeps the source hex at the 500 stop and regenerates every other stop by holding H and S from `hexToHsl` and substituting a fixed lightness table `RAMP_L = [.97,.93,.86,.76,.65,.53,.45,.37,.29,.21,.13]` against `RAMP_KEYS = [50,100,…,950]`. Roles come from `pickRoles(colors)`: split into vivid vs neutral by `s < 0.14 || l < 0.07 || l > 0.96`; primary = first vivid; accent = first vivid whose hue distance from primary exceeds 60° (using circular distance `min(|a-b|, 360-|a-b|)`); secondary = next vivid WITHIN 60°; neutral = first neutral with `0.2 < l < 0.8`. Each with a hardcoded fallback.
The six emitters differ only in wrapper: `css` → `:root{ --color-role-500: … }`; `tw4` → identical body under `@theme{}` (the only difference between the two is the opening line); `scss` → `$color-role-500: …`; `tailwind` → a module.exports with `JSON.stringify(colorObj, null, 8).replace(/"/g, "'")` to produce single-quoted JS; `shadcn` → converts hex to space-separated HSL components (`${round(h)} ${round(s*100)}% ${round(l*100)}%`) and maps ramp stops onto shadcn's semantic names (background=n50, foreground=n950, primary=p600, muted=n100, ring=p500, radius = md/16 rem); `w3c` → `{color:{role:{500:{$type:'color', $value: hex}}}}`.
The format chooser is a chip row (`#exportTabs`) using event delegation on `.fchip[data-fmt]`; the output lands in a `<pre id="exportPre">` with copy and download buttons, and the download picks its extension from a lookup `{css:'css', tailwind:'js', scss:'scss', json:'json'}` defaulting to `txt`. A separate `.chip.modern[data-modern]` set downloads named files directly (`tailwind-theme.css`, `shadcn-theme.css`, `design.tokens.json`).
mechanisms.location: sidepanel.js:117-148 (buildRamp/pickRoles), 1697-1815 (genExport + wiring); sidepanel.html:288-302

mechanisms.name: Keyboard forwarding from the panel to the inspected page
mechanisms.problem: While the picker is active the panel may hold keyboard focus, so arrow keys, Enter and Escape go to the panel and the in-page tree navigation appears dead.
mechanisms.how_it_works: A `NAV_KEYS` Set of `[ArrowUp, ArrowDown, ArrowLeft, ArrowRight, Enter, Escape, d, D, s, S]` (the last four are the download-HTML and screenshot shortcuts). One document-level keydown listener registered with `capture: true` so it runs before any control in the panel can consume the key; it returns immediately unless `pickerOn && NAV_KEYS.has(e.key)`, then `preventDefault()`, `stopPropagation()`, and `relay({type:'NAV_KEY', key})` to the page. The shortcut table in the Inspect tab documents the same keys visually, with the arrow group wrapped in `<span class="kbds" dir="ltr">` so ←/→ don't reorder.

Option (2) is strictly better than the extension's approach, which had to re-implement the key handling on the page side.
